In cases where baggage reconciliation is performed manually in the baggage collection area: 1. The baggage tag is examined visually to check the flight number and the destination. 2. One of the small baggage tags is attached to the Bingo Card (ULD/Baggage card). 3. The loading order is numbered to facilitate the baggage offloading processes, it is ensured that the baggage is loaded in a numbered sequence (by loading order). 4. Tagged baggage is placed on the ULD/baggage trolley properly without throwing it. 5. In order that there is no remained baggage, the expected baggage number and the loaded baggage number are compared with each other.  k.   When the ULD/baggage trolley is full or loading is complete: 1. The ULD/baggage trolley is properly closed and the seal is fitted. 2. ULD/baggage trolley is arranged to be loaded in coordination with the ramp employee responsible for dispatch.  l.   The wheelchairs and the vehicles of the passengers with reduced mobility delivered at the check-in area for carriage; 1. It is necessary to make sure that the vehicles of the passengers with reduced mobility have been received at the check-in area and taken away to the area allocated to the out of gauge baggage determined as per the airport regulations. In some areas, it may require security checks for these vehicles to reach the allocated area. 2. The vehicles of the passengers with reduced mobility are accepted in compliance with the requirements specified in DK.41.011  Dangerous Goods Regulations (DGR)/2.3. Table A. 3. It is necessary to make sure that the person responsible for planning and loading of the aircraft has been given information on the number and types of the vehicles of the passengers with reduced mobility, which have been received for transportation. This information is sent to the next station through LDM or CPM.  m.   Where baggage reconciliation is performed in the hold: 1. The baggage that comes by being loaded on the baggage trolleys is unloaded to the conveyor belt in the aircraft hold to be loaded. 2. Baggage tag barcodes are scanned. 3. It should be verified that the loading is performed for the correct flight and passenger. 4. Unmatched or faulty baggage is set aside for re-verification. 5. The loaded baggage of the denied passenger is unloaded, set aside as unaccompanied baggage, and processed according to the rules specified in 2.9.1.1. Storage of Lost/Found/Unidentified/Unclaimed Baggage. Planned emergency measures for disruptions in baggage operation should be reviewed.  a.   Predicting possible disruption scenarios,  b.   Planning equipment for possible disruption,  c.   Ensuring that manual operations are available in case of problems by restarting planned software maintenance works in case of possible failure.  2.8.2. Dealing with Baggage Irregularities 2.8.2.1. BRS (Baggage Reconciliation System) Interruption  In case of baggage reconciliation system failure, baggage tags for the relevant flight should be collected and baggage should be included in the system with bingosheet application.  2.8.2.2. Baggage Handling System Interruption  Most major airports have baggage handling systems in place to transport relevant baggage from the check-in area to the designated collection area. In the event of an outage in the baggage handling system, as per the airport authority procedures,  a.   the baggage remaining on the baggage belts is collected,  b.   the pending baggage that cannot be given to the system must be collected in the areas designated by the manual method. Local procedures must be established in such a way that the handling of baggage (security screening, dispatch, collection, etc.) does not reduce airport capacity in case of BHS failure.  2.8.2.3. Equipment Problems  Equipment to be used in the operation planning stage should be reviewed, and unusable ones should be separated and repaired.  2.8.2.4. Employee Irregularities  In case of disruptions in the working order of the employees (strike, disaster, etc.) due to force majeure, alternative conditions must be considered in order not to disrupt the operation.  2.8.2.5. Diverted Flights  Things to consider when diverting a flight to a station other than its destination are:  a.   Flight documents/messages must be checked and it is necessary to make sure that the rules are met for baggage requiring special handling such as mobility aids, live animals, etc.  b.   According to the passenger's decision, the baggage is diverted to the relevant area;  1.   If the aircraft changes, the baggage is transferred to the new aircraft.  2.   If passengers are transferred to other flights, the baggage is transferred to the next flight or a space is allocated for them to pick up their bags.  3.   If the passengers will go by land, the baggage is delivered to the appropriate areas so that they can take their baggage and delivered to the passengers.  2.8.2.6. Canceled Flights  Once a flight is canceled;  a.   Baggage is shipped to the alternate flight provided.  b.   It is delivered to the areas allocated to the original flight so that passengers can collect their baggage.  2.9. Baggage Irregularities or Unclaimed Baggage/Forgotten Item  In case of loss of or damage to any accepted baggage or item, the Company is liable for the arising inconvenience. However, loss and/or damage giving rise to the inconvenience must have occurred during the carriage performed by the airline. The passengers whose baggage has been delivered late due to any irregularities are required to apply to the carrier in person or in writing with documents for urgent need expenses within 21 days as of the date when their baggage was delivered. Introduction  In the relevant section, the baggage systems used in the Company are mentioned.  2.10.2. Baggage Reconciliation Systems 2.10.2.1. Baggage Reconciliation (BRS)  In accordance with international civil aviation and security regulations, any baggage belonging to a checked-in passenger should only be loaded on board the aircraft if such passenger travels on the flight for which s/he has been checked-in. Any baggage of any passenger, who does not fly, should not be loaded into the aircraft, and if such baggage has been loaded into the aircraft, then it should be identified and unloaded from the aircraft. The detailed information on the security checks and measures applied to the hold baggage of the passengers who will travel with the Company aircraft is given in the requirements in   EK.10.15.001 Security Program/section 4. Security of Hold Baggage. Baggage and passenger reconciliation is being carried out through Baggage Reconciliation System (BRS) in the flights of the Company. At the stations that do not have Baggage Reconciliation System, or have Baggage Reconciliation System but cannot use it due to a general failure, after it has been understood that the baggage belongs to the relevant flight by checking their labels, the ULD or the compartment   into   which   the   baggage   has   been   loaded   is   specified   by   using   FR.67.0356   Bingo   Sheet,   and   by   logging   in  bingosheet.thy.com, the passenger baggage from the departure airport is recorded by having their labels read by means of scanner or manually. The baggage manifest that indicates the feature and position details of the loaded baggage is emailed automatically to the destination station. Any baggage, the owner of which could not be determined upon passenger and baggage reconciliation, shall not be loaded on board the aircraft for security purposes in any manner for whatsoever. For baggage of each passenger checked-in electronically through DCS, the system creates a standard BSM (Baggage Source Message) message in order for identification of the baggage and forwards the same to the Baggage Reconciliation System (BRS).  a.   The baggage reconciliation system ensures that only the baggage that has been matched with passenger baggage, authorized and checked for rush baggage is loaded and shipped.  b.   The details of the manual baggage reconciliation application are available in   TL.67.094 Instruction on Bingo Sheet Application. For automatic baggage reconciliation, the Automatic Baggage Reconciliation system used at the relevant stations is applied. Purpose  The Baggage Reconciliation System (BRS) is used to;  a.   prevent inaccurate baggage loading,  b.   ensure security with a view to carry the passengers together with their baggage,  c.   minimize or to eliminate liabilities arising from inaccurate baggage loading and losses, as well as to contribute to the prestige of the Company by preventing passenger dissatisfaction,  d.   be able to receive details in relation to all loading reports retroactively on flights basis, all processes carried out in relation to baggage and the persons who have performed the same,  e.   prevent any delays arising from any baggage irregularities. Containers with barcode or baggage cart tags (container sheet) generated through "Work Station" shall be scanned through HHT and the required ULD (AKE/AKH, etc.) or CAR (baggage cart) number shall be typed with HHT and upon scanning of the baggage, the baggage to which system grants loading authorization shall be loaded on board the aircraft.  b. Baggage unloading processes shall be performed through HHT.  d.   Loading position of the container on board the aircraft shall be determined by HHT.  e.   Baggage scanning to containers must definitely be carried out by using container tags. Baggage shall be scanned to bulk loading compartments of the aircraft after specifying the relevant loading position (Example:H1, H52 etc.). In the event that baggage barcode could not be scanned, then baggage tag number shall be entered manually by HHT, then the baggage shall be scanned.  f.   In the event that the baggage details are not recorded on TROYA DCS when the baggage was scanned or in case of any interruption of BSM due to any system failure, then the Baggage Reconciliation System (BRS) shall give the warning "Unidentified Baggage" on HHT in respect of such baggage. In that case, HHT user shall enter the other passenger details on the tag to the system (passenger name, PNR etc.), and shall ensure that such details are displayed on the "Work Station". By checking the list of unidentified baggage on the "Work Station", it shall be ensured that only the baggage of the passengers, who are admitted to the flight, are carried by performing k-edit on TROYA DCS, or by correcting and identifying the same through (BSM) passenger-baggage reconciliation. Thus, any baggage not authorized by the "Work Station" cannot be loaded on board the aircraft.  g.   Any baggage unaccompanied by the passengers (Rush baggage) cannot be loaded on board the aircraft without having been identified and authorized. Rush (RUSH), Security (SEC) and Crew (CREW) baggage (in respect of Rush baggage, in case of any system failure while generating BSM) shall be recorded to the Baggage Reconciliation System (BRS) and shall be then loaded.  2.10.2.6. IATA 753 Resolutions  IATA 753 Resolutions define baggage tracking for all airline companies. They define the points of tracking throughout the entire journey of the baggage and determine the mandatory tracking points.  2.10.2.7. Factors that are considered to be beyond the passenger's own will;  a.   The passenger or their baggage is transferred to another flight without the passenger's demand,  b.   The passenger boards the transfer flight, but their baggage cannot be transferred between two flights due to unpredictable reasons,  c. Baggage Handling System  The baggage systems are designed to direct the baggage from the check-in areas to the certain point at which the baggage pieces will be brought together. Since the baggage screening tools are integrated into the system, it shall be responsible for the transportation and security of the baggage at the airport in general terms. Baggage Handling Systems have different handling features that enable different segregations of a flight (according to their class or different destinations). Other baggage handling system functions also allow baggage to be diverted to carousels where several flights can be made at the same time. These special points and sorting, the configuration of the baggage handling system are made by the Airport authority.  2.10.4. Baggage Message Systems  All movements of the baggage are tracked and processed into the Baggage Reconciliation System by means of baggage messages. Baggage messages are also defined in Type B and Recommended Practice (RP) 1745 and RP 1755 for modern baggage messaging, respectively. Messages are sent directly from airline to airline, through link or message distributors such as DCS or 3rd party service provider such as SITA (Societe Internationale de Telecommunications Aeronautiqes).  2.10.5. Baggage Management Systems  Baggage management system is a system that combines information from other systems in order to provide complete information for the control and loading of baggage information of the flight, provides instant tracking of baggage movements, and allows assignment of tasks to different crews for baggage transportation.  2.10.6. Baggage Re-Flighting Systems  Re-flighting baggage system is used to allocate an irregular baggage to a new flight. The system must be able to generate baggage messages and tags to support baggage movements. The relevant system allows the automatic allocation of baggage directly to a new flight. DCS check-in system or automatic BRS systems can be used for this. 3. GENERAL SAFETY OF AIRCRAFT/SERVICE CONDITIONS  3.1. Apron Safety in Aircraft Service 3.1.1. Introduction  Apron safety rules and procedures promote and maintain safe ground operations. Therefore, the minimum safety rules must be understood and followed by the ground handling agents and their employees who perform service in the ground operation of the Company. All employees on duty at the apron are required to wear the apron identification card in a visible manner. Damage to aircraft may endanger passengers, employees, and the aircraft. Disruptions may also negatively impact safe airline operations. Even a slight scratch or dent on an aircraft may result in a serious accident. If any damage is seen or caused to the aircraft structure, it should be reported by entering AQD 1.7 GSR and 1.10 for cargo processes. Smoking or the use of lighters/matches/e-cigarettes is not permitted on the apron area, unless there is an area designated by the local airport operator/regulator.  3.1.2. General Apron Safety 3.1.2.1. Engine Hazard Areas  There is serious injury risk in the aircraft intake and blast areas. When the aircraft stops for any reason and then uses extra force to move again, this risk increases more.  While the aircraft engines are running and/or the anti-collision/beacon lights are on, the vehicles and the employees must stay out of ERA. (excluding the employee who put the nose block and connect the GPU).  a. Blast Area  The area located behind the aircraft and affected by the blast wind and exhaust gas of the running engines. While the aircraft engines are running or the anti-collision/beacon lights are on, there must be no employee, vehicle, and equipment in the zone affected by the blast area, nor must that zone be used for pass-through. Exhaust gas at high temperatures may cause skin burns when a person stands too close. Ground operations employee and/or equipment must stay away from the intake and blast areas.  b. Intake Area  The area in front of the jet engines. There must be no employee, vehicle, and equipment within the zone affected by the intake area while the engines are running or about to be started. Intake power of the running jet engines is 5 times stronger than a hurricane. Therefore, it poses a risk that people and other objects around might get caught into the engine due to its suction power.  c. Venting Area  As specified in Figure-6: Venting Area, the venting area is a global area around the fuel valves of the aircraft where flammable gas fumes may form in the course of fueling.   This area shall be kept under surveillance by taking special safety measures. When it is not windy, this area shall be regarded as venting area for three (3) minutes longer, even after fueling has finished.  NOTE:   In the event that the surface wind exceeds 25 knot, the danger area shall be extended by 20%. The parked equipment is kept away from the danger zones (blast and intake areas). The aircraft is never approached before its engines stop. Do not approach the distance where the engine intake is effective. Approaching may have fatal results. The jet aircraft engines have different suction forces. The danger zones created by such a suction force vary by dimensions and engine output of aircraft, (See LS.67.043 List of Blast Areas and Intake Areas ) Closer to the aircraft, this suction force is more dangerous. Therefore, approaching is always forbidden.  Note:   The Company's fleet does not include propeller aircraft. Figure-8: Equipment Restraint Area  3.1.2.4. Foreign Object Debris  Foreign Object Debris (FOD) is a generic term used for all unattended objects that are dangerous for the safety and integrity of aircraft and employee, and thus must not be left in any area where they may create a risk. Every individual has a responsibility to ensure that the risk of damage to aircraft from FOD is minimized. All wastes must be collected the moment they are found, before becoming FOD, and the collected FODs must be put into the FOD box. FOD is often caused by the carelessness of the employee working airside and their lack of understanding of its consequences, or the movement of foreign objects into airside locations during high winds.  Examples of FOD:  Plastic and paper, nylon bags/plates, rags, Metal nuts and bolts, Empty oil and hydraulic fluid boxes, tools, and equipment, Natural objects (stones, pebbles, pieces of wood), Other debris (exploded ballast bags), Suitcase handles, casters, etc.  Caution! Results of FOD:  Foreign object debris may be ingested by the aircraft engines and damage the engine. This situation is especially critical if it occurs in flight, particularly during the take-off phase. It also creates a tripping/falling hazard for personnel working on or around the aircraft. Additionally, damage caused by FOD can occur to tires, the undercarriage, control systems and other parts of the airframe. All such damage could lead to inflight failures.  FOD Checks:  Before any movement or servicing of the aircraft, the following checks must be made:  a.   The parking areas near the operation area, where the ground equipment is prepared and positioned, must be checked.  b.   Routine checks of ground equipment (including the floors of enclosed cabinets) must be carried out to ensure that everything is safe and functioning and will not fall to the ground and create FOD.  c.   In the ramp areas, anything carried in or on a vehicle must be secured.  d.   Before arrival of the aircraft, the aircraft parking area must be checked on foot, and all the FODs found must be collected. Safety Instructions for Use of Ground Support Equipment on Apron 3.1.3.1. General Safety Instructions  a.   The employee to be assigned to the operation of ground support equipment is required to be qualified and hold an operator's certificate for the relevant vehicle. Only the authorized and certified employee can use ground equipment.  b.   Ground support equipment must not be moved in the following situations:  1.   -hen the aircraft is taxiing to the parking position or during push back,  2-   During passenger boarding and deboarding processes,  3-   During the passage of emergency vehicles.  c.   When docking or undocking ground support equipment, aircraft contact points must be checked for possible damage.  d.   Any contact or suspected contact, especially on composite body aircraft, must be reported immediately to the immediate supervisor.  e.   Where contact has occurred or is suspected to have occurred, ground support equipment must not be moved until an inspection to determine damage has been completed and conformity has been confirmed.  f.   The employee must protect themselves from situations where loose clothing, long hair, and accessories can become caught and entangled in vehicles and ground support equipment.  g.   Ground support equipment must never touch the aircraft. They must be no closer than 2 inches/5cm, or they must be positioned when the distance sensors (if any) stop their movement.  Attention:  The operator of the ground support equipment performs the required visual inspections (damage, contact, etc.) before and after the approach/separation maneuver of the aircraft to the contact zone, and in the event that s/he detects a dent or a notch on the fuselage, s/he immediately notifies her/his supervisor in respect thereof, and does not continue to approach to the area where damage is detected. The station official, the commander, and the technical employee are given information. All safety devices such as proximity sensors, bumpers, guardrails and stabilizers on the ground support equipment are used during servicing of the aircraft. While positioning the ground support equipment, it is necessary to avoid that the protective tire bumpers contact the fuselage, and have sufficient clearance when pulling up near the aircraft, considering the probability that the aircraft weight might change and the aircraft might move vertically. WARNING:   Any incidents mandatory to be reported as well as situations posing noticeable hazards during ground operation shall be reported through   Safety Reporting System (SRS). Detailed information is given in Chapter 6/Operational Supervision of Airside Safety.  3.1.3.2. Basic Start-up Conditions for Ground Support Equipment  a.   To prevent any personal injury or material injury and/or damage to the aircraft, ground support equipment cables and hoses must be securely stowed away when the equipment is not in use or before transfer to another location. Great care must be taken when positioning, lifting and maneuvering ground support equipment.  b.   Ground support equipment should not interfere with ground operations of other aircraft in the areas where it is positioned.  c.   It is necessary to ensure that all areas of ground support equipment (GSE) are free from contamination and FOD, and that the equipment is safe for use prior to and throughout the operation.  d.   Before using ground support equipment in aircraft services, it is necessary to check physically and visually, especially the "parking" brakes and tire protection pads, fuel and battery levels, safety systems (beam lights and all other lights and signals), and the service life of fire extinguishing equipment. When not in use, vehicles and equipment should always be put on parking brakes to ensure that they are secured against movement. If any failure is detected, it is recorded in the Vehicle Use Follow-up book, or by using the follow- up method, if any, determined by the department using the vehicle. Meanwhile, the relevant authority shall be informed of this detection (via radio/phone). Equipment should be labeled “Out of Service” and decommissioned.  e.   All safety rails (except fixed ones) shall be fully retracted/lowered during positioning and removal, where possible.  f.   No personnel can be carried on or in vehicles that do not have extra seats.  g.   Seat belts must be worn except in equipment that is repositioned within the same operational area, for example a parking area or chute.  h.   Before moving any ground support equipment/vehicle, ensure that all doors, if any, are closed.  i.   It is prohibited to use mobile phones, car phones and similar communication devices while using vehicles, tools and devices in the PAT zones.   In addition to these devices, portable music players and portable game consoles are also prohibited. Operators use handheld electronic devices with “hands-free” capability when operating ground equipment.  j.   Vehicles should only be used for their intended purpose.  k.   Before any ground support equipment or vehicle moves, its route must be checked to confirm that there are no people, equipment or other obstructions.  l.   The platform of the equipment whose level can be adjusted must be kept at the lowest level, except the final position when it approaches the aircraft (the elevating section must be kept at the lowest position).  m.   Platforms shall not be used when GSE is in motion.  n.   In order for the operator to maneuver safely around the aircraft when ground support equipment is positioned on or moved close to the aircraft and operator visibility is restricted, A second employee using standard hand signals shall be present. If visual contact with the assistant personnel is lost, the operator must stop the equipment immediately. Equipment shall not be moved until visual contact is established. Equipment should be supported by proper proximity detection and warning prompts and/or visual aids such as cameras and mirrors.  o.   While the motorized or electric-powered ground support equipment is serving the aircraft or giving a service near the aircraft: Apply the parking break with the gear selector in park or neutral. Turn off the engine, unless required when in operating/servicing mode. Install GSE wheel chocks. If equipped with self-stabilizers, ensure they are deployed before GSE is used for operation. If it has other safety devices, they must also be positioned before the operation. When equipment is positioned close to the aircraft and used in operating mode, the user should be within easy reach of emergency controls. Stand next to the tow bar when connecting or disconnecting dollies, make sure the tow pin is properly engaged before disconnecting. The tow bar handle must be used to connect and disconnect dollies.  h.   During transfer with baggage cart and dolly, the load must be secured by using suitable lock, curtain, strap, and safety rail.  i.   The overall height of the load must allow for the regular unloading and loading of each part of the load from the baggage cart by ground employee.  j.   Light packages must not be tucked between heavy pieces.  k.   While using tarpaulin/canvas, all straps must be fastened to the baggage cart securely.  l.   If the ground support equipment is equipped with a fixation system, that system must be positioned before the service. Other fixation devices, if any, must also be positioned.  m.   If equipment like a maintenance ladder will be used to open and close the doors of the cargo compartment; The ladder must have extendable/retractable safety rails to prevent falls. Maintenance ladders must face towards the accessed panel. The extendable/retractable safety rails of the ladder must be raised or pushed forward during positioning before any worker can use the ladder. The ladder cannot be moved with employee on it.  n.   The towable GPU, APU, and PCA may not be connected to the aircraft, unless they are disconnected from the towing vehicle. Before driving such equipment away from the aircraft, the operator must make sure that they are disconnected from the aircraft.  o.   The brakes/locks of the baggage carts must be set when not in use.  Danger:  While the movement of carts and dollies by hand is very simple, it can result in injuries. Therefore, additional care shall be taken.  3.1.3.4. Safe Use and Parking of Ground Support Equipment in Equipment Restraint Area  While using or parking the ground support equipment in the equipment restraint area, the operators must follow the following warnings to test that the equipment operates properly and the apron surface:  a.   Before entering the ERA area or at a distance of 5 (five) meters from the aircraft, ground support equipment must stop completely and check the brakes.  b.   The ground support equipment may not be used faster than walking speed (5 km/h, 3 mph).  c.   In order to avoid personnel injury and/or aircraft damage, ground support equipment must be maneuvered carefully, and A distance of at least one (1) meter must be maintained between the vehicle and the aircraft fuselage.  d.   When equipment is attached to vehicles no sharp turns shall not be made near aircraft.  e.   When positioning or towing ground support equipment to the aircraft, the operator shall: Marshalling should approach with a guide using hand signals, if the guide loses eye contact with the person(s) he/she should stop the vehicle he/she is using immediately, Appropriate proximity sensing systems on vehicles should be supported by visual aids such as cameras and mirrors when approaching the aircraft or positioning ground support equipment.  f.   The ground support equipment not used directly in the ground operation or other services given to the aircraft must not be used or parked in the Equipment Restraint Area (ERA).  g.   Ground support equipment and vehicles must not be operated or parked under the fuselage and/or wings. However, in the event that ground support equipment is required to be maneuvered or parked under the fuselage and/or wings; always make sure that necessary clearance is kept, and that maneuvers are guided by a guideman. h.   Great caution must be exercised during the positioning, lifting and maneuvering of ground support equipment to avoid injury to persons or property and/or damage to aircraft.  3.1.3.5. Passenger Boarding Bridge  Before using the bridges, the checks must be performed:  a.   While the bridge is moving, only the employee trained and authorized to use the bridge must be on it.  b.   Before using the bridge, it is confirmed with the bridge operator that the bridge is active.  c.   If the bridge has any defect, this must be informed and reported to the relevant person/unit.  d.   The walking surface of the passenger boarding bridge must be checked to see if it is safe (not wet/slippery) to use.  e.   While the bridge is moving, only the employee needed for use of the bridge must be on it.  Danger:   There is a risk of falling from height and operator distraction.  f.   At the aircraft arrival and departure times, the passenger boarding bridge must be in retracted to the allocated safe area.  g.   When the passenger boarding bridge is not retracted into the aircraft, it must be ensured that the security strip/doors are closed.  h.   It is necessary to make sure that the movement path is clear before moving the bridge.  i.   If the operator’s vision is limited while positioning the bridge at the passenger door, assisting employee is used. It is necessary to make sure that the assisting employee evaluates the distance correctly and guides the operator properly with his/her signs. If the visual contact with the employee is lost, the operation must be stopped immediately.  Note:   If the passenger boarding bridge is equipped with a system (like a sensor) enabling the operator to evaluate the distance properly and dock with and separate the bridge correctly, there is no need for assisting employee.  j.   During passenger boarding bridge positioning, the slide rails and canopies should be fully retracted and only extended when the bridge is in place.  k.   The passenger boarding bridge should be moved slowly towards the aircraft, avoiding contact with the sensors and protrusions of the aircraft, until the protective bumpers touch the aircraft (rain canopy, auxiliary equipment such as motion sensors) or the approach sensors stop movement. If the equipment used does not have a proximity sensor, it should never touch the aircraft. Contact must be avoided, especially on composite body aircraft. In case of even the slightest contact with composite fuselage aircraft, the responsible captain, technician or station officer must be notified. See item (s) 3.1.3.2 Basic Operating Conditions for Ground Support Equipment.  l.   It must be ensured that the passenger boarding bridge does not touch the wing root leading edge trim or any other sensor or other trim that extends below the cabin door.  m.   Once the passenger boarding bridge is positioned, care must be taken to ensure that all safety rails and canopies are fully extended. It is necessary to check that the bridge has docked at the aircraft without leaving any gap between the aircraft and the bridge so as not to cause anybody or any object to fall there.  n.   When the passenger boarding bridge is positioned/separated, the control panel must be secured and isolated to prevent unauthorized persons from intervening.  o.   Sufficient clearance must be left between the passenger boarding bridge and the underside of the cabin access door or as indicated on the cabin access door markings. This clearance is to prevent the risk of damage to the aircraft door by the passenger bridge when the aircraft is positioned during loading and unloading.  p.   The safety system or automatic level adjustment system, if any, must be activated. If the bridge does not have an automatic leveling feature, an operator must accompany when it is positioned on the aircraft.  q.   Before separating the passenger bridge, it must be ensured that the cabin door is closed. r.   The ground power cables and PCA hoses integrated with the passenger boarding bridge are disconnected from the aircraft before movement of the bridge unless they are necessary for operational purposes.  3.1.3.6. Passenger Stairs  It is necessary to follow the following warnings while using passenger stairs:  a.   Before using the passenger staircase, it must be checked that it is operational and that the surface of the staircase is clear of any slippery material (water, snow, ice, garbage discharge, oil, de-icing fluid, etc.).  b.   Before moving the passenger stairs, it must be checked that there are no workers, equipment/vehicles and no obstacles in the maneuvering area.  c.   The towable passenger stairs that will be docked to the aircraft must be separated from the tractor and braked after being manually pulled to the aircraft.  d.   The passenger stairs must be positioned outside the ERA before docking and after departing the aircraft, and it must be ensured that all railings and canopies are fully retracted during docking and departing the aircraft.  e.   When manoeuvring the passenger staircase towards the aircraft, contact with any sensors or projections must be avoided: The protective rubber bumper should approach without touching the aircraft, see 3.1.3.2.(s) It should be moved slowly until the approach sensors stop it. If the passenger stairs operator’s vision is limited while approaching the aircraft, assisting employee is used.  f.   It is necessary to make sure that the assisting employee evaluates the distance correctly and guides the operator properly with his/her signs. If the visual contact with the employee is lost, the operation must be stopped immediately.  Note:   If the passenger stairs are equipped with sensor or system that enables the operator to adjust the distance and approach and disengage properly, there is no need for assisting employee.  g.   Sufficient distance must be left between the passenger stairs and the underside of the cabin door, as high as the riser or as indicated on the cabin door markings to prevent damage. This distance must be checked during the entire operation. The handrails must be extended when the cabin door is opened. The cabin door must be closed before the passenger stairs disengage.  h.   If the passenger stairs have any safety system and automatic lifter feature, they must be used. If the passenger stairs do not have automatic lifter, the height of the passenger stairs must be observed and adjusted as necessary.  i.   If there is stabilizer, it must be positioned. No one but the operator must be allowed to use the stairs before positioning the stabilizers.  j.   The passenger stairs must be positioned so as to allow using the cabin door as a clear escape route in case of emergency. If the stairs are not adjacent to the aircraft, they must be kept sufficiently away from the slide deployment area for emergencies.  k.   Passenger stairs should not be retracted from the aircraft unless the cabin access door is closed.  l.   After the cabin door has been closed, confirm that there is no employee on the stairs, and then, retract the stabilizers of the stairs.  m.   If the stairs are separated from the aircraft by towing, they must be towed to a convenient position manually before connecting them to the tractor.  Danger:  The cabin doors must be opened only if there is ground support equipment or boarding gear positioned at the door. The cabin doors must never be opened unless the abovementioned equipment is positioned at the door. There is the risk of falling while opening the cabin doors. Slide deployment may be deadly. If an armed door is opened, it is necessary to avoid trying to hold the door, as this creates a serious risk of injury and death.  3.1.3.7. Belt Loader  The following precautions shall also be taken when operating a belt loader:  a.   The belt is not operated while the employee is on the conveyor.  b.   It is necessary to avoid standing or walking on the conveyor belt while the handrails are down. Handrails must not be lowered and raised when there is an employee on the belt.  c.   Do not sit, walk or stand on the conveyor belt while it is operating.  d.   Conveyor belts shall not be used to transport baggage, cargo or other items from one place to another, except for inflight operation.  e.   Belt sections of belt loaders must never be positioned in the cargo compartment of the aircraft. (Certain special design conveyors can be positioned in the compartment.).  f.   Position and remove a belt loader to/from the aircraft in a straight line.  g.   Allow tractors/trailers to access the belt loader without impeding slide deployment areas and passenger evacuation routes. Besides, the conveyor must be positioned in such a manner that no employee and load will fall through a gap between its rubber part and the cargo door threshold. Rubber part of the belt loader should never come into contact with the aircraft.  h.   Once the belt loader is positioned ensure the wheels are left in straight ahead position.  i.   As the belt loaders are positioned, the safety rails should be raised immediately. Ensure that the security rail does not touch the aircraft fuselage (security rails can be lowered for loading or unloading of large loads).  j.   Safety rails should also be raised when the belt loader is used to access the cargo compartment. However, great caution should be practiced where there is limited clearance from the fuselage or engine of the airplane.  k.   Ensure proper separation between articles on the belt loader to prevent jamming.  l.   When placing the aircraft on the conveyor for loading or unloading, care must be taken to ensure that it is balanced and positioned correctly on the belt.  m.   It must be ensured that there is no contact with the aircraft body/cargo hold door while unloading or loading cargo between the aircraft cargo hold and the conveyor belt.  n.   To prevent loads from falling off the belt, the rear section preparations of the conveyor belt (baggage cart, container) must be made and checked correctly.  o.   Conveyor guardrails can be lowered to allow large loads to be loaded during loading and unloading.  p.   Ensure the conveyor belt is clear of the aircraft or other obstacles before making a turn.  Danger:  Speeding up operation of the conveyor belt using the accelerator pedal/handle is not permitted.  Danger:  Care shall always be taken when working around a moving belt. Personnel shall remain vigilant to trap hazards while raising/lowering the safety rails. Hands and fingers must be protected from the end and edges of the belt. Belt movement shall be stopped before any attempt to clear any obstructions.  3.1.3.8. a.   It is necessary to check that the walking and loading surfaces of the loader are clean and safe for use.  b.   While the ULD loader is maneuvering, both platforms must have been lowered.  c. Except the ULDs that are too heavy to move only manually, the ULDs must not be moved by using external mechanical power support.  w.   While raising the ULD loader elevating platform, or during the transfer, the ULDs on the platform must not be turned.  x.   All employees must stay away from the platform during raising or lowering of the elevating platform.  y. The ULD loader must be driven backwards on a straight line at walking speed by observing that all directions are clear.  aa.   Before starting its turns, the path of the ULD loader must be cleared of all obstacles.  bb.   When the ULD is on the loader, the following must be ensured while moving the ULD:  1.   There must be no one on the platforms. Elevating Equipment  The following measures must be taken while using elevating equipment:  a.   To raise lift equipment, it must be ensured that all safety barriers/rails are secured in place before the platform is moved up.  b.   Before the lift is raised or lowered, it must be ensured that the loads in the vehicle are secured (wheelchair, stretcher) and all access doors are closed.  c.   Doors of lift equipment that are not used for service to the aircraft should be closed and locked.  d.   Lift equipment must be approached at the appropriate level/height so as not to interfere with the movements of the cabin doors and the service.  e.   While it is at the elevated position (final position) at the aircraft door, the lift equipment must allow a safe working area so that the employee and items do not fall. The distance between the aircraft and the platform must be minimized.  f.   Before accessing the platforms in front of and behind the lift equipment, it must be ensured that the platform and the lift are at the same level.  g.   The mobile ramp/ladder of the lift equipment must be placed carefully, as necessary, on the sill of the cabin door from the vehicle's platform direction.  h.   The equipment (catering trolley, etc.) and the passenger in wheelchair must be pushed forward and pulled towards the aircraft. There must be no material on the platform. There is no lifting equipment on the platform; and the unattended materials (like catering equipment) are not carried on the cart.  i.   It is necessary to watch the gap between the lift equipment platform and the aircraft continuously.  j.   When the process of giving service to the aircraft is over, the mobile ramp/ladder is towed back and retracted carefully and safely from the vehicle platform direction, and the aircraft doors are closed as shown in   article 4.4.2. Cabin Access Doors.  k.   The passenger and/or cargo in the lift equipment must be secured properly. The passengers must sit down and fasten their seatbelts. The wheelchairs of the passengers in wheelchairs must be secured while the lift equipment is moving.  l.   Before lowering the lift equipment, it must be checked whether there is any obstacle on both sides of the equipment.  m.   The platform of the lift equipment must be kept at the lowest level, except the final position when it approaches the aircraft (the elevating section must be kept at the lowest position).  n.   When the lift equipment service has been completed, its doors must be closed, and the equipment must be secured.  o.   For the gap around the lift equipment stabilizers and FOD, a walk-around check must be made.  p.   If the visibility is low, it is necessary to employ assisting employee. The assisting employee must assess the gap fully and inform it to the operator/driver by signs. If the visual contact with the assisting employee is lost, it is necessary to stop immediately.  q.   When the wind speed is 40 knots, the lift equipment operation must be paused. Danger:  Do not enter or place any part of the body inside the scissor area beneath the elevating equipment.  3.1.3.10. Ambulift  When using an Ambulift, in addition to the obligations in 3.1.3.9. Elevating Equipment, the following measures must be taken:  a.   Ambulift must be checked by the vehicle operators before use in order to ensure patient and employee safety, to identify possible technical defects or deficiencies that may arise during use, and to ensure such deficiencies are corrected.  b.   The vehicle’s fuel must be checked every night and must be topped up if necessary. It must be cleaned inside and out every night. Vehicle cleaning is the responsibility of the operator and must be done whenever necessary, regardless of the time.  3.1.3.10.1. Inbound Passenger Operation  a.   In line with the information given by the relevant department and/or assistant health employee, the Ambulift is driven to the aircraft parking position. Ambulift shall be ready at the relevant parking area at least five (5) minutes before the aircraft lands.  b.   When the parking position of the aircraft is reached, the forward or aft door of the aircraft is approached depending on the information provided by the relevant employee/assistant health employee.  c.   In order to stabilize the ambulift on the ground, the legs of the vehicle are lowered, the front door of the vehicle cabin is opened, and the lift is raised to the door level of the aircraft so that the front platform with the relevant/assistant health employee is seen.  d.   Safety measures are taken by placing the guardrails on the front platform.  e.   The crew waits for the patient/disabled passenger to be placed in the ambulift. The wheelchair/stretcher is mounted on the fixing points in the ambulift cabin.  f.   After the passenger is placed, the safety railings are raised as per the information provided by the relevant/assistant health employee.  g.   The lift is lowered, provided that the front platform with the relevant/assistant health employee is seen, and the front door of the vehicle cabin is closed.  h.   Ambulift goes to the terminal exit gate indicated by the relevant/assistant health employee. Upon reaching the terminal exit gate, the vehicle is parked safely.  i.   The vehicle operator brings the Ambulift rear platform to a horizontal position, opens the safety railing barriers behind the cabin, and closes and locks the door of the railing barriers.  j.   The rear platform is raised to the level of the passenger cabin by the vehicle operator.  k.   When the rear platform is at the same level as the passenger cabin, the relevant/assistant health official is given the necessary confirmation. The relevant/assistant health employee first completes the necessary safety checks after receiving the confirmation and then takes the patient/disabled passenger out of the cabin and onto the platform.  l.   Only one health employee and one passenger in a wheelchair and that passenger's companion may be present at a time on the rear platform of the vehicle during the lowering and lifting process. However, the number of assistant health employees may be increased to two depending on the condition of the patient/disabled passenger. In the case of a passenger on stretcher, a minimum of two (2) and a maximum of three (3) health employees accompany the passenger on stretcher, depending on their condition. When the passenger transferred by stretcher is taken to the ambulift platform, the accompanying passenger must not be taken to the platform.  m.   The passenger and the employee are waited to be ready on the rear platform. The rear platform is lowered by the vehicle operator upon the information given by the relevant/assistant health employee.  n.   When the rear platform touches the ground, the guardrails are opened by the vehicle operator and the relevant/assistant health employee is allowed to exit safely.  o.   After the rear platform railings are closed, they are lifted and closed.  p.   After the passenger transfer is completed, if there is no other instruction, the vehicle returns to its location. 3.1.3.10.2. Outbound Passenger Operation  a.   The vehicle is driven to the terminal exit gate where the passenger will be picked up according to the information provided by the relevant department or the relevant/assistant health employee.  b.   Ambulift is parked safely based on the information given by the relevant/assistant health employee.  c.   Ambulift rear cabin door is opened. The vehicle operator opens the rear platform and lowers the platform until it touches the ground, and opens the guardrail barriers.  d.   After the passenger is placed on the rear platform of the vehicle by the relevant/assistant health employee, the vehicle operator closes and locks the door of the guardrail barriers and lifts the platform up according to the information given by the relevant/assistant health employee.  e.   There are 2 people on the rear platform of the vehicle at a time: only one relevant/assistive health employee and one passenger in a wheelchair. (Only in passenger on stretcher operations, an additional relevant/assistive health employee may be present on the rear platform.)  f.   The passenger is waited to be placed in the Ambulift and the platform is closed after the back door is closed.  g.   Ambulift is moved to the parking position where the aircraft is located according to the information provided by the relevant/assistant health employee.  h.   The forward or aft door of the aircraft is approached depending on the information provided by the relevant employee/assistant health employee.  i.   The front platform door of the vehicle is opened. The vehicle operator lifts the front platform with the relevant/assistant health employee on it, and docks the vehicle by the aircraft door. Safety precautions are taken and the guardrails of the front platform are installed.  j.   The passenger is waited to be transferred and placed in the aircraft.  k.   After the transfer and placement of the passenger in the aircraft, the platform is lowered and the front door of the vehicle is closed upon the information provided by the relevant/assistant health employee.  l.   After the passenger transfer is completed, if there is no other instruction, the vehicle returns to its location.  3.1.3.11. Tractor/Electric Baggage Cart  It is necessary to follow the following warnings while using tractor:  a.   The tractor must drive the tractor within the speed limits as per the local airport authority's rules, and avoid sudden tight turns, abrupt movements, and sudden stops.  b.   A maximum of four full or six empty baggage carts or "dollies" can be attached to baggage towing tractors. If there are loaded baggage carts and "dollies" among the baggage vehicles being towed the total of baggage carts and dollies must not exceed four including empty ones. The maximum numbers of baggage carts and dollies that can be towed may vary by local authority regulations.  c.   No tight turn is performed when too close to the aircraft.  d.   It is necessary to stay minimum 1 m (3 ft) away from the aircraft fuselage.  e.   During the operation, the tractor must approach so as to be one (1) meter away from the conveyor. When it becomes necessary to place the baggage carts closer than one (1) meter to the conveyor, the position of the baggage carts must be adjusted manually.  f.   The brake check must be made in compliance with the conditions specified in article 3.1.3.4. Safe Use and Parking of Ground Support Equipment in Equipment Restraint Area.  g.   Before moving with the towed load, it is necessary to ensure that there are no employees between or near the towed load.  h.   The appropriate dolly type must be used to carry the load depending on the ULD type.  i.   During the loading and offloading process, a suitable distance must be left between the dolly and the loader. To prevent ULD falls, if the distance between the loader and the dolly is nonconforming, the dolly must be realigned.  j.   It is necessary to make sure that the ULD is fully transferred to the loader before moving the tractor. ULD Transporter  It is necessary to follow the following warnings while using ULD transporter:  a.   Do not stand or sit on the cylinder bearing.  b.   Do not stand and walk between the ULD transporter and the ULD loader and dollies.  c.   For safe transfer of the load, the ULD transporter should be positioned at a 90° angle to the ULD loader/dollies.  d.   If there is elevating platform: The ULDs must not be sent to the ramp area while the platform is in the elevated position. The platform is not elevated until it is positioned at a convenient distance from the aircraft.  e.   If the operator has low visibility for any reason, guideman must be employed (e.g. when he does not have camera or mirror to see their path clearly while moving backwards with ULD on the transporter.) If he loses visual contact with the guideman, the operator must stop the ULD transporter immediately.  f.   The ULD transporter should be used in low gear and at less than walking speed when maneuvering in the ERA site.  Note:   For more warnings on the combined ULD transporter/loader equipment,   see article 3.1.3.8. Loader.  3.1.4. General Rules for Driving Vehicles at Apron  a. Vehicles, tools and equipment for which inspection has not been done or which do not comply with other conditions cannot work on the PAT zone until the fault/violation is resolved by the concerned company and the airport operator inspects it and issues conformity documents.  f.   Any vehicles, tools and equipment that have a malfunction on the PAT zones are moved off the site informing the airport operator tower and/or apron management as soon as possible.  g.   The repair/maintenance of vehicles, tools and equipment can only be done by authorized organizations/corporations and official in designated locations.  h. In case of brake unit and landing gear fires to occur on the apron (including also the other aircraft fires), the ground employee is required to report the fire to their superiors immediately when they see it; they or their superiors must call the fire brigade urgently; the ground employee must wait for the fire brigade and avoid responding to the fire themselves.  3.1.7.1. Fire Extinguishers  Portable Fire Extinguishers;  a.   Must always be available for emergency use.  b. Must meet the applicable standards and be periodically checked in accordance with the local regulations.  d.   Must be available in all apron vehicles.  e. Fire Prevention and Protection  The employee must always be aware of fire hazards and potential sources of fire in their area of operation and try to mitigate and eliminate these hazards during operation (e.g. refueling, open cables, dangerous goods handling, GPU connections and use of electrical equipment).   To eliminate situations that could lead to fire:  a.   The employee must never smoke on the apron area except in a designated smoking area.  b.   All employees must know the location and use of fire extinguishing equipment, fire alarms, fuel hydrant system emergency shut-off button, etc.  c.   All employees must know the muster areas.  d. Garbage must be disposed of in designated garbage bins, and no accumulation of garbage must be allowed.  g. Smoke from GSE and vehicles must be reported immediately.  i.   No GSE/equipment must be refueled while the engine is running or electronic equipment is in use.  j.   GSE/vehicles must only be parked as follows: 1. In defined equipment parking areas, 2. In such a way as not to obstruct access to fire-fighting equipment and the fuel hydrant emergency shut-off valve.  3.1.7.3. Actions to be taken in case of Ground Support Equipment (GSE)/Vehicle Fire  The fire is intervened with available fire extinguishers.  GSE/vehicles on fire are removed from the aircraft and the operational area as far as possible. If the GSE/vehicles on fire are not moved, the adjacent GSE/vehicles are removed to prevent the fire from spreading.  3.1.8. Security incidents.  When any of the emergencies that may occur in the ramp area occur; a. Lay down the person, and cover her/him with a blanket or coat, jacket etc. Press down the blanket etc. by using your hands to cut off the supply of oxygen to the burning part. Remove the blanket, coat or jacket, etc. slowly and carefully after you are sure that the fire is extinguished. The   detailed   information   is   available   in   the   requirements   in   EK.10.74.002   Fuel   Manual/Chapter-2   Aircraft Fuelling/Defuelling Procedures.  Warning:  In case of manual fueling due to technical malfunction, the fueling duration takes longer than automatic fueling. In order to control the fueling process and avoid delays: Contracted company officials to provide fuel service and the technician who will do the fueling shall be informed of the manual fueling process, Fueling equipment and technician shall be present at the parking lot before the arrival of the aircraft at the station, As fueling will take a long time, the ground handling employee acting as operations coordinator shall coordinate with the technician and cockpit crew and prepare for the process described in section 3.2.3.  Fueling/Defueling with Passengers on Board.  3.2.6.1. Refueling Operations while One Engine is Running  Refueling an aircraft with one engine running is a non-routine emergency operation, and safety precautions must be taken. The application must only be used when the aircraft engine cannot be restarted due to the unavailability of the ASU (Air Starter Unit) service. The aircraft must be positioned at least 50 meters away from the passenger boarding/deboarding area of the terminal, any other building, and other aircraft. The nose of the aircraft must be turned into the wind. Additional supervisor or fuel employee must be present during refueling. Refueling shall not start until all passengers have deboarded the aircraft and all employees assigned to the operation are at least 50 meters away. (Except for refueling employees). Refueling employees must not approach the running aircraft engine. Before starting refueling with one engine running, the fire brigade must be on standby near the aircraft. Refueling is not done from the side of the running engine. The   detailed   information   is   available   in   the   requirements   in   EK.10.74.002   Fuel   Manual/Chapter-2   Aircraft   Fuelling/Defuelling Procedures.  3.3. Winter or Slippery Apron Conditions  Winter weather brings extra hazards. The employee assigned to the apron is required to be more aware and careful to prevent operational accidents. Plan additional time for all ramp activities and take extra care when walking across apron surfaces, which can be slippery.  b.   Take extra care when driving, especially when approaching the aircraft. It is necessary to consider that the vehicles need longer distance to stop safely. On receipt of a stop order; Stop fueling. Fueling hoses cannot be left attached to the aircraft during any thunderstorm/lightning event. Discontinue aircraft communication by headset. Figure-11: Calculation Method Graph  Note:   Figure-11: The time shown in the Calculation Method Graph is the time between the flash of lightning and the sound of thunder.  1. If the period between the stroke of lightning and the sound of thunder is shorter than 15 seconds, the risk level is red. This indicates that the lightning has stricken a place nearer than 5 km. 2. If the period between the stroke of lightning and the sound of thunder is between 15 sec. and 25 sec., the risk level is orange. This indicates that the lightning has stricken a place at a distance between five (5) km and eight (8) km.  3.3.4. Danger:  Winds aloft cause serious damage and injury risk.  3.3.6. Heavy Rain and Flood  Heavy rains, winds and dense cloud cover are often precursors to thunder and lightning events, alerting individuals to take precautionary action. Heavy rainfall can cause rain to splash off hard surfaces, restricting visibility and pooling water on the aircraft door, the ground and ground support equipment.  Figure-12: Heavy Rain and Flood  In heavy rain and floods, the following measures should be taken as a minimum: Employee must wear appropriate personal protective equipment (raincoat, boots, etc.). In case of flooding, seek shelter in a protected area with proper conditions. Ensure that the GSE is parked on the parking brakes and secured with additional chocks. Check that all cargo and passenger doors of the aircraft on ground standby are closed before the operation. In case of heavy rain, loading of catering should be managed against the risk of heavy rain at the aircraft service gate and loading of baggage/cargo should be handled under control against the risk of rain inside the hold.  CAUTION!  Heavy rainfall coming into contact with the interior panels of the aircraft may cause the aircraft to AOG. Check that container Velcro fasteners are closed to prevent the baggage brought by container from getting wet, and that the tarpaulin on the baggage trolley is closed for baggage brought by baggage trolley. Avoid keeping baggage and cargo under rain for a prolonged period of time to prevent them from getting wet, even if all precautions are taken. In rainy weather, BULK/ULD cargoes, especially DG cargoes and those with the risk of getting wet and damaged should not be loaded on the aircraft.  Figure-13: Example of Wet DG That Should Not Be Loaded onto an Aircraft  Upon arrival of aircraft with bulk loaded cargo, the unloading should be carried out using a container used for baggage transportation or a covered baggage trolley as much as possible. Unloading time should be kept short if using containers is not possible. In the event of heavy rainfall that may affect the visibility of the operator while servicing the aircraft and prevent the GSE (push back, conveyor, etc.) from functioning, the senior supervisor shall be informed. Operation shall be suspended until sight is restored upon instructions from the superior officer. Introduction  The following hand signals are defined in order to standardize the communications between two ground operations employees, or a ground operations employee and flight crew:  a.   Guide Employee Hand Signals are used by the guide employee in direct contact with the equipment operator to facilitate the movement of any ground support equipment.  b.   Marshalling Hand Signals are used by the ground employee who helps the flight crew while the aircraft starts its engines and maneuvers.  c.   Technical/Service Hand Signals are used by the ground employee to give technical/service information to the cockpit crew, and by the cockpit crew to give technical information/service aircraft service information to the ground employee.  Note-1:   Use manual signals only when verbal communication is not possible. (If a headset malfunction is detected before the pushback operation starts, hand signals are not used. After the new headset arrives, the operation continues. In case of a headset failure after the pushback operation has started (while starting the way to taxiing or on the way to taxiing), the operation is continued with hand signals.)  Note-2 : It is necessary to make sure all signals are received by the flight crew.  d.   Aircraft Movements Hand Signals are the hand signals used during connection/disconnection with/out towbar, from start to finish of the aircraft ground movement operation.  3.4.2. Situations when Hand Signals are used  The person using the hand signals;  a.   Must have been trained and certified.  b.   Must use the approved hand signals only.  c.   Must wear a distinctive fluorescent identification vest -different than other employee- allowing the cockpit crew to know that s/he is the Marshal responsible for the marshalling operation.  d.   Must use signal wands in highly visible colors under daytime conditions. Must use light signal wands under low visibility or nighttime conditions. (The requirements of the local airport authority shall be followed).  e.   Must act as the single person in charge of the procedure from the beginning to the end.  f.   Must keep visual contact with the other ground operations employee and flight crew from the beginning to the end of maneuver. If visual contact is lost, the operation must be stopped and not be re-commenced until visual contact is re-established. All Clear  Figure-69: Hand Signal for All Clear  Raise one hand, thumb up and the other fingers down. This is the acknowledgment of completion of all ground operations.  3.5. Lavatory Services 3.5.1. Introduction  The service given for the aircraft toilet waste tank covers the processes of discharging, rinsing, and disinfecting. Lavatory service and water supply process must be carried out by the qualified ground operations employee. The toilet liquids are abrasive. Before opening it, it is necessary to make sure that there is no leak (blue ice) from the lavatory servicing panel and its covers are closed (if there are leaks from the water supply and drain panels, ice forms while the aircraft is on ground and in flight under the adverse weather conditions, and while it is in flight under normal conditions. This ice may break off after a while, and cause damage to the aircraft and engines). In case of a potential leakage, the cabin crew and/or the station officer must be informed of it immediately, and this leakage must be cleaned before giving service to the aircraft. After completion of the cleaning, a second check must be made for leakage. If the aircraft is to lay over for a long period of time under cold weather conditions, the water and lavatory tanks shall be discharged by the responsible officials.  3.5.2. Hygiene Measures  a.   As specified in the requirements of   DK.41.012 Airport Handling Manual (AHM)/440 Portable Water Servicing article 10.1., the employee assigned to lavatory servicing must absolutely wear special clothes protecting their face and body as well as rubber gloves to protect their hands.  b.   The distance between the toilet water servicing vehicles, trucks, etc. and the clean water supply vehicles must be more than 30 meters.  c.   Toilet service vehicles and water supply vehicles may not be filled with water from the same source. The detailed information on water supply service is available in   PR.67.016 Procedure for Management of Drinking and Potable Waters on Board.  d.   The toilet servicing and water supply may not be carried out simultaneously.  e.   As specified in the requirements of   DK.41.016 IATA Ground Operations Manual (IGOM)/article 3.5.2.   Hygiene Precautions, the employee who supplies water may not give both lavatory and water supply services within the same day.  3.5.3. Lavatory Service Procedure 3.5.3.1. General  a.   The aircraft toilet servicing vehicle must approach the aircraft absolutely through marshaling, the parking brake must be set, and the vehicle must be chocked before commencing the operation. The operations on the aircraft must be started after taking these measures. The toilet servicing process must be completed before boarding of the passengers.  b.   The toilet servicing processes must be carried out in compliance with the requirements specified in the Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM-38) of each aircraft type.  c.   It is necessary to use non-calcareous water for toilet servicing process.  d.   The toilet system must be serviced in the amounts specified in Table-16: Rinsing Process and Disinfectant Amount by Aircraft Type.  e.   The toilet liquids must not contact the aircraft body. a.   Before starting the necessary process, wear personal protective equipment (gloves, mask, apron, etc.).  b.   Before opening the toilet servicing panels, check the panels for any dirt around them.  c.   While opening the servicing panels, stay away from the panels and monitor if there is any leakage.  d.   Stay away from the discharge connection covers and check if there are leakage symptoms.  e.   Before starting the discharge process, check that the draining hose is connected to the aircraft servicing valve correctly.  f.   Connect the discharge line.  g.   Turn and pull the drain valve in order to discharge the tank.  h.   Monitor the draining hose during the discharge process in order to make sure that the tank is completely empty. At the end of the process, shake the hose for a few seconds in order to make sure that the wastes have been discharged from the hose to the vehicle tank completely.  i.   Tanks are discharged one by one for optimum result.  j.   Once discharge is complete, the rinsing process is started.  k.   In the event that the servicing panels cannot be opened or the tank cannot be discharged, information on the situation is given immediately to cabin crew and/or station official. In the event that a considerable amount of waste splashes on the employee performing the process during the discharge, that employee informs their immediate superior by radio, and that superior assigns another employee to the task. The employee exposed to waste splash must take off their clothes and wash themselves immediately. The ground handling agents are responsible for performing the medical checks in addition to the other necessary checks.  The rinsing process is for cleaning the residual wastes in the tanks. The ground operations employee shall  connect the rinsing line while the discharge line is connected.  feed the sufficient amount of pressure water in the manner appropriate for the aircraft type. (Table-16: Rinsing Process and Disinfectant Amount by Aircraft Type)  rinse the tank twice and drains it again. do not disconnect the discharge line before the rinsing process is over. return the drain valve to its initial position to turn it off and disconnect the discharge line from the aircraft. close the service hatch after waiting for 5 (five) minutes after disconnecting the discharge line.  a. Use of Disinfectant  The disinfectants are used to prevent the microbiological pollution and foul smells in the tanks. The disinfectant amount to be used is specified in Table-16: Rinsing Process and Disinfectant Amount by Aircraft Type.   The ground operations employee shall  feed clean water mixed with disinfectant into the aircraft after completion of the rinsing process. disconnect the rinsing line after completing the process and keep the service hatch open for five (5) minutes. must check the service covers or the service panel and the connection hose visually for any fluid leakage in order to avoid corrosions that will damage the aircraft body. wipe the service covers with a clean cloth before closing in order to prevent icing, and then close the covers securely. take off their personal protective equipment after completing the servicing process, and wash their hands with water and soap.  3.5.3.3. a.   In case of Boeing aircraft, when the air temperature is at or below freezing point, if the aircraft systems do not function, the waste tank must be discharged absolutely. The station officer or the technical department must be informed of the situation immediately.  d.   When the aircraft is going to be assigned to an operation, in order to make sure that the water in the waste tank will not freeze, antifreeze fluids may be added to the tank at the pre-filling stage. Since foams can form when the antifreeze fluids and detergent mix with each other, it is necessary to pay attention to type of the fluids used. In order to prevent this situation, the manufacturer instructions of the antifreeze fluids must be checked. For cargo aircraft, the process is carried out according to the details in   PR.61.001 Procedure Of Freighter Cleaning.  3.8. Safety in De-icing/Anti-icing Operations 3.8.1. General  No aircraft shall attempt takeoff when frozen or freezing contamination is present or an adhering to the wings, propellers, control surfaces or other critical surfaces. This is known as ICAO Clean Aircraft Concept. Compliance with this requirement can be achieved by appropriate use of anti-icing or de-icing procedures, or where necessary a combination of both. Detailed procedures and requirements for de-icing and anti-icing are available in   EK.10.67.002 De-Icing/Anti-Icing Manual. This section provides the general guidelines for safe de-icing/anti-icing operations. The term de-icing shall be used throughout this section, but it shall be considered to refer also to the anti-icing process. De-icing operations shall be performed with extreme caution to prevent injury to employees and damage to aircraft and equipment. De-icing operation is not permitted before completing the fueling operation.  3.8.2. Employee Safety  The safety factors given below are designed to ensure that safety is not compromised for employee performing aircraft de-icing tasks:.  a.   Appropriate Personal Protective Equipment shall be checked for serviceability and worn by all employee engaged in de-icing operations.  b.   When necessary, the cones shall be removed to allow access to the aircraft surfaces. If the aircraft is not departing, upon completion of the de-icing operation, the cones shall be returned to their assigned points.  c.   To prevent injury, caution must be taken when filling de-icing vehicles with hot fluid. When refueling the de-icing vehicle with fluid, care must be taken to prevent possible spills and to prevent employees to contact with the fluid.  1.   During use and handling of de-icing fluids, it is necessary to avoid spillage and comply with the local environmental and health rules as well as the fluid manufacturer’s safety data sheet.  2.   Before de-icing operation starts, the operation shall be coordinated between the de-icing and ground operations employee.  3.   De-icing/anti-icing fluids may be 60°C or warmer. The nozzle exit temperature of the fluid or fluid-water mixture planned to be used for de-icing purposes on the aircraft is a minimum of 60°C. For maximum values of the fluid or fluid-water mixture, the limits of the fluid manufacturer shall be consulted. For maximum values of the aircraft surface temperature, the aircraft manufacturer's documentation must also be taken into account. In order to prevent injuries, the ground employee, passengers, and the flight crew must be prevented from walking near the aircraft during de-icing process.  4.   Slippery conditions can exist onthe ground and equipment surfaces during and following the de-icing processes.. Caution shall be exercised, particularly in low humidity or nonprecipitating weather conditions, due to increased slipperiness following the use of glycol that is not diluted by the weather element.  5.   During the de-icing operation process, all ramp equipment, including the stairs, must be removed from the application area to prevent the avoid contamination by de-icing/anti-icing fluid. When de-icing on a stand, all ramp equipment, including steps, should be clear of the area to be sprayed to avoid contamination by fluid.  6.   Care should be taken to avoid contamination on the ground handling equipment (e.g. steps, passenger bridges), aircraft interiors and aircraft cargo holds by walking. Operation with Open Basket Vehicle  When the de-icing operation is carried out with open basket vehicle, the following measures must be taken:  a.   While performing de-icing operation with open basket vehicle, it is necessary to make sure that the fall prevention/restriction device is connected safely and the safety belt is always fastened.  b.   It is necessary to make sure that the basket door or the safety chain is locked securely.  c.   In the event that the auxiliary power unit (APU) is active, caution shall be taken to avoid exposure to potential safety risks (fire risk, etc.).  3.8.4. Operation with Closed Basket Vehicle  When the de-icing operation is carried out with closed basket vehicle, the following measures must be taken:  a.   Ensure that the safety belt is always fastened.  b.   Ensure the vehicle cabin windows are clean. In order to carry out the de-icing operation in compliance with the regulations, the vehicle cabin wipers and the wiper fluid level must be checked.  c.   Ensure the cabin access door is securely closed.  d. Ensure that the vehicle cabin heater/ventilation systemair-conditioner do not have any defect. The detailed information on and all requirements related to de-icing/anti-icing processes is given in   EK.10.67.002 De-icing/Anti-icing Manual and   EK.10.73.001 Operations Manual Part-A/section 8.2.4 De-icing and Anti-icing on Ground.  4. AIRCRAFT DEPARTURE AND ARRIVAL PROCESSES  4.1. Aircraft Arrival  4.1.1. Actions Prior to Aircraft Arrival  a.   It must be ensured that employees responsible for aircraft arrival and post-arrival services are knowledgeable about the safety and operational requirements of their duties. (For example, aircraft malfunctions that may affect ground handling operations, equipment positioning and operational requirements.).  b.   In order to prevent Foreign Object Damage (FOD), the ramp area must be cleared of all debris and ensure that there are no exposed elements.  c.   It is necessary to make the parking are sufficiently clear of ice, snow, etc. to ensure safe aircraft movement.  d.   It is necessary to make sure that the necessary ground support equipment is ready in active status, and such equipment must be positioned out of ERA, at a safe distance from the arrival path of the aircraft.  e.   If an automatic call system is used, it must be ensured that it is active and only works when it is not unsafe for the aircraft to approach the parking position. If an automatic call system is not used, make sure the marshalling employee is present in the parking lot.  f.   If necessary, there must be extra assisting employee (like wingwalker).  g.   It is necessary to make sure that the taxiway and the ramp area to be used by the aircraft are free of any objects that may be collided with by the aircraft or jeopardize the safety of others due to "jet blast" effects of the engines.  h.   Especially in night conditions, the headlights of the equipment/vehicle coming to the aircraft for service must not face the cockpit of the approaching aircraft, and must be turned off if the equipment/vehicle is parked in the standby position.
