Danger:  All employees not assigned to the arrival operation must wait at a safe distance out of ERA area until arrival of the aircraft and not approach the aircraft until the following processes are completed.  1.   Until the engines are switched off and stop.  2.   Until the anti-collision lights are turned off.  3.   Until the main landing gears are chocked.  4.   Until the ground operations official responsible for the arrival flight approves (if available).  4.1.2. Arrival Procedures  a. Standard arrival procedure at a stand without an automated guide-in system or at an open ramp:  As aircraft approaches the stand area, the marshaller points to the guide-in line on the ramp to be followed by the aircraft by standing at the top of the guide-in line and giving the “Identify Stand” signal (See article 3.4.7.1. Identify Stand). If necessary, Wing Walker should be positioned approximately one (1) meter (3 feet) from the wingtip. Wing Walker shall be in visual contact with the person responsible for guiding the airplane until the airplane comes to a complete stop. While the aircraft taxies along the guide-in line, the marshaller must give the “Continue to Taxi ahead” signal with marshalling wands. (See article 3.4.7.2. Continue to Taxi Straight Ahead) The nose wheel should follow the lead-in line all the way to the appropriate stop point according to the aircraft type. “Turn Left” (from the flight crew’s point of view) or “Turn Right” (from the flight crew’s point of view) signals should be used to correct the track of the aircraft as required. (See articles 3.4.7.4. Turn Right (from the Pilot-In-Command’s Point of View) and 3.4.7.5. Turn Left (from the Pilot-In-Command’s Point of View)) If, at any time during aircraft movement, marshaller is unsure or identify an imminent danger, the marshaller should signal “STOP/EMERGENCY STOP” to the aircraft. (See, article 3.4.7.6. Stop/Emergency Stop). If, at any time during aircraft movement, Wing Walker is unsure or identify an imminent danger, the Wing Walker should signal “STOP/EMERGENCY STOP” to the marshaller. (See article 3.4.7.6. Stop/Emergency Stop). As the aircraft approaches the stop position, the “Slow Down” signal should be used if required (See, article 3.4.7.3. Slow Down). As the nose wheel reaches the stop point, the wands should be slowly crossed in the “STOP” signal. (See 3.4.7.6. Stop/Emergency Stop) The information that the chocks are inserted is given via the headset, by the marshaller signaling "Chocks inserted" (see, article 3.4.7.13. Chocks inserted) or by pressing the "Chocks on" button on the bridge, if available.  b. Standard arrival procedure at a stand with an automated guide-in system:  The ground employee responsible for arrival operations shall ensure that the equipment is operational and the correct aircraft type has been selected. The employee responsible for operating the emergency button shall have an unobstructed view of the arriving of the aircraft and be within reach of the system to the stop the aircraft if needed. It is essential to maintain a continuous unobstructed view between the employee responsible for operating the emergency stop button and the ground employee (“Wing Walker”) ensuring clearance. If the emergency stop is activated, and only after verification by the ground employee operating the guidance system that the risk has been eliminated, the aircraft docking guidance system can be reactivated. If not reactivated, standard aircraft arrival procedures shall be followed. If required, Wing Walkers should be positioned approximately one (1) meter (3 feet) from the wingtip. Wing Walkers must be in visual contact with the marshaller for guiding the airplane until the airplane comes to a complete stop. For positioning of the wing walker during the aircraft’s arrival at the parking position, see Figure 70:   Wing Walker Positioning for Aircraft Arrival. All cargo access doors, All access panels and servicing access points, Aircraft fuselage, Aircraft engine cowlings/propellers, Aircraft cabin doors including service doors.  d. Note 1:   If any damage is detected, the station official/immediate superior is informed of it; and the damaged area is never approached with ground support equipment.  Note 2:   Spooling down of an engine can be identified as follows: reduced engine noise, visible fan or propeller speed reduction, or reduced engine speed. Placement and Removal of Safety Cones  Safety cones are portable warning signs that provide a warning to ground service vehicle drivers servicing the aircraft warning them not to drive under the wing and/or between the engines, and setting the safety distance. These cones signify a safe working area. Cones protect parts of the aircraft against collision by GSE. Prior to the arrival of the aircraft in the parking position, make sure there are sufficient serviceable safety cones. The required safety marker cones shall remain in place until the activities of the ground support equipment and vehicles around the aircraft have ceased prior to take-off.   (except ASU and GPU/FPU.) Before the safety cones are collected, it must be ensured that all other vehicles, except ground support equipment required for the take-off operation, such as ASU, Pushback and GPU, are removed from the ERA. Design of Cones  The design requirements of the cones are defined in   DK.41.012 Airport Handling Manual (AHM)/462 Safe Operating Practices in Aircraft Handling.  a. Warning:  In order that they can grab attention in the visuals, the cones in the document have been colored differently. Use of Cones upon Arrival of Aircraft  The cones are placed after the aircraft has come and stopped completely at the parking position, the chocks have been placed, and the "anti-collision" beacons indicating that the engines of the aircraft are still running have been turned off.  Before the ground support equipment starts their maneuvers to approach the aircraft (except for PBB and GPU), the cones must be placed at the wingtips, in front of the wing-mounted engines, and external side of the engines in such a manner that they will not block the movements of the equipment during the ground operations process. When there is a service road or the service vehicles ride behind/in front of the aircraft, under low visibility conditions, in the MARS parking areas, and when the ground clearance is low, it is necessary to place cones in the nose and tail areas of the aircraft as well.  The cones must never be placed on the taxiway and/or vehicle lane. As long as the ground handling processes continue, the cones must not be removed from their positions. In order to achieve their intended use, the cones must be positioned at a distance of 0.5 to 1 m to the areas that must be protected. Warning:  Coning may vary by country or authority regulations. However, the number of cones must not be less than the number specified herein.  4.4. Aircraft Access Doors 4.4.1. General Safety Requirements  Aircraft access doors are passenger entry, service, and cargo loading/offloading doors. The employee carrying out the door opening/closing process must have received the required training and certificates. If any difficulty emerges during the door opening/closing operations, assistance must be requested from the technical employee. If any damage is detected on the aircraft surface, it must be reported to the immediate supervisor, technical maintenance employee, or flight crew. A320 Family   If the wind speed exceeds 65 knots, do not open the passenger/crew door. A330 CAUTION! Regardless of which party wants to reopen the door, first the flight crew gives approval for reopening of the door, and then the abovementioned steps are followed.  g.   If the door is not permitted to be reopened, do not attempt to open the door until you have received approval from the flight crew.  4.4.3. Before closing the door: In the bulk loading cargo compartments, the door protection doors must be stretched safely and in compliance with the rules. If there is no AVIH carried, the compartment lights must be tuned off. It is necessary to pay attention that the door sill and the area around the door are clear of stones, water, ice, foreign objects or debris. A visual inspection shall be carried out to check for any sign of damage on or around the doors, after the doors are closed.  If any nonconformity/irregularity is detected during visual check, it must be reported to the authorized technician and the commander.  It is necessary to make sure that the latches/locks on the door threshold are raised.  b.   The activation of the door lock indicators should be checked and adjusted accordingly. The door latches of the compartments configured for ULD loading must be operational and locked. The door must be properly locked, the door handles must be even with the body and properly closed. Aircraft Loading and Unlloading  4.5.1. Supervision of Aircraft Loading and Unloading 4.5.1.1. Introduction  The employee who supervises the aircraft loading operation is responsible for the protection of the cargo carried as well as the safe and correct execution of the aircraft loading and unloading operations. This task will ensure that the aircraft is loaded in accordance with the weight and balance calculation specified in item 5.3.   Duties in the Weight and Balance Calculation Process, the relevant loading processes and conditions in item 5.2.2.   Loading Instruction/Report (LIR), and unloaded in accordance with the load distribution message (LDM)/container pallet message (CPM) or other incoming messages.  Note:   The loading and unloading operation should begin with the employee responsible for loading and/or unloading ready for duty in the hold.  4.5.1.2. Communication  Pronunciation and understanding of the letter and number combination when verbal communication is used is very important to the sender and receiver of the message by radio or telephone, regardless of the employees’ native languages. The ICAO   phonetic alphabet and numbering system in article 0.27. Phonetic Alphabet should be used by all parties involved in aircraft departure and arrival activities. In order for all loads to be calculated correctly before departure, uninterrupted/open communication should be established between the employee responsible for the loading and loading plan, and the following items must be mutually approved.  1.   Flight Number and Aircraft Registration Mark  2.   Flight Legs (if needed)  3.   LIR Edition number  4.   Positions of all loads in the compartment, including NIL positions  5.   Standby loads not loaded onto the aircraft  6.   Information on all loads If verbal communication is carried out between the employee preparing the Loading Instruction/Report (LIR) and the employee performing the loading in the hold, when the employee preparing the Loading Instruction/Report (LIR) receives the information in the above-mentioned items, s/he must repeat them and it should be mutually confirmed.  Note-1:   The rules above are applicable in cases of verbal communication between the cargo control office and the employee in charge of the loading, and in cases of verbal communication between the loaders and the crew leader responsible for the loading.  Note-2:   Standard communication should be established in order to avoid communication problems in aircraft loading and unloading operations   and   flight   close   out   operations,   especially   in   cases   of   inconsistency/change   in   loads.   Standard   communication   is established in the situations listed in Table-19: Table of Situations where Standard Communication should be established in case of Inconsistency/Change   in   Loads.   Additionally,   this   process   is   applicable   between   the   employee   preparing   the   Loading Instruction/Report (LIR) and the employee performing the loading in the hold, and between the loaders and the crew leader responsible for the loading.  Note-3:   In verbal communication, a headset, telephone and a powerful radio device should be used due to the necessity of strong and understandable communication. In this way, the inability to understand that can be created by the noisy environment in the hold can be prevented. Aircraft Balance in Ground Operation  Loading or offloading may unbalance the aircraft or cause tail tipping. Although tail pole or nose rope is used for some aircraft, such apparatuses are not used on the Company's passenger aircraft.  As any other objects, aircraft also has a center of gravity and equilibrium. Each object is attracted towards the earth surface in proportion to its mass. However, each object has a point of equilibrium. This point is the midpoint of the gravitational force that affects every part of the object, i.e. the center of gravity. For numerous aircraft types, the center of gravity is as crucial in ground operation as they are during flight. It must be within a range that does not allow change of the balance of the aircraft on ground, tail tipping as a result of shifting of the center of gravity toward the aft of the aircraft, injury to the employee/passengers, and damage to the aircraft. The offloading process can be specified in Loading Instruction/Report (LIR). The measures required to be taken to prevent any problem in safe operation are as follows.  a.   Unloading must be started with the aft hold (including also the bulk).  b.   While unloading the compartment, it is necessary to make sure that there is more load in the section before the wing than the section after the wing.  c.   Unloading must be finished with the front hold.  d.   Loading must be started with the front load.  e.   While loading the compartment, it is necessary to make sure that always there is more load in the section before the wing than the section after the wing.  f.   Loading must be finished with the aft hold (including also the bulk).  g.   For cargo aircraft, the loading sequence should be as follows: front hold, maindeck compartment, rear hold/bulk, and the unloading sequence should be as follows: rear hold/bulk, maindeck compartment, and front hold.  Refueling, loading, and unloading processes cause change in the weight of the airframe, and that change causes height difference. If such changes are ignored and no measures are taken, unintended consequences may emerge. The balance center of the aircraft may be affected by the fuel and the other loads. In order to prevent tail tipping during the towing process, it is necessary to make sure that the actual balance center of the aircraft is ahead of its critical balance center on the basis of the loads on board the aircraft. If it is not possible to establish this situation, it is necessary to consult with the load control employees verbally.  CAUTION:  If it is not possible to unload the aft cargo hold (including also the bulk) due to any reason, the passenger disembarkation must not be started unless coordination is established with the cockpit crew.  CAUTION:  The ground operations employee acting as the operations coordinator must observe the stability of the aircraft on the ground while the aircraft is parked. When he detects any abnormal situation (the oleo strut is very high and continues to rise visibly, etc.), he must give information to the cockpit crew immediately and E K . 1 0 . 6 7 . 0 0 1 | R e v i s i o n 1 6 G r o u n d O p e r a t i o n s M a n u a l ( G O M ) QMS Document Template Number: FR.18.0001 | Revision 12 Document Template Reference Document Number: TL.18.006 Page: 232 | Total Page: 464 Copy of this document has been generated on 4.02.2026 16:42. During the entire transportation process, it must be ensured that there is no damage, leakage, or seepage of packages or “overpacks” containing dangerous goods. During the entire transportation process, packages must be inspected physically and ground handling operations must be carried out in accordance with the labels and markings on them. If leakage or seepage is detected during transportation, transportation of damaged packages showing leakage and/or seepage must be stopped. Depending on the damage, the emergency procedures specified in   EK.10.63.002 Dangerous Goods Manual Chapter 20. Emergency requirements are applied, and the person who detected the defect notifies their immediate supervisor. Packages or overpacks containing hazardous materials and cargo containers containing radioactive materials should be checked for signs of damage or leakage after they are unloaded from the aircraft or unit load unit (compartment/ULD). If there is evidence of damage or leakage, the area where the hazardous materials or unit load unit are stowed on the aircraft shall be checked for damage or contamination. It must be ensured that dangerous goods are transported, secured, and stowed in a way that meets the following conditions:  i.   Damage to packages and containers must be prevented during aircraft loading and unloading.  ii.   In case of leakage, separation and stowage of packages on board the aircraft must be ensured to avoid contamination.  iii.   Movements that may change the direction of the packages on board must be prevented.  iv . Dangerous goods must be checked for compliance with the information (NOTOC) given to the captain. If the dangerous goods package appears to be damaged or leaking, the following must be ensured:  i.   Damaged or leaking packages must be prevented from being loaded onto the aircraf.  ii.   In case of leakage, an evaluation must be carried out to identify and prevent the transportation of other cargo, baggage, or means of transport contaminated by the leakage of the dangerous substance.  iii.   If damaged or leaking dangerous goods are loaded on board, the package or consignment must be removed from the aircraft.  iv.   Immediate notification must be sent to the authorized person of the Company and the relevant authority. While loading the cargoes on top of each other, the stowage must be performed very carefully. In order to prevent the packages from being crushed, the packages must be stowed as if putting up a wall to minimize the force applied on the central points of the boxes. The   detailed   information   regarding   the   preparation   of   wet   cargo   is   defined   in   EK.10.61.003   Cargo   Operations   Manual/article  4.4.12.   Wet Cargo.  e. Perishable and Temperature-Sensitive Health Products  During transportation, loading, and unloading of perishable and temperature-sensitive health products:  1.   It must be brought to the aircraft hold in such a way as to minimize the waiting time.  2.   It must not be exposed to adverse environmental conditions.  Notes: 1.   The perishable substances must be put in a warehouse (e.g. cold, freezer) depending on their types in accordance with the requirements of   DK.41.018 Perishable Cargo Regulations (PCR)/4.2 Types of Perishables.  2.   Pharmaceuticals must be put in a warehouse (e.g. cold, freezer) depending on their types in accordance with the requirements of  DK.41.023 Temperature Control Regulations (TCR)/4.2 Types of Pharmaceutical Products.  f. Dry Ice  Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) is used as a refrigerant for return catering supplies, temperature-sensitive healthcare products such as vaccines and other life-unit products to ensure that they are kept at the required temperature throughout the supply chain.  1.   In cases where the cargo being loaded or unloaded contains dry ice, the employee must be aware of the necessary precautions to ensure that there is no risk of asphyxiation from the high CO2 levels resulting from sublimating dry ice.  2.   For requirements regarding the loading and unloading of dry ice as a hazardous material and the maximum quantities allowed by aircraft type, see the   Technical Data Sheet dry ice transport limits.  3.   Documentation of the use of dry ice as a coolant must be verified (ICE code) and employee must be allowed to ventilate the cargo compartment after opening the cargo access door and before entering the cargo compartment.  4. After opening the door of the cargo compartment, it is necessary to retreat. No one must enter the hold. The cargo compartment with dry ice must be ventilated after opening the cargo compartment door.  5.   Cargo access doors must be left open to clear dry ice vapors before the employee enters the hold or compartment.  Danger: 1.   There is a risk of suffocation when entering a compartment containing dry ice.  2.   Employees entering the cargo hold before the dry ice vapor has dissipated may experience dizziness and shortness of breath due to lack of oxygen. In such cases, the employee must be immediately removed to fresh air and, if their breathing is severely affected, sent to a physician or health facility.  4.5.4. Offloading 4.5.4.1. Process of weighing Suspicious Loads  If the cockpit crew is suspicious of the Loadsheet, or a warning is made by the cockpit, the cockpit crew may request that the loads on board the aircraft be weighed at the destination station. (Weighing all cargoes and baggage on board the aircraft). The weighing process will be coordinated by the airline representative. No load shall be offloaded and/or no passenger shall be disembarked from the aircraft before starting to weigh all loads on board the aircraft.  4.5.4.2. Safety Requirements for Offloading  a.   Before docking ground support equipment and/or opening cargo doors, the doors or their surroundings must be visually inspected for any damage.  b.   Check the loads to make sure that they have not slipped during the flight. If any variability is detected, the responsible employee must be contacted. Check of Cargo Hold  4.5.5.1. General  a.   The cargo hold must be checked in the following processes: After completing the aircraft unloading process, If the loading will not be started immediately after the offloading (in cases where the process before arrival and departure is long), before the commencement of loading, When the aircraft is left unattended between offloading and loading; or If the persons responsible for loading and supervision of the aircraft change (shift change, etc.).  b.   The employee who has assumed the cargo hold check must perform a visual check of the following in all cargo holds to be sure:  There is no damage to hold floor, walls, ceiling, door frames, panels, and doors, There is no missing, damaged, or defective floor latch, any condition requiring to restrict the loads, or missing net, There is no spilled fluid in the compartment, In case of station with multiple destinations, that there is no load but the transit/transfer loads left on board the aircraft, That the other loads (empty catering trolleys, used blankets, etc.) required to be offloaded from the cargo compartment after the arrival have been offloaded.  c.   The employee (usually the foreman) responsible for checking the cargo holds must confirm to the ground operations employee acting as the operations coordinator of the departure flight that the check was performed, before the commencement of loading of the aircraft. If this cannot be confirmed, the control must be carried out by the ground operations employee acting as the operations coordinator.  d.   If there is any damage of nonconformity detected, this must be reported immediately to the ground operations employee acting as the operations coordinator, and if any restriction is to be applied, to the Load Control employee who will prepare the Loadsheet.  Note:   Even if it is reported in the counter station LDM/CPM information that the compartments are empty upon arrival, it is necessary to open all cargo doors and check visually that the relevant compartments are empty.  e.   It must be confirmed absolutely that the aircraft has been unloaded except for the technical equipment like EIC, etc.  4.5.5.2. Cargo Hold Damages  Any tear, puncture, or damage to the components in the compartment affects the efficiency of the fire extinguishing systems negatively. For this reason:  a.   The ground operations employee acting as the operations coordinator is required to report any technical defect, damage, and irregularity immediately to the Pilot-In-Command and/or the relevant technical department.  b.   In order to prevent damage inside the aircraft, the floor weighing capacity and height limits must be observed during loading. Flow/Leakage/Spillage of Loads  a. RLM  4.5.6. Loading 4.5.6.1. Load Delivery  The handover process between the cargo depot, baggage preparation area and ramp must be carried out systematically for safe departure. Cargo, mail and baggage should be handed over to special points on the apron in accordance with the airport infrastructure and/or regional agreements.  4.5.6.2. Carrying the Load  Before carrying the cargo and/or mail and baggage from the cargo storage area or baggage preparation area, the equipment operator must pay attention to the following:  a.   The ground support equipment to be used for carriage must be in operating condition as required by the light loads and/or the loads prepared on ULD. (See 3.1.3.   Safety Instructions for Use of Ground Support Equipment on Apron)  b.   The baggage carts must be in operating condition, and the lids/covers/doors must be closed correctly before the moving process.  c.   The local authority's requirements regarding the maximum number of towable dollies must be observed.  d.   For all loads being carried, the following checks must be made: It is necessary to make sure that the cargo, mail and/or baggage being carried is the load of the correct aircraft. There must be no nets, ropes, protective materials that may be dragged on the ground or get jammed in the dolly cylinders, rolling balls, or casters.  Carriage of all cargoes/mails/baggage prepared must be performed safely; these loads must not skid, roll, topple downn.  The ULD container/pallet must not have any damage and defect.  e.   All transported loads must be protected from adverse weather conditions using tarpaulins or covered carts. Special attention must be paid to live animals and/or perishable cargo. When using a tarpaulin, all straps must be securely fastened to the cart.  4.5.6.3. Delivery of Load at Departure  Depending on the delivery point location, the employee responsible for supervising the loading operations of the aircraft or the employee responsible for receiving the load must pay attention to the following:  a.   He accepts all documents special to the flight, money bags, or special instructions.  b.   In order to secure all loads, he checks that It is the correct flight for the loads, Whether there is any damage occurred during the carriage, Whether there is any evidence to the load having been tampered with and spoiled (cuts, tears in plastic plate, etc.) Whether there are nets, ropes, or protective materials that may be dragged on the ground or get jammed in the dolly cylinders, rolling balls, or casters while maneuvering or during loading of the aircraft.  Before loading, a visual check of the ULD is made as specified in article 4.5.9.3. Control of ULDs,  Whether there is any sign of leakage from the ULDs,  It is necessary to make sure that all the cargoes loaded have been packaged properly and will not damage the aircraft, All ULDs must be handled safely to prevent them from slipping, rolling and tipping over while being loaded onto the aircraft. Failure to do so may result in the smoke sensors and fire suppression systems failing to function. The Sliding Carpet must never be removed from the aircraft, and the Sliding Carpet mechanisms must never be opened without the approval of the responsible technical employee at the relevant aerodrome. General Rules  The loads carried on board the aircraft must be secured as described below.  a.   The loads must not move during the flight. The weight distribution and balance of the aircraft must not be jeopardized.  b.   The cargoes loaded must not damage the aircraft structure or the other important parts of the aircraft.  c.   The cargoes loaded must not damage themselves and the other loads.  d.   The cargoes loaded must be secured so that they will not harm the passengers and the flight crew in case of an emergency landing.  e.   The loaded cargoes must not cause injury to ground handling employee during loading and unloading.  4.5.7.2. Safe Loading in BULK Compartments  a. Dangerous Goods (described in article 4.5.7.7. Securing Dangerous Goods),  Electric mobility devices (Battery-powered wheelchairs),  Scatterable/spreadable cargoes, Fragile cargoes.  b.   The following loads must move neither vertically nor horizontally during a flight. If the volume of the compartment or section is not full (three-quarters of the height), additional safety measures must be taken for the following cargoes. === Sayfa 254 ===
LINEAR LATERAL MOVEMENT   Vertical forces are effective during hard landing, turbulence, and tight turns. LINEAR UPWARD MOVEMENT   Vertical forces are effective in case of severe turbulence during landing and on board aircraft. Depending on the flight status, the final forces may be stronger than 1 g normal gravitational force. All loads must be secured against different forces on the basis of the force factor (g-factor). (Table-21: Force and Description) In the ULDs, the tarpaulins, nets used to prevent the movements of the loads must be strong enough not to be affected by different forces. Since the aircraft is subject to acceleration during take-off/landing as well as its airborne movement, all types of baggage and cargo, which may pose danger or damage the structure of the aircraft due to its form, density and content or which may cause significant variations in the balance of the aircraft as a result of movement of the aircraft, shall be tied-down. There are four reasons which might cause the load to move;  Acceleration during Takeoff:   Load tends to slide backwards.  Sidewards Movement (YAW)   Usually occurs under turbulent conditions. Load tends to move towards both sides.  Deceleration:   Load tends to slide forward.  Linear Upward Movement:   Load tends to bounce from the floor particularly under bumpy weather conditions (turbulence, etc.). The load shall be tied-down and secured considering the foregoing conditions. Sample Tie-Down Figure-83: Views of the Load Tied- Down and Secured. The load shall not be tied down with different fastening devices. Only straps or ropes shall be used for fastening. Loads shall be fastened on three sides, which include the front, rear and upper side. Each strap or rope must form a maximum 30-degree angle to the direction of tie-down.  Figure-83: Views of the Load Tied-Down and Secured  Tying the loads down with straps or ropes:  If it is first necessary to restrain the load with straps, the tying processes must be carried out as per the requirements specified in articles   DK.41.012 Airport Handling Manual (AHM)/311 Securing of Load and   DK.41.019 Unit Load Device (ULD) Regulations/Section 6 Operating Specification 6/07 Restraint Straps Utilization and Tie-Down Calculations on a Pallet. Opposite or Overall Tying of the Package  The opposite or overall method of tying the package is tying of a load by straps or ropes tied to opposite tie-down points on the floor and crossing all over the load. It is performed by using a second tie-down point on the opposite side. An ETSO/TSO-C172 strap whose strength is 2,250 kg can immobilize 4,500 kg load   when tied to opposite tie-down parts. Single fastening devices are fastened in three different directions depending on three straps or ropes. There shall not be more than one strap or rope in the same direction. Fasten the load from the point of restraint to a tie-down point in front of this restraint point in order to prevent backward movement. Fasten the load from a point as close as possible to it, preferably from the restraint point on the load, to a tie-down point on the opposite side in order to prevent upward movement. Fasten the load from both sides to the opposite side in order to prevent sidewards movement. Load with irregular shape or a high center of gravity requires to be fastened from both left and right. Standard fastening shall be used for loads of proper shape. Standard fastening requires four stud fittings, four fastening ropes and one safety rope. Two fastening ropes or straps shall be used against upward effects and two fastening ropes or straps shall be used against forward and backward effects. As the sidewards effects are already covered by the standard fastening, sides of the load do not require to be fastened individually. Also, when a high and narrow item with a height twice as long as its width is loaded, fastening against sidewards effects is required in addition to standard fastening. This additional fastening must be placed between half and two thirds of the height of the item and secured by two safety ropes to prevent it from sliding. Safety rope is used for preventing sliding of the ropes attached to prevent the forward and backward movement of the load. Additional fastening may be required depending on the weight of the item and the fastening devices used. Safe tying method Figure-88: is in Tie-down of the Planked Load to the Cargo Compartment . Use of Tie-Down Equipment  It is necessary to make sure that the tie-down equipment is in usable condition/undamaged.  a. Tie-down Ropes  The tie-down ropes must be tied to the designated parts of the aircraft floor/the tie-down hardware. (Figure-89: Rope Example) It is necessary to make sure that the overlapping ends of the tie-down ropes are sufficiently long and will not get loose in case of a sudden tension. It is necessary to make sure that the tie-down ropes have been fixed to the tie-down rings in such a manner enabling to untie the ropes easily during the offloading. The tie-down ropes must not be fixed to the other parts of the aircraft. They must be fixed by using the tie-down points only. (Do not use the blow out panel, fire panel, etc.) The compartment nets and the rope used to tie down another load must not be tied to the same tie-down point.  Figure-89: Rope Example  b. Fixing the Tie  The straps and ropes can be tied to/fixed on the load for once only in three different ways. (Figure-90: Examples of Immobilization), (one in upward direction, and two in opposite and horizontal directions). The forces created by the load must not move in multiple directions simultaneously at any time; the tie shall never be pulled by multiple straps/ropes. Therefore, multiple straps or ropes running in the same direction are not used to tie down the load. Tying examples Figure-90: Examples of Immobilization, Figure-91: Examples of Tie-Down Points on the External Side Latches and Lateral Auxiliary Parts, Figure-92: Examples of Tie-Down Points on Pallet and Tie-Down Anchor Plate and Figure-93: is in Examples of Tie-Down Points in the Bulk Compartment.  Figure-90: Examples of Immobilization  The tie-down rings must be fixed by passing them through the parts used as tie-down points on the aircraft floor only. Four (4) tie-down ropes/straps and one safety rope: Two (2) tie-down materials against upward forces, One (1) tie-down material against forward forces, One (1) tie-down material against backward forces, One (1) safety rope. The safety rope prevents that the load tied down against forward and backward forces from skidding. (Figure-96: Tie-Down Example)  Figure-96: Tie-Down Example  Lateral forces:  The effect of the lateral forces is normally prevented with upward, forward, and backward standard tying, but the ropes/straps must contact the load in a regular manner. (Figure-97: Tie-Down Example)  Exception:  If the height of the cargo to be loaded is more than twice its width:  a.   In addition to the standard tie-down, extra tie-down from the opposite side is performed against the lateral forces.  b.   The extra tie-down is placed between the half and two-thirds of the height ( extra two (2) ropes and four (4) tie-down points are necessary ).  c.   In order to prevent sliding, this tie-down process must be fixed by using two (2) extra safety rings. Figure-97: Tie-Down Example  Barrel/Drum Loading:  Barrels/drums are the loads that are difficult to tie down safely due to their round shapes and mostly sharp covers. In the fixing process, it is necessary to create a cubical structure that can be tied down by placing planks or wooden pallet under and only planks onto the barrel/drum consignments (Figure-50: Safe Barrel/Canister Fastening Example) and must be fixed to the aircraft floor. The requirement for planking in bulk loading is included in   article 5.12.2. Determination of Planking Requirements in Bulk Loading Aircraft.  Exception:   It is not required to put a plank beneath the cylindrical metallic packages containing Radioactive Material (RRY). However, it is necessary to put a plank above the cylindrical Radioactive Material (RRY) packages for safe fastening.  FR.61.0001 Special Load-Notification To Captain (NOTOC) is issued depending on its contents.  4.5.7.6.1. Automobiles  a.   Cars can be transported on wide-body passenger planes or cargo planes.  b.   LPG-powered automobiles are NOT ACCEPTED on board passenger aircraft. It is loaded only in cargo aircraft in accordance with the rules/requirements of   EK.10.61.003 Cargo Operations Manual/article 2.2.23.   Automobile Acceptance and Tagging.  c.   Fuel   tanks   must   be   empty   in   accordance   with   the   rules/requirements   of   EK.10.61.003   Cargo   Operations   Manual/article  2.2.23.   Automobile Acceptance and Tagging. Whereas the maximum amount of fuel in the fuel tanks of diesel vehicles shall not exceed 3/4 of the tank, the maximum amount of fuel in the fuel tanks of gasoline vehicles shall not exceed 1/4 of the tank. Some fuel shall be left in the tank in order to be used in cases of emergency.  d.   It should be checked if there is any oil or fuel leakage or not. It is not necessary to drain the engine oil.  e.   It should be checked that engine coolant and fuel tank caps are firmly closed. It is not necessary to drain the engine coolant.  f.   It is not necessary to deflate the tires.  g.   The batteries may remain on the vehicle, provided that they are tied down upright and firmly. However, the battery terminals must be insulated against short circuit.  h.   Engine must not be started while loading/offloading the automobile to/from the compartment. Where required for the automobiles with power steering, engine may be started to facilitate steering during loading or offloading. Spreading the Effect of Load on the Floor  If the total weight of the cargoes to be loaded exceeds the maximum floor load limit per square-meter or the maximum load limit of a certain section in the cargo compartment, the loading must be performed by spreading the weight so that it does not damage the compartment floor. While this applies to Heavy Cargoes (HEA) every time, it may also apply to the cargoes lighter than 150 kg (330 lbs) as well (the reasons such as smallness of the contact point, density of the load, etc.). The loads to be carried in this way must be limited. (See the following example). Wooden boards and planks can be used.  CAUTION!  The overloading exceeding the aircraft structural may damage the compartment floor, panels, and the other internal structure of the compartment. This damage may cause serious damage to the aircraft. This affects the safety negatively.  In some cases, the force the cargoes to be loaded to the aircraft will apply may be spread with the help of wooden boards or planks to be placed under the cargoes. (Figure-103: Example of Spreading the Load) As a result:  a.   The area/surface that will support the weight will be enlarged.  b.   The length of the load will be extended.  The operation coordinator and/or cargo official is required to know the subject of spreading the load and ensure that the relevant knowledge is reflected in the Loading Instruction/Report (LIR). Figure-103: Example of Spreading the Load)  4.5.9. ULD 4.5.9.1. General  ULDs are equipment such as pallets, containers, etc. used to ensure the safe transportation of loads such as luggage, cargo and mail within the aircraft.  a.   The ULDs in our inventory comply with IATA standards.  b.   ULDs are deployed manually or with mechanical power drives, depending on the weight and balance regulations determined by the aircraft manufacturer.  c.   Certified lashing equipment must be used to secure the shipment on ULDs.  d.   ULDs   must   be   prepared   in   accordance   with   the   requirements   specified   in   article   DK.41.019   Unit   Load   Device   (ULD)  Regulations/article 1.5.4 Ground Handling Agents (GHA).  e.   If the damage or dirt on the ULD exceeds the limits specified in   TL.61.015 ULD And Fastening Equipment Damage Limit Check Instruction , it cannot be used  f.   Damaged ULDs detected at stations should not be used for the inventories of the Ground Operations Directorate, and the  FR.67.0013   Damage   Assessment   Report   Form   should   be   prepared   and   immediately   notified   by   e-mail   to  HCCULDCONTROL@THY.COM and   TKM@THY.COM.  g.   For the inventories of the Cargo Operations Directorate, damaged ULDs detected at stations should not be used and the  FR.61.0042 ULD Serviceability Checklist should be prepared and information should be provided by e-mail to ULD@THY.COM within 24 hours after the aircraft lands.  h.   ULDs shall be carried empty only in following cases: While sending the surplus ULDs from the present station to the hub, While sending the surplus ULDs to   IST   station in need of ULD, in coordination with the hub. For ULDs that will be loaded empty, a ULD receipt must be created and placed on the ULD. The weights of ULDs must also be shown on the weight and balance form. Departure-arrival station, net weight of the company material carried, tare weight of the ULD, total weight, flight number and loading position must be written on the ULD receipt. In shipments made by pallet, the ULD plug is attached to the nets on the pallet. The ULD number shall be entered into the system even if the ULD is empty. ULD tare weights shall be specified as equipment in compartment (EIC) in the manual loading plan and the loadsheet. Procedures for the inspection of ULDs in order to determine airworthiness and serviceability during the acceptance phase of ULD are carried out by Turkish Technic Inc./Component Workshops Directorate. Since the containers are very voluminous, they are transported without being assembled in line with the interests of the Company. Container manufacturer companies provide training to the Component Workshops Directorate on the assembly of AKE and AKH containers and certification is carried out. After certification, the containers, which are assembled and passed the control criteria of the manufacturer, are delivered to Ground Operations Directorate and made available for aircraft operation. The ID and MDV numbers of the newly purchased ULDs to be used in passenger operation are sent by the Product and Service Management to Istanbul Operation and Apron Services Management by e-mail. After the installation of ULDs is carried out by the Istanbul Operations and Apron Services Management, the ID and weight information is sent to the Station DCS Coordination Managemnet via e-mail to be entered into the TROYA system, and to the Cargo Operations Directorate/Cargo Facility, Equipment and Logistics Managemnet via e-mail to be entered into the COMIS system. If there is a ULD exceeding the damage limits, it must be withdrawn from the operation and the   FR.67.0013 Damage Assessment  Report Form must be filled out and notified via e-mail to   ULD@THY.COM,   HCCULDCONTROL@THY.COM and   TKM@THY.COM.  c. In case of leakage or spillage, the authorized employee must be called in for inspection depending on the content of the load. For detailed information is available in article 4.5.5.3.   Flow/Leakage/Spillage of Loads.  d. ULDs must be cleaned of snow, water and ice etc. before loading. Snow and ice may prevent ULDs from being properly loaded and locked in the cargo compartment and may cause severe damage to the aircraft cargo loading system.  e.   ULDs must be loaded onto the aircraft using special ground equipment (high loaders) rather than using equipment such as a forklift.  f.   Authorized employee must ensure that loads are loaded into the correct location on the ULD and secured to the strap/clip locking points.  g. For cargo aircraft, notifications must be made through the CGR field 1.10 in the "eReports" section of the AQD System.  h.   After loading, ULDs shall be securely locked in their positions.  i.   The numbers of all ULDs loaded onto the aircraft must be obtained for use in the UCM message.  j.   After aircraft loading operations are completed, empty or full ULDs that have not been loaded for the flight should be transferred to ULD storage areas or facilities suitable for their type, without being abandoned in the parking area. When transporting pallets that are not loaded on a voyage, the pallet nets should be collected and actions that may damage the net should be avoided.  k.   Containers registered with the MDV of the Ground Operations Directorate are equipment used to ensure the safe transportation of loads such as luggage, cargo and mail within the aircraft and should not be used for purposes other than their intended purpose.  4.5.9.1.2. 4.5.9.1.4.1. Airworthiness of the ULDs  ULDs shall be completely ready for service. In order to prevent damage during loading and unloading of the aircraft loading system, ULDs are checked in the following stages according to   TL.61.015 ULD And Fastening Equipment Damage Limit Check Instruction ;  a.   After aircraft unloading,  b.   During receiving the ULD from the third parties,  c.   Before re-use for departure. Following the inspection process, the damaged equipment shall be classified damaged within and without limit. It is important to distinguish the damaged equipment from usable ones. Damaged equipment shall be divided as;  a.   Out-of-service equipment,  b.   Damaged but serviceable equipment. When a damaged container is detected,   TL.67.046 Instruction on Use of Container Damage Assesment Reports shall be followed. The damaged ULDs may: injure the employees, It may damage the aircraft structure, affect the on-time performance, It may damage the luggage, cargo etc. items inside and, may affect the weight-balance required for loading All business processes, including damage, loss, and tracking of pallets, containers, and similar ULDs included in the cargo inventory, are implemented as detailed in   PR.61.017 ULD Management Procedure..  4.5.9.1.4.2. This method ensures the utmost safety through clear/understandable information exchange throughout the takeoff operation. The ground employee assigned to the takeoff operation must be in contact with the cockpit crew continuously, and they are responsible for the ground movements.  The scope of this method is limited to tractors with and without drawbars and 4.7.   Open Area Take-Off Operation, push-back and aircraft that will walk under its own power.  Note:   The term “headset” is used for wired or wireless interphone systems.  Other employees are also involved in the take-off operation. The number and functions/responsibilities of these employees may vary depending on the following situations:  a.   Operating airline procedures  b.   Aircraft Type  c.   Ground Support Equipment used for maneuver  d.   Airport infrastructure  e.   Park position configuration  4.6.1.1. Pre-Flight Processes  It is necessary to make sure that the following processes were carried out before takeoff of the aircraft:  a.   It is necessary to make sure that there is no FOD.  b.   The apron ground must be sufficiently free of snow, ice, etc. so that the aircraft can move safely.  c.   Make sure that all persons not involved in the aircraft departure operation remain clear of the departing aircraft.  d.   Make sure that all persons not involved in the aircraft departure operation remain clear of the departing aircraft.  e.   Make sure that the additional ground operations employee (such as "Wing Walker") is present, if required.  f.   Verbal   communication   is   established   with   the   cockpit   crew   through   the   headset;   only   in   exceptional   cases   (breakdown   of communication, adverse weather conditions, etc.) the takeoff operation is carried out by using the hand signals without establishing headset communication. (If a headset malfunction is detected before the pushback operation starts, hand signals are not used. After the new headset arrives, the operation continues. In case of a headset failure after the pushback operation has started (while starting the way to taxiing or on the way to taxiing), the operation is continued with hand signals.)  g.   In cases where it is necessary to use ASU to start the engines, the cockpit crew is contacted for position of the ASU position and engine start order. Aircraft Maintenance Log (AML)  AML is the log book indicating that aircraft is released to service in an airworthy condition. The AML used for the aircraft available in the fleet of the Company consists of three (3) copies in white, green and red colors. The red page of the Aircraft Maintenance Log (AML) shall be received by the technical employee or ground operations employee, depending on the nature of the process performed, after the section “Pre-flight Inspection” is signed off by the pilot-in-command. Detailed information on these practices is available in   PR.50.028 Procedure for Usage of Aircraft Maintenance Log and   PR.50.051 Procedure for Managing of Aircraft  Maintenance Logs Pages. The following practice, explained in detail below, shall apply to the aircraft registered to the Company fleet: For IST Station;  For flights receiving or not receiving technical servic e, the red AML page is received and delivered to Line Maintenance Directorate of Turkish Airlines Technic Inc. reporting to Technical Directorate by the ground operations employee, together with the daily flight list. At Stations other than IST Station; The red AML pages of   the aircraft receiving technical service   are received and delivered to the department providing technical service by the ground operations employee. The red AML page of the   aircraft not receiving technical service   is received and retained for three (3) years at the concerned station by the ground operations employee. If the AML pages are archived together with the flight sets, then this period shall be equal to the period of retention of the flight sets. The white copy shall never be taken from the aircraft. In the event that it is taken out of the aircraft by mistake or that it is found to be missing, MCC (Maintenance Control Center) shall be informed. The Green AML pages shall never be taken by the ground operations employee.  4.6.2. Ground Employee’s Responsibilities 4.6.2.1. Ground Employee Responsible for Take-off  The responsible ground employee is defined as the person who ensures communication with the flight crew. There must be a responsible ground employee for the push-back operation of each unit of aircraft. This function can be carried out by persons who have different roles and positions. Ground employee responsible for takeoff operation:  a.   Must bear the responsibility for the entire push-back process, the cockpit crew must permit to start push-back.  b.   Must be sure that the towbar/towbarless tractor matches the aircraft type.  c.   In the event of a defect in the parking brake indicator (the indicator light does not illuminate), the flight captain and/or the technical department must be informed in order to record the defect.  d.   Must make sure that the “steering by pass pin” has been attached to the nose landing gear and/or the nose landing gear mechanism has been fixed as necessary for the pushback (if applicable by aircraft type), before connection of the towbar/towbarless tractor to the aircraft.  e.   Holds briefing with all the assigned employee to review the aircraft movement process, and agrees on how the aircraft will maneuver.  f.   Must connect the headset and carry out the communication to check the following: Whether the communication system operates. Must inform the flight crew of the developments in the apron operation. Must request permission to disconnect the ground power unit and disconnect the unit after receiving verbal permission.  g.   Must stay in contact with the cockpit crew through the headset.  h.   Must perform the pre-flight checks. Pre-Flight Checks around Aircraft  The final check around the aircraft shall be started as soon as possible after all ground services have been completed. It is necessary to walk around the aircraft at normal speed. The check must be started immediately before the takeoff. If any ground support equipment is connected to the aircraft during the check, or it is connected to the aircraft again after the check, the connection points must be rechecked. The pre-flight checks must include the following:  a.   The apron area must be cleared of all FODs that could damage the aircraft or pose a risk.  b.   It is necessary to make sure that passenger bridge, external power, air connection, static electricity grounding cable have been disconnected from the aircraft.  c.   The parking position must be cleared of all obstacles. The ground support equipment and vehicles must be positioned sufficiently away from the path of the aircraft.  d.   It is necessary to make sure that there is appropriate distance between the aircraft and the fixed facilities and barriers on its forward path, and that the forward path is clear of objects.  e.   All   doors   and   panels   must   be   closed   and   locked.   After   the   passenger   and   cargo   processes   are   completed   and   the passenger/service and cargo doors are closed; before starting the push-back process, a quick check must be made to make sure there are no open doors/panels on the aircraft, and it must be ensured that all open doors and panels (passenger, cargo doors, water- lavatory maintenance covers, GPU, "air starter", air conditioning connection panels) are closed by ground employee. If any panel other than the mentioned panels is detected to be open, the cockpit crew must be notified and a technician must be called.  Exception:   Excluding headset panels and external power. In order to realize the check procedure before flight, the employee must be qualified enough and get the defined trainings within the determined periods. Within the abovementioned service and the following responsibilities, the compliance of the operational and managerial cargo processes executed; By Sales Directorates, as they are the departments to which employee report, By Training Directorate, as it appoints to the relevant employee the trainings determined by their own Directorate and required to be followed, By the Office of Chief Operations Officer and Ground Operations Directorate, as he is the Manager in charge of Ground Operations, By Technical Directorate, as it determines the pre-flight check processes,  The necessary checks and improvements, By Quality Assurance Directorate, as it is responsible to the authorities for monitoring the compliance of the operational process.  4.6.3.2. Before the pushback vehicle is connected, the tractor can park in front of the aircraft or outside the ERA, but not behind the wings, as specified in the table in item 4.6.3.2.   Pre-Take-Off Check Table.  b.   Before connecting a push back vehicle, with or without a tow bar, to the aircraft, it must be ensured that the bypass pin is correctly installed. Diameter and length of the steering by-pass pin vary by aircraft type. Use a pin suitable for the aircraft type. Otherwise, steering system cannot be by-passed; and this may cause injuries and damage. Steering by-pass pin  1.   Labeled with the specific aircraft type(s) for which it can be used.  2.   Identified with a ''Remove Before Flight'' streamer.  3.   Checked regularly for proper technical condition, or as per manufacturer instructions.  c.   It is necessary to make sure that the aircraft is on park brake before connecting the towed and towbarless push-back vehicle to the aircraft; it must be connected to the aircraft after all ground support equipment has been disconnected. (except ASU, GPU/FPU).  d.   When using a vehicle with a towbar for pushback, a guide personnel should be deployed for the final approach of the towbar to the nose landing gear. When a towbarless vehicle is used, assistive employee must be used if the operator's vision is limited. It is checked whether the towbar match the aircraft type, and the towbar is connected first to the front landing gear.  c.   Make sure the towbar connection is secure and the lock pin is in place.  d.   When connecting the towbar, make sure it is aligned with the centerline of the aircraft.  e.   Raise the towbar to the same height with the tractor connection point.  f.   Approach slowly until the connection is aligned and the connection to the tractor is secured.  g.   Make sure that the front wheels of the tractor remain straight and that the tractor is in line with the centerline of the aircraft. 4.6.6.4. Takeoff Operation without Headset  The aircraft takeoff operation must be carried out by using always the headset communication.  If the headset is out of service or under exceptional circumstances where the headset cannot be used, hand signals for take-off (3.4.6. Pushback Hand Signals-from Wingwalker to Headset Operator, Tow-Car Operator, Marshaller, Cockpit Crew and 3.4.7. Aircraft Marshalling Hand Signals must be used and constant eye contact must be maintained with the cockpit crew. (If a headset malfunction is detected before the pushback operation starts, hand signals are not used. After the new headset arrives, the operation continues. In case of a headset failure after the pushback operation has started (while starting the way to taxiing or on the way to taxiing), the operation is continued with hand signals.)  4.6.6.5. Headset Communication Defect  Push-back operation requires headset communication. If the headset is out of service or the communication is lost, the following measures must be taken:  a.   In the event that the operation is carried out with single person, and if there is no other means of communication, the movement is stopped as per local situations and regulations, and assistance is requested to be able to continue the movement.  b.   Communication with the cockpit crew in case of an operation with more than one person 3.4.6. Pushback Hand Signals- Wingwalker to Headset Operator, Tow Operator, Marshaller, Cockpit Crew and 3.4.7. It is established using the hand signals described in the Aircraft Marshalling Hand Signals article. The push-back vehicle driver must be able to receive the visual signals given by the cockpit crew. The push-back can be continued after establishing the hand signal communication. (If a headset malfunction is detected before the pushback operation starts, hand signals are not used. After the new headset arrives, the operation continues. In case of a headset failure after the pushback operation has started (while starting the way to taxiing or on the way to taxiing), the operation is continued with hand signals.)  c.   If there is handheld radio, ATC is informed, and the movement is continued in cooperation with ATC as per the local regulations.  4.6.7. Pushback Maneuver  The process of pushing the aircraft, for any purposes whatsoever, by using a specially-designed vehicle with or without tow-bar is called "push-back". After passenger and cargo handling processes are completed and passenger/service and cargo doors are closed, before starting the push-back process always walk around the aircraft to check quickly and carefully that there is no ice, snow, sand, dust and FOD on the external surface of the aircraft, wings and around the engines.  The "push-back" process should be started after the landing gear chocks are removed. The chocks off acknowledgment must be given to the commander.  4.6.7.1. Anti-Collision Lights  In standard takeoff, after closure of the aircraft doors, the flight crew requests permission for push-back from ATC. After receiving the permission, the flight crew turns on the anti-collision lights of the aircraft.  Warning:  Anti-collision lights that are switched on are a visual indication to ground staff of imminent engine start-up or aircraft movement. Vehicle traffic shall stop until the aircraft has departed from the area.  Warning:  If the anti-collision lights are switched on unexpectedly (other than in preparation for the departure or towing operation), ground staff shall move away and remain outside the ERA. The responsible ground staff member shall check with the flight crew before resuming ground handling activities. Warning:  In case of the lower anti-collision light failure, the flight crew shall inform the personnel responsible for the departure operation to inform employee involved in the operations about the imminent engine startup or aircraft movement.  4.6.7.2. Pushback Requirements  a.   The pushback maneuver should not be performed at a speed higher than walking speed (5 km).  b.   Before the aircraft takes off, it must be observed that the park brake is released (the park break light is checked) and the anti-collision lights are on.  Note:   The park break light must be checked before the operation starts. If it does not work, the cockpit or the technical department must be informed of the situation.  c.   The headset operator will signal “Ready for Push” to the pushback vehicle driver and wing walkers (if applicable) when the aircraft brakes have been released by the flight crew and the flight crew has given approval for push back.  d.   It is necessary to select the appropriate gear in the push back vehicle and start moving slowly. The pushback must start in a straight line.  e.   After obtaining approval from the flight crew, the pushback operator should ensure that the taxiway through which the aircraft will move is clear of other aircraft/equipment/objects. If any obstacles are seen, the pushback should be stopped until the path of movement is clear.  f.   In order to avoid damage to the front strut during pushback, it must be ensured that the rotation limits are not exceeded. If the limits are exceeded, the cockpit crew must be notified.  g.   At the end of the maneuver, the aircraft/pushback vehicle must be positioned on the taxiway towards the center line.  Warning:  The flight crew shall be notified immediately in the event any connection between the tractor and the aircraft is lost during aircraft movement.  h.   When the pushback is complete, the headset operator will receive the “Vehicle Brakes On/Stop” signal from the driver of the pushback vehicle to verify that the parking brake of the pushback vehicle is set. (see. 3.4.5.4. Brake/Stop Vehicle) Before the pushback vehicle without a drawbar or tow bar is detached from the aircraft nose gear, the headset operator:  1.   The flight crew must be requested to set the aircraft's brakes and maintain the current position until the taxi clearance signal is given.  2.   When confirmation is received from the flight crew that the aircraft brakes have been adjusted:  i.   As per   DK.41.016 IATA Ground Operations Manual (IGOM)/3.4.5.4. According to the Vehicle Brakes On/Stop article, the “Vehicle Brakes On” signal must be given to the push back driver and wing walkers, if any. The pushback driver releases the parking brake of the pushback vehicle and shifts into neutral to relieve any pressure on the tow bar.  ii.   Authorization to disconnect pushback equipment must be given.  4.6.7.3. Employee Safety During Pushback Maneuver  1.   All employees walking on the ramp area during pushback operation with a towbar/towbarless vehicle must stay clear of the following areas:  a.   The area under any part of the aircraft,  b.   The path of the aircraft,  c.   The path of the pushback vehicle,  d.   Engine hazard areas. Pushback and Pull Forward  When performing the towing maneuver after the pushback maneuver, certain precautions must be taken at the end of the pushback and throughout the entire towing process. The following precautions should be implemented to prevent the aircraft from passing/pushing the pushback vehicle during the towing maneuver:  a.   Aircraft engines must be in idle thrust during all pushback and towing maneuvers.  Note:   If a pull-forward requirement is known in advance, consideration should be given to not starting the engines until the pull maneuver is completed.  b.   The towing maneuver must be performed in the lowest gear position of the pushback vehicle.  c.   Braking should be done smoothly and without jerking.  d.   If the aircraft cannot be controlled/sustained by the pushback device, the flight crew is warned to stop the aircraft by soft braking.  Note: 1.   The following situations increase the risks of aircraft passing/pushing the pushback vehicle and should therefore be considered: Aircraft type and number of started/running engines Parking area and taxiing slope Vehicle and towbar used to perform pushback/towing maneuvers. Adverse weather conditions.  Warning:  Care should be taken to avoid a jackknife situation between the aircraft and the pushback due to the asymmetrical push of an aircraft running one engine in a push-to-pull transition or vice versa. The manufacturer's maximum towing angles must not be exceeded.  Danger:  If the aircraft overtakes/pushes the pushback vehicle, the responsible ground staff member shall ensure they stay well clear of the path of the pushback vehicle and the aircraft NLG wheels. Flight crew and aircraft maintenance personnel must be informed if the aircraft overtakes/pushes the pushback vehicle, as both the pushback vehicle and the aircraft NLG may be damaged by the incident.  Danger:  If the nose wheels are not in the centered position, they can turn quickly to their centered position when the steering bypass pin is removed. This can result in personnel injury and aircraft damage.  Never increase or decrease the push-back speed drastically during push-back and always reduce speed at least three (3) meters before the final position, align the strut to the center and complete the push-back process in such a way that the nose tires face forward.  Do not signal the commander to set brakes before receiving the “push-back completed” signal from the “push-back” operator.  It is necessary to pay attention to the no tow line in order not to exceed the turning limits of the flight yoke/steering wheel during the "push-back” maneuver; if the flight yoke/steering wheel is tuned too much, the flight crew must be warned. For maximum turning angles, see the aircraft manufacturer AMM chapter 9.  4.6.7.5. Maneuvering During Wintery and Slippery Conditions  The adverse weather conditions (fog, rain, etc.) will affect visibility and road grip negatively. The pushback operator must reduce the vehicle speed and adapt it as the current conditions require. Under slippery apron conditions, extra measures are necessary not to lose the control of the tractor due to the skidding that will cause drift while maneuvering with the aircraft. Numerous factors (strong wind, slippery road surface, road slope, etc.) may play a part in the relevant hazard. The following minimum measures must be taken:  a.   Sudden turns, accelerations, and decelerations must be avoided.  b.   Except when ASU is used, the aircraft engine must not be started without doing the following:  It is made sure that the road condition provides reasonable grip. The aircraft parking brake is set. TThe aircraft is disconnected from the tow tractor/TWL tractor.  4.6.7.6. Maneuvering under Low Visibility Conditions  a.   The airport operator is responsible for developing low visibility procedures for the airport.  b.   Handling employee must have received appropriate training/authorization before undertaking aircraft movement operation in low visibility conditions.  c.   Handling employee must observe other regulations that always apply to the movement restrictions and airport low visibility procedures.  d.   An airside map must be available on the pushback vehicle.  e.   If the pushback operator has any doubts about the net position of the vehicle/aircraft, the operator should stop the vehicle/aircraft and inform ATC. Low visibility conditions (heavy rain, fog, poorly lit areas)  2. It shall be ensured that the ramp is clear of all FOD items in order not to harm persons, engines or environment during engine start- up or while the engines are running.  b.   Any abnormal conditions that may occur in the engines and the aircraft during engine start-up must be reported to the captain pilot in charge, specifying the location where they occurred (flame extension, smoke from the exhaust, fuel, oil leaks, etc.).  c.   Keep away from the danger areas while the engine is running. Strictly obey the warning signs where it is required to approach the aircraft. Take precautions for environmental safety. Also, if the engine has been started-up during push-back, keep an appropriate distance from the engine while walking.  d.   The engine on the opposite side shall be started-up first where it is necessary to approach an external air supply unit to the engines during engine start-up. Then, the air supply unit shall be removed from the aircraft and the other engine shall be started using the air supplied by the running engine.  e.   Wheel chocks shall be removed after all ground equipment around aircraft has been removed before engines start.  f.   The interphone connection shall be disconnected after all engines start and all ground equipment has been moved away from the aircraft. The marshaller carries out the communication thereafter.  g.   The flight crew shall be informed before disconnecting headset communication. The marshaller shall ensure the necessary communication with the flight crew if interphone connection is not used for communication with the flight crew. (If a headset malfunction is detected before the pushback operation starts, hand signals are not used. After the new headset arrives, the operation continues. In case of a headset failure after the pushback operation has started (while starting the way to taxiing or on the way to taxiing), the operation is continued with hand signals.)  h.   If there are more than one employee at ramp, all of them shall leave the aircraft at the same time. The commander may start taxiing after making sure that all ground operation employee has moved away from the aircraft. If the process of an aircraft left on the centerline for any reason takes a long time, the head set employee should be visible from the cockpit and use the phrase "Radio Check" to remind the cockpit crew via the headset.  i.   The marshaller shall move away from the aircraft after contacting the flight crew in case of occurrence of any failure during engine start-up. S/He shall proceed to the parking stand, direct the aircraft back to parking area, and inform the technical crew. If a failure occurs while no engine is running, the commander shall be requested to call in the "push-back" vehicle; the aircraft shall be attached to the vehicle again and towed to the parking stand after obtaining clearance from the commander.  j.   If the conditions are below the standard for a normal push-back operation (hazard, obstacle, slippery ground, icing), the headset operator must not give permission to start the engine until one of the following situations occurs:  1.   Until the aircraft is in a safe place to start the engine,  2.   When the push back is completed, the aircraft should come to a complete stop and engine start should be allowed if the parking brake is applied.  Note:   Engines shall be numbered from left to right, from the aft side view of the aircraft.  4.6.8.2. Engine Start Using Aircraft (ASU) and Ground Power Unit (GPU)  a.   During engine start-up, only the employee assigned to engine start-up or pushback operation and the equipment to be used stay in the ERA area.  b.   Communication is established with the cockpit crew, and the ASU position, total number of the engines to be started, the engine starting order to be used, and the number of the engine starting units are verified.  c.   All employees and equipment involved in the engine start shall remain clear of engine danger areas.  d.   Advise the engine start sequence to the ASU operator and any other ground staff.  e.   Wherever possible, the ASU must be positioned at the opposite of the engine starting side of the aircraft. Communication during Fire in Aircraft Engines  Engine Fire: Normally, the flight crew can detect a fire in the engine or APU. However, when the ground employee detects a fire in the aircraft engines, s/he must warn the flight crew immediately through the headset. The ground operations employee shall not attempt to extinguish it by using portable fire extinguishers, since the flight crew shall respond to the fire with the engine fire suppression system of the aircraft.  Exhaust Pipe/Exhaust Fire:  If a flame is noticed in the exhaust during engine start-up, the flight crew is immediately warned by indicating the location of the abnormal situation, as it may not be detected by the sensors and/or fire warning systems in the aircraft.  Warning:  The ground operations employee shall not attempt to extinguish it by using portable fire extinguishers, since the flight crew shall respond to the fire with the engine fire suppression system of the aircraft.  4.6.9. After removing the nose landing gear steering bypass pin, it is necessary to make sure that the mechanism is in place. After the headset communication is over, the connection must be disconnected with the approval of the cockpit crew and the access panels must be closed.  Attention:  It is necessary to make sure that the headset cover panel locks are fully engaged in their slots.  The aircraft must be moved away from the parking position to a safe position visible to the flight crew, and the bypass pin must be shown to the cockpit crew.  After establishing visual contact with the flight crew, the “all OK” signal must be given. Under the low visibility conditions, the crew will turn on the cockpit light. It is necessary not to leave the current position without the approval of the flight crew and before the aircraft starts taxiing.  Danger:  After the headset connection has been disconnected, no attempt should be made to approach the aircraft unless hand signals have been received from the cockpit crew. Takeoff Operation in Open Area  An open area is the area where the aircraft enters or exits the operation area. It is necessary to make sure that all employees and equipment are away from the aircraft, out of the ERA zone.  d.   Considering the Jet Blast and the intake effect, the employee and equipment must be outside the danger zone. According to aircraft types, the response area and the intake area are included in LS.67.043 List Of Blast Area And Intake Area . Back Force Operation of Aircraft  Not applied in Company operations.  4.9. Push-Pull 4.9.1. Introduction  Aircraft push-pull operation can be done for three different reasons:  a.   Maintenance: It is a push-pull operation with only a small amount of fuel when there is neither passenger nor cargo on board the aircraft.  b.   Operational: It is the push-pull operation of an aircraft loaded with passengers and/or cargoes and/or fuel to/from the terminal or to open parking positions. Ground Employee Responsible for Push-Pull Operations  The responsible ground employee must make sure that all requirements for the push-pull operation are met before initiating the push- pull operation. Brake Operator  When applicable according to the local procedures, the brake operator  a.   Becomes responsible for communication with ATC.  b.   Makes sure that all aircraft doors have been closed by the authorized employee.  c.   During towing, the brake operator sits with his seat belt fastened.  d.   Applies the “brakes on” and “brakes off” procedures in coordination with the headset operator.  e.   Turns on/off the anti-collision lights.  f.   Positions the seat to apply the brakes easily.  g . Informs the headset operator immediately in case of contact with any object.  h.   Applies the brakes during the towing operation only when instructed so by the headset operator or if it can be seen clearly that the connection between the aircraft and the tractor is broken.  Note-1:   For the relevant procedure, see the section “incidents during towing” (article 4.9.5.   Incidents during Push-Pull).  Note-2:   With the exception of the flight crew and the maintenance personnel, there must be no employee other than the brake operator on board the aircraft during maintenance or repositioning towing operations. The brake operator must sit with the seat belt fastened and, if necessary, be instructed to follow the safety instructions.  4.9.2.3. Headset Operator  Headset operator is responsible for establishing communication with brake operator and/or VHF operator.  4.9.2.4. VHF Operator  The VHF operator is responsible for communication with ATC and/or ground movement control (GMC).  Note:   Depending on the functions of the ground employee performing the push-pull maneuver, the VHF operator may be present in the pushback vehicle or in the cockpit.  4.9.3. Pre-Flight Checks around Aircraft.  b.   The requirements defined in the section 4.6.3.2.   Table of Pre-Flight Checks must be met.  c.   It must be ensured that the flight crew, authorized technician, or authorized brake operator (VHF operator if necessary) is present in the cockpit.  d.   Communication is established with the flight crew, authorized technician, or brake operator/VHF operator (when necessary).
