To ensure safe towing, the relevant apron lines must be used as a guide during the maneuver. It is necessary to be aware of the size of the towed aircraft.  b.   Maintain a minimum safety distance between vehicles to ensure sufficient space. If necessary, set the pushback vehicle brakes slowly.  c.   If you need to stop, stop 50 meters before the taxiway.  d.   On arrival at the respective assigned parking position, the aircraft must be moved a few meters more in a straight line to ensure that the nose wheels are in the straight ahead position. The stress on the landing gear and tires must be reduced.  4.9.4.2. Push-Pull Speed  Aircraft weight, vehicle performance, and air side ground structure affect push-pull speed. The push-pull speed should be kept to a minimum and the push-pull speed limit set by the towing equipment, aircraft manufacturer and airport authority should not be exceeded. If ATC requests an increase in speed due to an active runway crossing, ATC should be informed that this is not possible. If the push-pull speed is limited during the push-pull operation on the active taxiway, ATC should be notified that this may cause traffic jams on the air side.  4.9.4.3. Push-Pull Limits  Refueling, loading, and offloading processes cause change in the weight of the airframe, and that change causes height difference. If such changes are ignored and no measures are taken, unintended consequences may emerge  The balance center of the aircraft may be affected by the fuel and the other loads. In order to prevent tail tipping during the towing process, it is necessary to ensure that the actual balance center of the aircraft is ahead of its critical balance center. If it is not possible to establish this situation, it is necessary to consult with the load control employee.  Note:   In case of towing operation in bad weather conditions, the specified precautions should be taken and the relevant sections below should be referenced.  Operation in winter conditions 4.6.7.5. Maneuvering under Winter and Slippery Conditions article,  Operations in low visibility conditions (weather conditions and other reasons) 4.6.7.6. Maneuvering under Low Visibility Conditions article.  Attention:  Before the towing operation, the loads and the center of gravity of the aircraft must be checked. It is important for the operator's health and the aircraft's safety not to ignore this. Long-Term Parking of Aircraft 4.10.1. Introduction  Successful re-commissioning operation after long-term parking requires close coordination and cooperation between all relevant air side and stakeholders, including the airline operator, airport authority, ground handling provider, and maintenance provider. During long- term parking, "task cards" prepared by aircraft manufacturers according to parking periods, including parking and storage procedures, and business processes and activities detailed in   PR.50.063 Procedure For Management Of Aircraft Parking/Storage Check are applied.  4.10.2. Aircraft Movement  According to the airport parking plan, Note-1 should be followed to ensure that there is no damage to the aircraft before operation resumes from where it left off.  Note-1:   Ensure that the procedures in articles 4.6. Takeoff Operation through 4.9. Push-Pull are followed throughout the aircraft's ground movement.  Note-2:   Establish timely communication with the airport authority regarding the movement of the aircraft.  Note-3:   If any surface damage is observed, contact the airport management team as per airport directives. Long-term parking of the aircraft requires the adoption of a variety of special measures to ensure the continued safety, security and general airworthiness of the aircraft. These measures are included in the "task cards" prepared by the aircraft manufacturers according to the parking periods and containing the parking and storage procedures.  4.11. Preflight Preparations  4.11.1. Responsibility of Cockpit Crew  The process is described in detail in   EK.10.73.001 Operations Manual Part-A/article 8.1.11.5 Pre-Flight Inspection.  4.11.2. Responsibility of Ground Operations Employee acting as Operations Coordinator  a.   Ensures fueling in line with the fuel data received from the commander.  b.   Checks the fuel quality prior to fueling, or ensures that the same is checked.  c.   Carries out “Business Class” partition and seat setting arrangements in line with the cabin configuration, or ensures that the same is carried out.  d.   Checks if all passenger and service doors of the aircraft are closed before "push- back", upon closing of aircraft doors, or ensures that the same is checked.  e.   Checks for foreign object damage (FOD) or ensures that the same is checked, if the aircraft is to start the engine at the parking stand.  f.   Provides headset service to establish ground-cockpit communication, during "push- back".  g.   Collects AML pages from the aircraft in line with the explanations given in article 4.6.2.1. Ground Employee Responsible for Take-off. Detailed information is available in   PR.50.051 Procedure for Managing of Aircraft Maintenance Log Pages and PR.50.028 Procedure for  Usage of Aircraft Maintenance Log.  4.11.3. Load Lightening Procedure  Process of weighing Suspicious Loads  If the cockpit crew is suspicious of the Loadsheet, or a warning is made by the cockpit, the cockpit crew may request that the loads on board the aircraft be weighed at the destination station. (Weighing all cargoes and baggage on board the aircraft). No load shall be offloaded and/or no passenger shall be disembarked from the aircraft before starting to weigh all loads on board the aircraft.  Requirements for Consignments that require Special Processing  It is necessary to follow the rules for the loads that have special requirements. All consignments that require special loading instruction must be specified in the Load Distribution Message (LDM) or Container Pallet Message (CPM).  a.   It is necessary to make sure that the packages labeled with special handling labels are held in the correct direction. (see THIS WAY UP, CAO, MAGNETIZED MATERIAL, etc.)  b.   It is necessary to pay attention to the fragile articles.  4.11.4. Safety Measures for Unloading  a.   It is necessary to be careful in the handling process of heavy items. It is necessary to use the appropriate lifting techniques and ask for help if necessary.  b.   It is necessary to be careful while placing the heavy items on the conveyor. It is necessary to make sure that they are fixed and will not fall.  c.   During offloading, the ULDs must be checked for damage, leakage, and load balance.  d.   Check whether the ULDs have been loaded erroneously (latches not raised, latches or side rails crushed, etc.). If any nonconformity is detected, it must be reported.  e.   It is necessary to be careful if the load has shifted during the flight. Loading Procedures  Before starting the loading process, it is necessary to cross check the registration mark of the aircraft and the registration mark on the Loading Instruction/Report.  a.   The cargoes loaded to the aircraft, the weights, and the ULD numbers must be cross checked against the Loading Instruction/Report.  b.   It is necessary to make sure that the special tie-down equipment (tie-down straps, the hooks which the ropes run through, etc.) are ready before loading.  c.   It is necessary to make sure that the Loading Instruction/Report has been received and understood by the loading and offloading team.  d.   The cargo compartment and the latching systems must be checked before loading. In case of any damage/missing, it must be ensured that the operations coordinator, the flight crew, or the station official is informed of the same.  e.   In case of cargo, heavy goods, it is necessary to make sure that the load has been secured, and the straps have been stretched and tied down.  f.   It is necessary to make sure that the ULDs are suitable to be loaded to the aircraft and no damaged ULD is used.  g.   It is necessary to make sure that the cargoes bearing handling labels have been loaded in such a manner that their labels can be seen on the cargoes during offloading.  h.   It is necessary to make sure while loading pallets or containers that they are on the pallet and container loading tracks in the compartment, latched, and that the pallet height does not prevent opening of the cargo compartment doors.  i.   It is necessary to check that the other position latches will not prevent loading of ULDs to their positions.  j.   It   is   necessary   to   make   sure   that   the   separator   nets,   fire   panels,   doorway   nets,   pallet   and   container   latches   have   been fastened/locked safely.  k.   In case of bulk loading, the per compartment and per destination station numbers of the loaded baggage must be recorded.  l.   All changes in the load and loading must be shown on LIR (baggage position change, new container addition, etc.), and the final Loading Instruction/Report (LIR) must be prepared.  m.   Before finalizing the Loadsheet, it must be verified against the final Loading Instruction/Report (LIR).  4.11.6. Loading of Live Animal  Live animal transportation processes must comply with the requirements of   DK.41.013 Live Animals Regulations (LAR/Chapter 10). Besides, detailed information on the Company's rules is available in   PR.60.005 Procedure for Carriage of Live Animals and TL.67.092  Instruction on Tables for Loading Live Animals on Board. The “Cargo Temperature and Ventilation Table” published by the Technical Presidency   can   be   accessed   under   the   Aircraft   Systems   Engineering   Directorate   heading   at  https://teknikbaskanlik.thy.com/Pages/dokumanlar.aspx.  4.11.7. Wet Cargo Loading  Wet cargo refers to shipments containing liquids, or may substantially produce/excrete liquids by nature even though not included in the "IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations"..  Liquid cargo in watertight containers, cargo not packed in watertight containers as well as cargo packed with wet ice (fish, wet hides, etc.) which may produce liquids (such as certain live animals) are considered wet cargo. The loading/offloading team leader who is in charge of the loading must check the following.  a.   He makes sure that the wet cargo has been packaged properly and does not leak anything.  b.   Loads with torn, leaking or damaged packaging are NOT ACCEPTED.  c.   For bulk loading, nylon is laid on the compartment floor and absorbent pads are laid on the nylon, and crushing/damage of the packages is avoided during stacked loading. LOAD CONTROL  Load control practices for passenger aircraft are described in this section, and for cargo flights with cargo aircraft, Section 5. Necessary information other than the general information included in Load Control 5.15. It is described in the article titled Load Control in Cargo Aircraft.  5.1. Introduction  The purpose of this section is to determine the standards and publish them by IATA starting from AHM 500 and   DK.41.012 Airport  Handling Manual (AHM) /Chapter 5 Load Control and Turkish Airlines Inc. Establishing standard procedures for minimum requirements in the Load Control process. For operational safety, the Company’s rules and the national and international rules must be taken into account in the load control process. Load control is the process of loading the aircraft safely, optimally, economically (in a way that will have a positive effect on fuel economy) and as quickly as possible, within operational limits, taking into account the center of gravity parameters, and sharing the resulting values with the cockpit crew. This process begins with documenting the structural limits of the aircraft, then includes loading planning, loading supervision, reporting of final load, processing of reported load & loading, and weight and balance calculation. It is necessary to ensure that the information on the Loadsheet is consistent with the correct and actual loading information in the aircraft. The load control includes the following processes:  a.   Load planning; Checking the aircraft loading limits and the total dead load to be loaded in terms of quantity and content before and during planning, calculating and sharing with the loading plan, Taking into account information regarding hazardous materials and other special loads and sharing itwith the loading team, Planning the loading and producing the loading instructions/loadplan (LI), special instructions.  b.   Management/supervision of aircraft loading and unloading; Recording and approving of aircraft loading, ensuring that the aircraft is loaded in accordance with the loading instructions/load plan (LI), Preparing the final loading information on the loading instruction report (LIR) and transfering it to the load controller,  c.   Weight and balance calculation Ensuring that the aircraft's weight and balance conditions (load and loading) are correct and within operational limits, Producing a Weight and Balance Form (Loadsheet) according to the approved final information shared on the LIR (FLIR), E K . 1 0 . 6 7 . 0 0 1 | R e v i s i o n 1 6 G r o u n d O p e r a t i o n s M a n u a l ( G O M ) QMS Document Template Number: FR.18.0001 | Revision 12 Document Template Reference Document Number: TL.18.006 Page: 306 | Total Page: 464 Copy of this document has been generated on 4.02.2026 16:42. The Weight and Balance Sheet (Loadsheet) must contain the actual load & loading on the aircraft and all information including LMCs, Ensuring preparation, documentation and filing of other loading documents (NOTOC, Load&Trim Sheet Infirmotion, FLIR etc.),  d. In order to ensure the flight safety, all cargoes to be loaded to the aircraft must be planned, documented, and recorded down to the last detail. Control of the information exchange by keeping a written record prior to take-off is necessary to ensure that correct Weight and Balance calculations are sent to the Pilot in Command (PIC). Load Control is completed/ensured to be completed only by employees with active training qualification, based on the documented basic values of the aircraft (A/C), in accordance with company, airport, national and international procedures. The load control process can be carried out by certified employees of the Company or certified load controllers of the service provider either on-site (at the airport where the flight takes place) or remotely (CLC-Centralized Load Control-Remote Load Control) if approved by the load control supervisory of the Company. The Company load control process is managed by the TROYA Departure Control System (DCS) or TK's new Weight&Balance. Only at stations without TROYA DCS infrastructure, other Departure Control Systems (DCS) approved by the Company may be used by informing the Company's load control supervisory at   loadcontrol@thy.com and fully fulfilling the requirements of the Company. The expansion of the system to the stations will be carried out in accordance with the determined phases. In case of force majeure, manual LS generation by employee who have not gained experience in the last 3 months must be prevented; if a situation that poses a safety risk is foreseen,   loadcontrol@thy.com must be contacted to determine whether the load control process is conforming.  5.2. Load Control Planning Process  5.2.1.Minimum Requirements & Information in the Load Control Planning Process  The load controller, who will prepare the Loading Instruction/Loading Plan (LP), ensures that the loads are planned and distributed in a safe and optimal manner, taking into account the structural limits (area, compartment, hold, etc.) of the planned aircraft. Load control planning takes into account the following:  a.   Control of the aircraft's basic weight/index (BW&BI),  b.   Control of all items to be included in the operation weight & index (DOW&DOI),  c.   Checking the information in operational messages (total weight, index, vacant positions, etc.) for completeness and accuracy, including the special loads of the previous flight/leg  d.   Checking the limits or other restrictions on the flight that may limit load planning/loading,  e.   Calculation of estimated traffic load (Payload/Total of passengers, baggage, cargo, mail and company materials, regardless of whether revenue is generated or not),  f.   Control and planning of hazardous materials and special loads (DGSL) that require special loading rules, if any,  g.   Plan unit load devices (ULDs) taking into account expected loading figures, aircraft configuration and operating airline procedures. The graphics or tables in AHM 565 should be used to ensure the balance of the aircraft on the ground while it is parked. If any risk is foreseen, a new plan can be made by shifting the loads in the rear compartment to the front compartment and %MAC (% mean aerodynamic cord/Percentile of the average aerodynamic line of the wing surface) is determined for the time period in which the risk is seen against a possible tail tipping/towing limit risk. Before the calculation is made, the slope and wind strength of the parking lot must not be ignored. Method 1- Using the tipping and stability limit tables in AHM 565, an extra load plan is made for the front cargo compartment in order to ensure the balance of the aircraft on the ground together with the weight loaded in the rear cargo compartment. Method 2-Dead load index value/MAC%, a combination of the dead load in the received LDM message and the pre-departure dead load, is calculated and it is ensured that it is within the limits. (Not used in TK Operations). Method 3- A system application that can perform dynamic calculations can be used to ensure the stability of the aircraft on the ground. Each possible movement of the aforementioned loads in the aircraft in terms of balance can be calculated. (Not used in TK Operations).  n.   Generates Loading Instruction/Loading Plan (LI/LP).  5.2.1.1.Importance of Balance & Load Planning in Ground Operations  As any other objects, aircraft also has a center of gravity and equilibrium. Each object is attracted towards the earth surface in proportion to its mass. However, each object has a point of equilibrium. This point is the midpoint of the gravitational force that affects every part of the object, i.e. the center of gravity (CG). Besides, it is a movable point whose location changes under any effect on the object.   The point of equilibrium is on the chord where the wing is attached to the airframe   since the buoyant force is the force keeping the aircraft on air, which is generated only by the wings. Center of gravity and equilibrium are as crucial in ground operation as they are during flight. Weight calculation must be done manually or via DCS system (TROYA DCS, etc. approved DCS systems) or TK new Weight & Balance for each flight only by authorized and fully trained and up-to-date employees. For a safe flight, weight balance must be calculated and checked to see if it is within the safe %MAC limits set by the manufacturer before each flight. Structural %MAC limits determined according to aircraft types are available at  ahm.thy.com The actual weight of the aircraft (TOW) is determined by the sum of the structural empty weight (basic weight/BW) of the aircraft, fuel, catering, crew, passengers, deadload(cargo, mail, baggage, company material) and other weights, if any. These calculations are repeated once the available data is finalized and take their final form before take-off (Actual TOW/ATOW). Load distribution is made within the framework of loading rules, within the safe range operational field limits determined by the manufacturer and, if possible, within the right side of the ideal balance range, taking into account fuel savings. In order to ensure balance in ground operations, the load distribution is carried out in proportion to the compartments at the front and rear of the centre of gravity, while there is an equal passenger distribution on the main deck, and the rear (AFT) loading ratio is high. It must be ensured that the aircraft to be used for the flight are loaded within the safe trim line determined by the manufacturer and that the Loading Instruction/Report (LIR) and Weight and Balance Form (Loadsheet) processes for these flights are. completed fully. Loads shall be planned considering their categories, station of arrival and compartment limitations. For circular flights, the loads are sorted primarily with regards to destination. Then, the items for the same destination are loaded according to their order of unloading. Special loads under their loading conditions 5.10. Special Loads Requiring Attention (SL), Dangerous Goods (DG), Special Situation Team and Passenger Information are loaded according to the Triple Codes article. Load distribution must be performed in accordance with the principles of balancing and so as not to exceed loading limitations at each station of arrival. The messages (LDM/CPM) received from the previous station (transit/arrival station) must be checked, and transit load, if any, must be taken into account in planning. Negative situations in the following processes may cause the aircraft's balance to change and/or its tail to touch the ground while the aircraft is parked;  a.   Passenger boarding/deboarding,  b.   Loading/offloading baggage and cargo,  c.   Aircraft maintenance.  d.   Weather conditions  e.   Parking area slope The operations coordinator is responsible for watching the ground stability of the aircraft. When an abnormal situation is detected, he/she must immediately notify the cockpit crew and stop all operations such as passenger loading/unloading, baggage and cargo loading/unloading, and aircraft maintenance. Afterwards, procedures must be performed to ensure that the CG point moves forward.  Note: In the arrival operation in which unloading of the aft cargo compartment cannot be done immediately for any reason,  the passenger deboarding process must not be started.  In order to avoid the risk of aircraft tail tipping on the ground, the following rules must be followed. a.   If there is a plan, loading of the aircraft starts from the front hold, and unloading starts from the rear compartments. In the rear compartments, the loading order must be from front to back. The loading instructions for the relevant flight must be followed.  Attention:   B737-900ER/B737 MAX 9/A321–271NX (NEO) aircrafts have bigger tail tipping risk compared to the other aircrafts. For this reason, the rule that in outbound flights the load must be planned in the forward hold, the loading must be done starting from the forward hold, and in the arrival operation the loads in the aft hold must   be unloaded first,   is definitely applied . Additionally, the process of unloading the aft cargo hold of the relevant aircraft is completed before starting unloading of the forward cargo hold  regardless of categories (cargo, mail, baggage) of the loads. b.   The circular flights have bigger tail strike risk. While planning the load distribution in such flights, it is obligatory to take care to allocate sufficient loads to the compartments in front of the center of gravity, and pay attention to distribution of the transit load to ensure ground stability of the aircraft. At the next station, the loads remaining in the compartments must be distributed by paying attention to the aircraft balance limits.  c.   The arrival operations coordinator is responsible for coordinating the loading and offloading of loads in the correct order as per the Loading Instruction/Report (LIR) and the LDM/CPM messages respectively.  Attention:   Tire change process and refueling operation cannot be performed simultaneously. In such a case, the operations coordinator must be in coordination with the assigned technician on board the aircraft.  5.2.1.2.Crew, Passenger and Load Weights  Figures affecting aircraft weight calculations are listed below:  5.2.1.2.1. Extra Seat (EXST) Indication  Extra Seat is the seat paid for in addition to the passenger's own seat, as per the passenger’s request. In the TROYA DCS system or in case of purchasing an extra seat for TK new Weight & Balance flights, two seats are edited for a single passenger, the system perceives these two seats as a single passenger, therefore the total passenger figure in the Weight and Balance Form (Loadsheet) shows the number of passengers actually sitting on the plane. The extra seat is indicated in the BLKD field of the Loadsheet (in case of seats that cannot be used due to defect, etc., they are indicated in BLKD). For example, when extra seats are purchased for one male passenger, 2 seats in total are edited; the system (EXST) sees each two seats as one passenger. This information is sent to the system as 2 men for the total passenger figure and as 88 kg passenger’s weight for 1 occupied seats for the total traffic load on the Loadsheet. Single ticket is issued for the extra seat, and it is accepted as one passenger. The weight sent to the system is that single passenger’s weight (the weight of the passenger who has bought the extra seat). The ground operations employee acting as the operations coordinator informs the flight crew and the station of the number of extra seats.  Figure-108: Indication of Extra Seat on Loadsheet and ATOM  5.2.1.5. Additional Calculations  Calculation of actual weights as "+/-" due to operational requirements is under the responsibility of the operations coordinator. Significant differences shall be clarified prior to take-off. Weight and balance calculations are also obligatory to be made in training, technical and test flights. In the event of increase in planned weight (due to high number of passengers or load increase for some reason), flight plans shall be revised.  5.2.1.6. Loading Instruction/Report (LIR)  a.   Issue a Loading Instruction/Report (LIR) for each flight to be performed, by adhering to all safety parameters.  b.   Complete the load distribution for the flight by using the preliminary information on the flight and adhering to the Company requirements together with the requirements specified in   DK.41.012 Airport Handling Manual (AHM) sections 514 EDP Loading Instruction/Report and 515 Manual Loading Instruction/Report (LIR) without ignoring the segregation requirements.  c. 5.2.3. Cargo Offloading Instructions  a.   Close to arrival of the aircraft, an offloading instruction may be prepared by using the top "Arrival" section of the Loading Instruction/Report (LIR) by considering LDM/CPM information.  b.   At the point where the transit loads will be offloaded for transit flights, an offloading instruction can be prepared as per the requirements in the sections 514 EDP Loading Instruction/Report and 515 Manual Loading Instruction/Report (LIR) of DK.41.012 IATA  Airport Handling Manual (AHM).  c.   During the process of offloading loads and passengers to ensure the balance of the aircraft on the ground, the ground stability of the aircraft is monitored continuously.  5.2.4. Notification To Captain (NOTOC)  NOTOC is used to give the captain information on the dangerous goods and special loads (DGSL-Dangerous Goods and Special Loads) carried as baggage (AVIH, etc.), cargo, and mail. The   cargo   department   is   responsible   for   sending   the   DGSL   information   to   the   employee   who   will   prepare   the   Loading Instruction/Report (LIR) in a legible form if the same will be sent in a handwritten form, or in a printed or digital form if the same will be sent electronically. For the live animals accompanied by passengers and accepted to the cargo hold, the operation department issues  FR.61.0001 Special Load-Notification To Captain (NOTOC). The employee responsible for preparation of the Load Instruction/Report (LIR) prepares Load Instruction/Report (LIR) by considering the compatibility and segregation criteria related to DGSL. The information in NOTOC is forwarded to the Loading/Offloading Team Leader (Foreman) employee who is responsible for loading and supervision of the aircraft. The team leader who has received the information:  a.   Checks visually that DGSL is undamaged and not leaking.  b.   Makes sure that DGSL has been loaded in the positions specified in the Loading Instruction/Report (LIR) and NOTOC.  c.   Reports to the operations coordinator the actual loading positions of the DGSL on board the aircraft.  d.   Signs   FR.61.0001 Special Load-Notification To Captain (NOTOC) that includes the actual loading positions or delivers it to the operation coordinator to be signed by him.  e.   After the operation coordinator's or the foreman’s signature,   FR.61.0001 Special Load-Notification To Captain (NOTOC) is signed by the pilot-in-captain. The details related to the activities of sharing the NOTOC with all respondents and filing of it are available in all requirements in  TL.61.001 Instruction on Cargo NOTOC Preparation and E K.10.63.002 Dangerous Goods Manual. The DGSL information is given to the station where the aircraft will land at before the aircraft lands (LDM/CPM). NOTOC is issued in compliance with the requirements of   DK.41.012 Airport Handling Manual (AHM)/section 381 Special Load- Notification to Captain (General) and   DK.41.011 Dangerous Goods Regulations (DGR)/article 9.5.   Provision of Information.  FR.61.0001 Special Load-Notification To Captain (NOTOC ) is issued by cargo departments for the special cargoes and dangerous goods accepted through the cargo channel and by the operations department for the special cargoes and dangerous goods carried by passengers (Live animals, if any, accepted as registered baggage with the passenger,   dry ice used for the storage of catering items carried in the cargo compartment,   hygiene kits, etc.)  FR.61.0001 Special Load-Notification To Captain (NOTOC)must bear the signatures of the employee who has issued it, the operations coordinator who coordinates the loading of the cargoes, and the pilot-in-command. The EDP NOTOC to be prepared in TROYA system is viewed with the “NC” command. For circular flights,   FR.61.0001 Special Load-Notification to Captain (NOTOC) Form is issued so that there will be one copy for each destination including the final station by giving information to the pilot-in-command of the flight when special loads are being carried. Duties in the Weight and Balance Calculation Process  5.3.1. General Duties  The purpose of the Weight and Balance calculations is to cross check the Loadsheet against the following and make sure that the Loadsheet is final and correct:  a.   The final Loading Instruction/Report (Final LIR) obtained from the Loading/Offloading Team Leader (Foreman) after completion of the loading process,  b.   Final passenger figure,  c.   Final fuel figure,  d.   All structural and operational limits by aircraft registration mark,  Note-1:   If a preliminary Loadsheet has been issued during the process, one or more criteria (baggage and passenger information, etc.) may be finalized.  Note-2:   The employee assigned with the duty of making the weight and balance calculations makes sure that the necessary information in the manual or EDP Loadsheets are finalized and verified.  e.   The correctness of the Loadsheet must be checked before generating the Loadsheet and maintained by monitoring the following matters before delivery of the final Loadsheet to the cockpit: Flight number and date control, Aircraft tail name control, Checking the DOW/DOI by the catering weight, the number of the cockpit and cabin crew members, and potable water ratio, Underload/overload check (Total Traffic Load (TTL) must not exceed the Allowed Traffic Load (ATL).), Checking the final fuel figure, Checking the accuracy of the transit/transfer load information received from the connecting flights and transferred to the Loadsheet, Checking the passenger figure Checking the addition of the ULD tare weights to the Loadsheet issued for ULD loaded aircraft, Checking that hold baggage and gate delivery baggage are shown on the Loadsheet, checking the actual loading positions of the DGSLs specified on the NOTOC, Final status control of balance calculations including LMC data made according to predetermined limits, Loadsheet control according to Loading Instruction/Report (LIR) and other information related to actual loads, Checking   adherence   to   the   Company   regulations   and   the   special   requirements   specified   for   the   load   control   process   in EK.10.67.001 Ground Operations Manual and the other Company documents ( EK.10.63.002 Dangerous Goods Manual/16. Ground Handling Services,   TL.67.051 Loading Instruction,   TL.61.004 Load Master Flight Preparation, Loading and Unloading Instruction, etc.), Checking the manual/EDP signatures of the documents that must be signed.  f.   Checking that the generation format and contents of the Loadsheet meet the minimum requirements of AHM 516 Manual Loadsheet, AHM 517 EDP Loadsheet, AHM 518 ACARS Transmitted Loadsheet specified in   DK.41.012 Airport Handling Manual   (AHM), E K . 1 0 . 6 7 . 0 0 1 | R e v i s i o n 1 6 G r o u n d O p e r a t i o n s M a n u a l ( G O M ) QMS Document Template Number: FR.18.0001 | Revision 12 Document Template Reference Document Number: TL.18.006 Page: 326 | Total Page: 464 Copy of this document has been generated on 4.02.2026 16:42. Indicating Trim/Auxiliary Tank Fuel Information on Loadsheet  Some aircraft types in the company fleet (A332, A333, A321NEO) are equipped with ACT/TRIM TANK. While preparing Loadsheet for the aircraft equipped with ACT/Trim Tank, correct transfer of the fuel distribution is important to calculate particularly the take-off balance point (MACTOW) correctly. The value specified in the ‘Trim/Aux.Tank Fuel’ field of FR.67.0272 Load and Trim Sheet Information filled out by the pilot-in-command, or under the ‘Trim/Aux.Tank Fuel’ tab if the fuel information is sent through ACARS must be entered in the system after verifying it (it is mandatory to enter zero ‘0’ even if there is no fuel at all), and must absolutely be specified in the SI field of the LOADSHEET. For detailed information, see   TL.67.050.Instruction On Loadsheet Preparation. The values coming to the ATOM/TMAN systems and the values indicated in the Loadsheet must be cross-checked by the Load Control Employee (who prepares Loadsheet) and the Ground Operations Employee acting as the Operations Coordinator. In cases where ACARS/ATOM/TMAN systems are inactive or the information contained in FR.67.0272 Load and Trim Sheet Information cannot be transmitted to ATOM/TMAN systems through ACARS for any reason, if the load controller and the operations coordinator in the field are different officials, FR.67.0272 Load and Trim Sheet Information is filled out manually and its readable image is shared through phone/teams and transmitted to the Load Controller.  5.3.1.10. Load Control Operation in Cargo Loading in Passenger Aircraft Cabins  Details regarding Central Cargo Control processes for cargo operations/flights performed with passenger aircraft of the Company are defined in LS.67.050 List   of Cargo Carriage Operations to be performed with Passenger Aircrafts. In line with the relevant process, the signed Load Control documents are kept by the station official.  5.3.2. Last Minute Changes (LMC)  a.   After LS is prepared, changes in traffic load within the limits (Passenger, Baggage, Cargo, Mail, Equipment) defined in Table-40: LMC Limits Table, a new LS may not be sent to the aircraft and corrections may be made on the form. These kinds of corrections are called Last Minute Changes (LMC). If there is an LS sent through EFB, LMC is not made; the relevant approval/signature processes are completed by preparing a new LS and sending it again through EFB. Standard Process: The Loadsheet delivered to the commander must include all LMC information. Such changes must be done as per the Company LMC rules.  b.   Alternative Process:   For some special cases, the Loadsheet may be delivered to the pilot-in-command without making LMC.  However, this process is not executed in the Company's flights .  NOTE:   In case of the local authority compulsion requiring that the LMC is shown on the Loadsheet, the Company's authorized persons are required to contact the local authority. When a last minute baggage offload occurs in the Company DCS system, the baggage is not deleted from the system, so there may be a difference in the number of pieces in the LS to be received (for example, if 5 pieces of baggage of 2 passengers do not make it to the plane at the last minute, 5 pieces of baggage will be shown in the LS to be received). If a similar situation occurs, the baggage weight must be realized on TROYA. However, since the number of parts cannot be edited in the system, the number of parts on EDP and ACARS LS are initialed and the actual number of parts (including EXP and HBG) is shown. In the EFB LS process, the correct luggage piece number must be shown in the SI column of the LS and a new LS must be produced (Ex: ACT (Actual) BAG PCS 272. LMC FOR EFB). Since the changes made in the TROYA system for baggage weights are reflected in the new LS, there is no need to re-write the weight in the SI column.  c.   The pilot-in-command is informed of the LMC only by the employee in charge and only after all changes have been finalized and entered in all copies of the Loadsheet.  d.   If   the   pilot-in-command   has   been   informed   about   the   LMCs   verbally   or   directly   through   the   aircraft’s   internal   means   of communication (interphone, headset, acars, etc.), s/he must record the following details on the Weight and Balance Form (Loadsheet) in writing: Name and surname of the operations coordinator, E K . 1 0 . 6 7 . 0 0 1 | R e v i s i o n 1 6 G r o u n d O p e r a t i o n s M a n u a l ( G O M ) QMS Document Template Number: FR.18.0001 | Revision 12 Document Template Reference Document Number: TL.18.006 Page: 338 | Total Page: 464 Copy of this document has been generated on 4.02.2026 16:42. Examples of cases where LMC can or cannot be made: In narrow body aircraft, when LMC has been made for (+) 400 kg baggage in the compartment 2, no LMC can be made for (-) 200 kg baggage in the compartment 3. Since the total load difference will be 600 kg, it is necessary to issue new Loadsheet, as the LMC limit will be exceeded. In narrow body aircraft, when LMC has been made for (+) 300 kg baggage in the compartment 2, no LMC can be made for (-) 300 kg cargo in the compartment 2. Since the load category will be changing even if the loads are in the same compartment, it is necessary to issue new Loadsheet. When LMC has been made for (-) 300 kg baggage in the compartment 3 of narrow body aircraft, another LMC can be made for (+) 300 kg baggage after receiving information on that the same baggage can be loaded again. Since there is no difference in terms of load category and compartment, and the LMC limit is not exceeded, there is no need to prepare a Loadsheet again. It is checked that the maximum weight limitations (MZFW-MTOW-MLAW) of the aircraft are not exceeded. While making a “LMC”, care is taken not to exceed the weight limit, the maximum combined load limit, and the maximum cumulative load limit of each compartment and each ULD position. While making a LMC, the calculation related to the passenger weight segregation is made by considering the details explained in  PR.74.622 Aircraft Weight and Balance Data Management Procedure The Weight and Balance Form (Loadsheet) is given to the cockpit crew as soon as it reaches the aircraft, there is no need to wait for a possible LMC. The FOCC Dispatch unit must be immediately and verbally informed of LMC changes in order to avoid delays that may occur due to fuel purchases. New Loadsheet is issued to ensure the maximum level of flight safety.  Take-off Weight –TOW: a.   "ADJ TOW" weight is found by subtracting and/or adding "LMC TOTAL" weight from/to "ACTUAL TOW".  b.   ADJ "TOW INDEX" is found by subtracting and/or adding "LMC TOTAL" index from/to "LITOW". This index value is used to calculate ADJ "TOW MAC %".  c.   The adjusted “TOW, TOW index” and “TOW MAC %” found are written on the “ADJ” line in the “AFTER LMC” box.  Zero Fuel Weight -ZFW: a.   "ADJ ZFW" weight is found by subtracting and/or adding "LMC TOTAL" weight from/to "ACTUAL ZFW".  b.   ADJ "ZFW INDEX" is found by subtracting/adding "LMC TOTAL" index from/to "LIZFW".  c.   This index value is used to calculate "adjusted ZFW MAC %".  d.   The "adjusted ZFW, ZFW index” and “ZFW MAC %” found are written on the “ADJ” line in the “AFTER LMC” box.  Landing Weight-LAW: a.   "ADJ LAW" weight is found by subtracting and/or adding "LMC TOTAL" weight from/to "ACTUAL LAW".  b.   ADJ "LAW INDEX" is found by subtracting/adding "LMC TOTAL" index from/to "LILAW".  c.   This index value is used to calculate the adjusted "LAW MAC %". General Information Exchange  All data relevant to the aircraft Weight and Balance calculations shall be transferred to the load controller who prepares the loading plan. This transfer shall be documented by using any one of the following methods.  a.   Digitally,  b.   In writing on any document,  c.   Verbally by using any one of the following communication methods (Information on the load control process, including situations where instant verbal communication is required on the Company's flights, must be written down before all aircraft doors are closed/All Doors Closed (ADC)), To ensure the accuracy of the information obtained orally from radio, telephone or other electronic means, reading the information by reciprocally repeating it (Verbal communication must be written down before ADC), All verbal communication is recorded manually/digitally (not used on company flights), All verbal communication is recorded with a voice recording system (not used on company flights),  d.   The written information exchange and digital information exchange are the methods always recommended by the Company. If instant verbal communication is necessary, the following details must be recorded during the communication: Name and surname of the operation coordinator, Time of briefing, Acknowledgment that the party receiving the information (Captain, foreman, load controller, etc.) understands the changes, Retention of the record in the flight file.  5.3.3.2. Qualifications & Requirements of the Employee (Loading Team Leader) Who Will Forward the Final Aircraft Loading to the Load Controller  In all flights, all communication regarding final loading information (FLIR) and aircraft loading, especially in loading changes outside the loading plan and in cases where loading cannot be done in accordance with the plan, is carried out by the Loading Team Leader (Foreman) or an authorized person who meets the following requirements:  a.   The person responsible for aircraft loading communication must receive certified training for the turnaround period from the landing of the aircraft to the next take-off in accordance with “ DK.41.012 Airport Handling Manual /AHM 1110 RMP 18 RAMP SERVICES- TURNAROUND COORDINATION”.  b.   Must be able to communicate directly with the operations coordinator, if any, regarding aircraft loading and unloading duties.  c.   If the operations coordinator is not on duty, he/she must be able to communicate directly with the load controller regarding Load planning & Loading.  d.   Must   be   able   to   use   communication   protocol   in   accordance   with   the   procedures   and   principles   specified   in   the   4.5.1.2. Communication section.  e.   As stated in the Information Exchange section of the GOM Load Control Process, written communication methods shall be used instead of verbal communication. In routine operation only verbal communication regarding loads within the LMC limits is permitted. However, the final confirmed information must be put into writing before the ADC and, if necessary, LMC must be performed.  f.   In exceptional cases where verbal communication is required (Earthquake, Internet Outage, Storm, etc.), all information related to the load control process will be repeated and the process will be advanced. Sample Case: Operations Coordinator: Due to overload problem, PAG seven-three-eight-seven at position 11P will not be loaded, offload it! Loading team leader: It is understood that the PAG in 11P will be reduced to seven-three-eight-seven and will be taken out of the ERA area. Remote Load Control  This is the process where the load planning (LP) and loadsheet (LS) calculations of the departure flight are performed from a location other than the departure station. The remote load control requests other than the ones coming from the Company load control supervisory can only be fulfilled with the approval of the relevant station and the Company load control supervisory.  a.   The main duties of the load controller that fulfills the remote LP & LS process: Performing load planning (LP) duty, To perform the necessary calculations for Loadsheet (LS) by establishing healthy/continuous communication with the departure station,  b.   The main duties of the departure station/the official delegated by the station for data transfer: To supervise the loading and unloading operations as stated in the 4.5.1.1. Introduction, To communicate with the remote load controller in case of any irregularity and/or discrepancy/change that may occur during loading and unloading processes (failure to load as per LP, offload, extra last minute load arrival), To report the final loading of the aircraft to the remote load controller with Final LIR (FLIR), Sound/uninterrupted flow of information is indispensable for safety of the remote load control process. Data sharing is carried out directly or indirectly between the central load controller, the departure station and the flight crew, using designated communication tools (ACARS, Teams, EFB, etc.). Instant communication applications that can be used in Company systems are then put into writing and transmitted using radio, etc., subject to confirmation. In   cases   where   it   is   necessary   to   generate   the   Loadsheet   centrally,   it   is   generated   by   the   Ground   Operations   Safety Management/Load Control and Coordination Supervisor's Office (GLC) employee or the centrally approved certified load control employee (CLC). The information transfer is made centrally as detailed in   PR.67.024 Procedure For Centralized Management Of Load Control by using the means of communications determined in advance by the load control, departure station, and the cockpit crew. After landings at airports other than the planned destination (divert, technical landing, emergencies, etc.), the follow-up flight is created on the DCS system by the Station DCS Coordination Directorate. The loadsheet for the next flight is primarily prepared by the   station   officer.   If   it   cannot   be   prepared   by   the   station,   Ground   Operations   Directorate/Ground   Operations   Risk Management/Load Control and Coordination Supervisory is notified of the necessity of a loadsheet by the Integrated Operations Control Directorate/Stations Operations Control Management via e-mail. In this case, the loadsheet prepared by the Load Control and Coordination Directorate is transmitted to the relevant flight via the ACARS system. If all these stages cannot be completed, the loadsheet is prepared by the flight crew of the flight. It is possible to make contact with the Ground Operations Safety Management/Load Control and Coordination Supervisory through the e-mail address   loadsheet@thy.com , extension numbers, or 24/7 available mobile phone number   00905051605959 .  5.4. Responsibilities in Load Control Process  The responsibilities of the employee who performs the load control duty may vary in accordance with organizational formation.  a. Employing trained and qualified employee in the operation, in the number sufficient for the operation, for the purpose of ensuring the competence and security of the load control services safely and in compliance with the national/international rules and the Company's rules,  b.   For the flights with multiple destinations, the departure station is responsible for sending information on the loads to the next station to avoid any problem at the intermediate point, and for sending the LDM, CPM messages after the flight has become "PD" in the relevant system if it has been prepared over DCS, or after the flight has closed the doors if it has been prepared manually,  c.   The station at the intermediate point is responsible for checking the LDM, CPM messages sent by the previous station and preparing the Loadsheet by considering the load and passenger weight changes made,  d.   Ensuring that documents and records (Loading Instruction/Report, Loadsheet, NOTOC, etc.) concerning the performed load control duties are retained,  e. At stations where the Loadsheet is prepared in electronic media, it is mandatory that employee of the ground handling agent performing this duty has received DCS training. The department of the ground handling agent, responsible for issuing the Loadsheet, shall be obligated to communicate telephone, fax, e-mail, SITA and correspondence address details, etc. of the departments carrying out database entries into the DCS computer system used at stations where the Loadsheet is prepared in electronic media, as well as any changes in such details to the relevant department.  5.5.3. All documents related to load control shall be issued by the trained employee in accordance with the basic limitations and load control functions of the Company. IOCC/SOCC. In this case, the loadsheet prepared by the Load Control and Coordination Supervisory is transmitted to the relevant flight via the ACARS system. Before each loading, the cargo compartment must be visually checked. It must be ensured that there is no damage to the cargo compartment and that there is no cargo left in the cargo compartment from the previous flight [(except for transit cargo specified in the Loading Instruction/Report (LIR))] and that the compartment is empty, then any cargo, if any, is loaded into the cargo compartment.  b.   On each flight, the aircraft is loaded in accordance with the written Loading Instruction/Report (LIR).  c.   In terms of weight and balance of the loading, it is ensured that the aircraft is loaded in accordance with the specified limits.  d.   Load items shall be loaded so as not to cause any damage to each other or the aircraft.  e.   While loading/offloading the dangerous goods from the aircraft and while securing the relevant load, the process must be carried in such a manner so as not to damage the package or the container.  f.   Loads must be secured and its movement in any direction within the compartment must be prevented, since the changes in the position of loads (including dangerous goods) affect the center of gravity.  g.   Load weighing 150 kg or more shall be secured tightly, irrespective of the fact that it occupies the compartment or net section fully. Heavy loads must always be settled on the floor, and planks must be used if necessary by considering the floor load capacity or linear restraint limitations.  h.   The loads (liquids, barrels, protrusive/sharp loads) that may cause damage/harm to the employee or aircraft due to their form, density or structure must be secured by tying them down inside the aircraft.  i.   Special loads [dangerous goods, live animals, human remains, liquids, etc.] must be loaded in accordance with the handling labels (hold upright, etc.) they bear and their own regulations.  j.   Unlabeled loads shall be identified and re-labeled, before loading. k. Damaged and torn cargoes, if any, must be detected before loading, and the cargoes must never be loaded into the aircraft unless they are made airworthy. Baggage shall be loaded into separate sections depending on baggage tags so as not to be mixed up.  l.   Pay attention to cargo with priority (special cargo, or packages containing dangerous goods) and substances which must not be loaded together.  m.   Mail is a priority load.  n.   Loads must be protected against rain, snow, etc. at the ramp prior to loading and after the arrival.  o.   Nets in the compartments shall be stretched properly, loads shall be prevented from moving during flight.  p.   It shall be ensured that the ULD locks are fully seated. If the entire cargo hold is empty, it is not necessary to raise all locks.  q.   The compartment nets must always be tied in order to prevent movement of the loads and all nets must be tied even if the compartment is empty.  r.   Before each flight, it is necessary to check that the compartment nets are present, have the missing nets completed, and have the damaged nets replaced by reporting them to the relevant units.  s.   Before the compartment doors are closed, protection nets shall be secured carefully.  Attention:  Before each flight, the nets, clips, and poles in front of the cargo compartment door must be checked for airworthiness. When they are damaged, this causes the loads to move during the flight, and that the cargo compartment door cannot be opened. If any damage is detected, the cockpit crew and the technician must be informed of it immediately.  t.   In order that the smoke and fire detectors in the cargo compartments operate soundly, it is necessary to make sure that the detectors are not blocked by the load, and leave minimum 5 cm gap between the load and the cargo compartment ceiling. u.   Every loading area has a maximum load capacity, and these limits are specified in the "Weight and Balance Manuals" by the aircraft manufacturers. These limits must never be exceeded to avoid any damage to the aircraft floor.  v.   In order to prevent any damage to the cargo compartment door, wall, panel and ceiling, the loads must be admitted into the aircraft after checking their volumes and heights.  5.5.5.1.Loading/Offloading  Loading shall definitely start from the forward during ground operation. Items shall be loaded in line with the loading instructions for the flight. Loading order:  a.   Cargo  b.   Mail,  c.   Baggage (must be loaded last to be offloaded first)  d.   In the circular flights, the loading must be started with the loads of the last destination station and continued with the loads of the first station; and during this loading process, attention must absolutely be paid to the weight and balance separately for each one of the two stations by considering offloading of the loads at the first station.  NOTE:   When necessary (no suitable hold version, unsafe in terms of load and balance, etc.),   cargo can be loaded in front of the baggage.   In specified cases, verbal or e-mail approval must be obtained from the responsible station manager. After the approval of the relevant station manager, cargo is loaded in front of the baggage and the relevant status is written in the LDM/CPM messages to be sent to the destination station. Before accepting any load on board for carriage, the load dimensions shall be compared to cargo door dimensions. Other load limits shall be checked for items that can be loaded passing through the cargo doors. See "Maximum Package Chart" in the relevant aircraft manual for this purpose. Offloading must always start with the aft compartment. For the offloading processes, the necessary measures must absolutely be taken as per the LDM, CPM messages. The offloaded items must be protected against weather conditions such as rain, snow. Load support devices (plank, rope, strap, net, etc.) unloaded from the compartments shall be collected to be sent back. Unless otherwise requested, the ballast loads must definitely be offloaded and retained to be used later on. Loads may be refused or unloaded due to following reasons; volume problem, overload, compartment limitations (height, area load limitation, floor panel limitation, etc.), weight problem, ventilation, heating-cooling problems (AVIH, PER, etc.), balance problem, load incompatibility   (AVI/HUM,   etc.),   exceeding   quantitative   transportation   limits   (Radioactive   material   TI   limit),   packaging   problem (inappropriate packaging), extremely dirty load or live animals with a heavy odor or causing discomfort. The concerned cargo department is informed, through the means of communication (telephone, radio, etc.), concerning the cargo and mail to be unloaded. In the bulk loaded compartments, the volume of the load must be compared with the details provided in the Loading Instruction/Report (LIR) generated in DCS through estimation and comparison; and if any significant difference is detected, its cause must be found out, and the Ground Safety Report must be issued on   aqdportal.thy.com. It must be made sure that all compartments have been offloaded completely at the final station of arrival. Upon arrival of the flight, it is necessary to make sure that there is no damage to the compartment, there is no problem with the floor latches/net systems, and there is no leakage, spillage in the compartment. The process regarding sliding carpet is included in article 4.5.6.4. Loading Procedures. If crew baggage is temporarily offloaded and loaded back, it must be made sure that the baggage is loaded in the correct positions and completely. The live animals (AVIH) carried as registered baggage must be offloaded with top priority and taken into the terminal without keeping them waiting, to deliver them to the passenger as soon as possible. The baggage claim belt must never be used to deliver live animals (AVIH). If the live animal cannot be received soon, it must be left in an air-conditioned waiting room. In case of delay or injury, “AVIH” must be processed with top priority. Baby bassinets and wheelchairs tagged as delivery at door are delivered to the passengers at the aircraft door as soon as possible. The baggage, cargoes, or mails that are damaged, or whose identifying details are lost/missing,   are reported to the concerned departments verbally and/or in writing   and not accepted for flight. When the aircraft doors are being closed, the ground operations employee acting as the operations coordinator shall gather and communicate such details as total number of passengers checked-in (total number of male, female, children and infants), total baggage weight in kg, seating distribution of passengers as per each "zone" in the cabin according to seating layout plan, operational weights, fuel amount, cargo and mail details and special load details to the employee drawing up the Loadsheet. First baggage, then mail, and lastly cargo is offloaded, as opposed to the loading order. Priority of baggage claim as per the baggage type shall be as follows; “Short connection” baggage, Transfer baggage, VIP baggage, “Priority” labeled luggage, Internal/local luggage, Rush baggage (Lost property baggage), This order may change, where required. c.   Loading Into Passenger Cabin  Items loaded in the passenger cabin consist of fragile, valuable and diplomatic baggage, musical instruments, gold and banknotes, pets, and assistance animals accompanying disabled passengers.  The cabin load capacity per seat is 75 kg. Seats to be loaded with cabin load shall be determined and blocked by the passenger handling. The weight of the cabin load reserved by blocking during passenger "check-in" process must be communicated to load control department. In the weight and balance calculations made for the aircraft, the weight of the cabin load must be included in the traffic load by using the "CBG" code and considering the cabin zone where it has been loaded. The weight shall be added as dry load in cabin baggage into the Loadsheet. Details of this special load shall be entered in the section "SI" of the Loadsheet.  d. Stowing Load in Passenger Cabin  The armrests of the middle seat shall be lifted, if necessary/possible. The seat shall be protected with blankets, if necessary. The load shall be placed on the seats. The load shall be secured with seat belts. In the event that use of straps or ropes is required due to dimensions of the load, the seat tracks shall be used for the installation of fastening devices, or the straps/ropes shall be attached directly to the seat-frame.  5.5.5.2. Points to consider in case of Composite Body Aircraft  Due to the composite material structure, it is more difficult to notice damage on AIRBUS A350-900 and B787-9 Dreamliner aircraft caused by external impact compared to the aluminum body. Although no damage is seen externally, there might be internal damage; and therefore,   in case of any tiny or big contact to the aircraft , the ground handling employee   must absolutely inform the cockpit crew or the technician of the same verbally and/or with a   written report   so that the necessary examination can be made.  It must be ensured that   no   ground support equipment (all vehicles to be positioned next to the passenger, service, and cargo doors and give service to the aircraft)   touches   the aircraft.  While positioning the ground support equipment, it is necessary   to prevent the bumpers from contacting the fuselage , and leave sufficient clearance when docking at the aircraft, considering possible changes in the aircraft weight; considering the fact that the fuel, passenger, load changes will change the ground clearance of the aircraft, the distance between the ground support equipment and the aircraft must be checked throughout the turn-around period.  The   operator   of   the   ground   support   equipment   must   perform   the   required   physical   inspections   before   and   after   the approach/separation maneuver, and in the event that s/he detects any damage to the fuselage, s/he must immediately notify her/his supervisor verbally or in writing in respect thereof. After the detection, the station official, the pilot-in-command, and the technical employee (if available) must be notified verbally or in writing. It must be ensured that all cargo doors to be used for loading with High Loader are opened/closed with mobile stairs. It is prohibited to  open/close   the compartment doors through the High Loader.  Extra practices special to Composite Body (B787 and A350) aircraft:  Since the BULK cargo compartment (CPT5) doors are on the left side and close to the aft passenger (4L) door, in cases where passenger boarding/deboarding and compartment loading/unloading processes have to be simultaneous, the baggage carts must be disconnected from the baggage tractor and docked/removed manually. In case of loading of the BULK cargo compartment, it is necessary to consider that the volume of the BULK compartment is limited, and the minimum BULK load must be planned for the ER flights. Bulk Loading  Process of loading by using equipment utilizing a band system called a conveyor. There are nets separating each compartment inside the hold, and preventing mingling of the loads. There are separate locking systems for container and pallet loading on the cargo compartment floor.  b.   Before take-off, the locks on the ULD loaded positions must be raised. (If the hold is completely empty, there is   no need   to raise the ULD locks.)  c.   Tare weights of ULDs is included in the traffic load as company material (EIC) in the manual Loading Instruction/Report (LIR) and the Loadsheet.  d.   The ULDs may be sent empty. Calculate the empty "ULD"s by including them in the traffic load of the station. The "ULD" number must be entered into the system, regardless of the fact that "ULD" is loaded or empty. If a "ULD" contains loads for multiple stations, tare weight shall be included in the weight calculations of the final station. After introducing the ULD serial numbers to the TROYA system, the ULD tare weights are calculated by the system automatically. Since the tare weights vary by ULD serial number, it is necessary to make sure that the absolutely correct ULD serial numbers have been entered into the TROYA system.  e.   AKHs must be loaded to the aircraft as per the correct loading visual given in article “r” of   TL.67.051 Loading Instruction/section 6.2 ULD Loading.  f.   NOTOC form shall be delivered to the pilot-in-command against signature where special loads are carried in flight.  g.   AKH loading in wide body aircraft is carried out by considering the loading rules.  h.   PKC loading in wide body aircraft is carried out by considering the loading rules.  i. Points to consider while loading Boeing 777-300ER:  It must be checked manually that each latch is in operating condition. However, since the latching system of the B777-300ER aircraft is different, the containers are grouped when more than one container will be loaded. Grouping is a process that must be done consecutively. (28L, 27L, 26L, 25L, or 28L/R, 27L/R, etc.) The grouped containers must not be latched individually. It is unnecessary to raise the latches between the containers loaded as grouped.   If the latches in between are raised, it is not possible to load the containers safely.   In case of such loading, the groups must be secured by latching, and the container group must be secured by raising the latches in front of and behind the group reciprocally. In case of pallet loading, however, each pallet loaded must be secured by latching them always individually after the loading.  Note: Positions 43R and 43L cannot be loaded with ULDs alone. After the loading has been completed and all ULDs have been secured by latching them, the latches in all no-fit positions are also secured by raising them. Checks the parking stand where the aircraft will be parked for FOD, takes a full tour around the parked aircraft before any equipment approaches it and checks the airframe, mainly the cargo and cabin doors, for any damage. If he detects any damage, he reports that damage to the station official of the Company, the pilot-in-command, and technician (if any) in the given order. (In cases where an Operations Coordinator cannot be planned for the arrival flight, these tasks are performed by the Loading/Offloading Team Leader (Foreman).)  b.   Obtains the MVT that indicates the estimated time of arrival of the aircraft and the LDM/CPM messages that indicate the information on the load distribution at arrival, and meets the aircraft.  c.   Checks and/or ensures that the equipment required for offloading (container, "dolly", baggage cart, bus, etc.) is readily available in parked position prior to aircraft landing.  d.   Informs the relevant departments in the event that the equipment needed for passengers requiring special attention is not in parked position at the time of passenger disembarkation.  e.   Performs the offloading (local/transfer/transit) check upon arrival of the aircraft as per the LDM/CPM messages, and if he finds differences (contents, weight, position, etc.) between the loads in the compartment and the Loadsheet and LDM/CPM, reminds the Loading/Offloading Team Leader that he is required to report the same to him. Acts on the basis of the findings (stopping the operations/cleaning/taking pictures/reporting/damage reporting, etc.) Starts the process of sharing such findings with the station official of the Company immediately. The station official of the company reports the incident through the AQD; and in case of differences (contents, weight, position, etc.) between the Loadsheet and the LDM/CPM, s/he informs the Ground Operations Safety Management of the same in writing.  f.   Ensures that the special cargo/dangerous goods are unloaded in accordance with international rules ( DK.41.011 Dangerous Goods  Regulations (DGR) ,   EK.10.61.003 Cargo Operations Manual/4.4.34. Dangerous Goods, 5.10. Special Loads Requiring Attention (SL), Dangerous Goods (DG), Special Situation Crew and Passenger Information, Triple Codes etc.) and Company documents.  g.   Ensures that the damaged ULDs detected in the arrival flight are reported and repaired/returned.  h.   If he detects damaged lock, net, structural interior component of the compartment, lighting system, or panel, he informs the technical department of the situation so that the corrective action can be taken. Reports to his immediate supervisor, in writing, whether the technical official has responded to the incident.  i.   If he detects any missing, damaged, defective, illegible, worn-out, erroneously numbered placard in the cargo compartment, he reports the same to the commander and the technician verbally so that the same is recorded in the aircraft maintenance log.  j.   Takes necessary measures and informs the relevant departments about the damaged loads and/or loads damaged during offloading.  k.   Takes necessary measures so that the baggage is delivered to the passengers/transferred to the connecting flight as quickly as possible.  l.   Makes sure, with the help of the Loading/Offloading Team Leader (Foreman), that the loads in all cargo compartments of the aircraft have been offloaded at the end of the baggage offloading process.  m.   Makes sure, with the help of the Loading/Offloading Team Leader (Foreman), that the cargo compartment is clean after the offloading process.  n.   Directly reflects the loading of the arriving aircraft on the arrival section of the Loading Instruction/Report (LIR).  o.   Retention of flight documents; All flight documents shall be placed by the cabin chief in "Co-mail" bag in sealed envelope and delivered to "Co-mail" officers at IST airport. The relevant envelopes are delivered to the Flight Operations Support Management/Flight Operations Support Supervisory by the "Co-mail" officers. In cases where there is no “co-mail”, the flight envelopes are placed in the flight envelope storage boxes at the domestic and international arrival gates by the cockpit crew. At other stations, all flight documents shall be received from the captain or cabin chief of the flight in a sealed envelope, and shall be retained at the station for three months. Upon expiry of the three-month retention period, the documents inside the flight envelopes shall be disposed of, and the envelopes shall be used for subsequent flights. Calculates the estimate zero fuel weight (EZFW) of the aircraft to be used in creation of the flight plan and forwards it to the FOCC department. On board AIRBUS A350-900 and B787-9 Dreamliner aircraft; in case of loading in the bulk cargo compartments, the volumetric constraints of the bulk compartments and the excessive number of the crew baggage pieces on the ER flights must be considered, and the BULK load must be planned accordingly.  e. Pays attention to the following, if s/he enters AVI in the system as special load. Enter the weight of the live animal accompanying passenger as zero (0), as this weight is included in the total registered baggage weight. Shows baggage weight in the compartment or hold where the live animal has been loaded, which is equal to the weight of the loaded live animal.  Figure-134: AVI Entry Examples  f. Number of passengers with reservation, estimated baggage (number and weight), manifest received from cargo department ( FR.67.0432 ULD/BULK Load Weight Statement Form (UWS) or COMIS Deadload Statement / Screen in process: It is suitable for use via OPR063. application information, see section 5.2.1.1.   Importance of Balance & Load Planning in Ground Operations All employees assigned to the load control process must observe the following rules:  a.   Safety is always the primary principle in all loading operations.  b.   Load distribution shall be performed in compliance with aircraft weight and balance limitations as well as values published by the aircraft manufacturer.  c.   The capacities set for aircraft compartments shall never be exceeded.  d.   Loading regulations and restrictions as well as special loading regulations in accordance with the relevant aircraft type shall be followed to maintain aircraft balance on the ground.  e.   Maximum height limit (line) by aircraft type shall not be exceeded.  f.   Each station shall access first to its own load and baggage on arrival.  g.   If loads from different stations are carried inside the same compartment, they shall be separated in such a manner to avoid mixing up.  h.   Proper planning shall be made to prevent the load from shifting from its position due to balance at intermediate stations.  i.   Baggage, dangerous goods, live animals and special loads shall be loaded in accordance with their regulations.  j.   Special loading rules must be applied for the minimum/maximum quantity of live animals and/or perishable materials allowed subject to loading restrictions based on the heat limits.  k.   All loads distributed to and secured in cargo compartments must conform to loading instructions and Loadsheet.  l.   All values provided on the Loadsheet shall reflect the actual aircraft loading values.  m.   For fuel economy, center of gravity of the aircraft shall be within the ideal index range.  n. Actions required to be taken after Detection of any Error in Load Control Process  Every incident related to the load control and/or loading activities shall be reported. It is the operational duty of all stakeholders in the cargo control process to report their findings in order to take actions to prevent recurrence of such incidents.  a.   After issuance of the Loadsheet, any discrepancy found on the form must be reported to the load control employee and gotten corrected by them. If this discrepancy is found after the closure of aircraft doors, the load control employee must ensure that the pilot- in-command is given information by sharing the reissued Loadsheet with   socc@thy.com without delay. After confirming that the new and correct values have been shared with the cockpit crew, the incident must be shared with   GLC@THY.COM for follow-up and reported through AQD.  b.   In case of a warning/tail strike suspicion notification from the cockpit in relation to the cargo control process, s/he may request weighing of the cargo on board at the destination station (Weighing all cargoes and baggage on board the aircraft). No load shall be offloaded and/or no passenger shall be disembarked from the aircraft before starting to weigh all loads on board the aircraft. The relevant cockpit/cabin crew must be contacted about the warning/suspected sound, and detailed information must be obtained. The result   of   the   weighing   performed   in   such   cases   and   the   relevant   findings   are   shared   with   the   Ground   Operations   Safety Management/Load Control and Coordination Supervisor's Office first by e-mail. Afterwards, reporting is made by the station official who performed the weighing by filling out the Ground Safety Report (1.7 GSR) through AQD.  c.   The station official is required to compare the information on the Loading Instruction/Report (LIR) with the LS and BRS systems; and if there are excess differences, s/he is required to find their reasons and fill out the Ground Safety Report over   aqdportal.thy.com.  d.   If the operations coordinator finds differences (contents, weight, position, etc.) between the loads in the compartment and the Loadsheet and LDM/CPM, reminds the Loading/Offloading Team Leader that he is required to report the same to him. Acts on the basis of the findings (stopping the operations/cleaning/taking pictures/reporting/damage reporting, etc.) He/she starts the process of sharing such findings with the station official of the Company immediately. The station official of the company reports the incident through the AQD; and in case of differences (contents, weight, position, etc.) between the Loadsheet and the LDM/CPM, s/he informs the Ground Operations Risk Management of the same in writing.  e.   For   the   mandatory   events   related   to   the   Load   Control   process,   the   Ground   Safety   Report   (1.7   GSR)   is   filled   out   over  aqdportal.thy.com.  5.9.Other Topics Concerning the Load Control Process  5.9.1. Transferring information to Turkish Airlines TROYA DCS or TK Yeni Weight & Balance is also carried out with the same process and all the processes mentioned below for handling agencies also include Turkish Airlines TROYA DCS. If procedures are carried out electronically, passenger and load data shall be entered into the DCS system by the ground handling agent. Aircraft load and balance calculations must be made manually (manual Loadsheet published on   ahm.thy.com) by using Load&Balance manuals and AHM 560/AHM 565-EDP (Semi Permanent Data for Check-in and Load Control) document, or automatically (EDP Loadsheet) through the DCS system where such up-to-date data have been defined for all aircraft types. The detailed information on TROYA EDP Loadsheet entries and all TROYA DCS commands are available in DK.56.011 DCS Action Code Guide and LS.67.018  Ramp Services DCS Codes List. Details in relation to repairs, etc. and the way of reflecting weight and moment variations as well as the results of weighing reports on the "basic weight, basic index" values of the aircraft are issued by Integrated Operations Control Center/Flight Planning Performance Management.  5.9.2.Check-in and Seating Layout  The seat numbers assigned to passengers during check-in are not only grouped as aisle and window side, but they are also divided into zones in the cabin for the load and balance control. Any changes in the seat number of the passenger shall definitely be indicated on DCS.  In cases where it is predicted that it will pose a risk in terms of load and balance control of the aircraft, the seat numbers can be blocked in the system to prevent admission of passengers to these seats. The detailed information on defective seat practices is defined in   PR.67.034 Procedure For Defective Seat DCS System, whose ticket and baggage handling processes have been completed, are admitted to the aircraft, as soon as it is ready for flight.  5.9.3. Passenger Boarding Process (Boarding)  It is the process of admitting passengers whose ticket and baggage transactions have been completed to the plane as soon as the plane is ready for departure.  Company requires that each passenger who will be traveling in its flights, and their hand baggages to be checked by the relevant safety or private security unit before the boarding. (Every passenger traveling in the company aircrafts and their hand baggages shall be subjected to security scans and checks in accordance with the security practices set by the state authority within the scope of national and international requirements.) Boarding processes are specified in 1. Passenger Handling heading.  5.9.4. Closure of Flight  Information regarding flight closures is available in section 1. Passenger Handling.  5.9.5. Flight Lists and Print-Out  Necessary lists of the flight are kept ready for the check-in procedures. Stations without system failure shall contact Station DCS Coordination Department through the numbers provided below in order to receive the relevant lists. These lists shall be accessed through   online.thy.com if it is available at the station. Station DCS Coordination Management: 17180-17181-17182 Station DCS Coordination Management E-Ticket Help Desk: 17185-17186-17195  5.9.6. It is recommended to load close to the aft cargo compartment door so that HUB Containers can be dispatched quickly to the transfer flight.
