Special   Loads   (SL)   Requiring   Attention,   Dangerous   Goods   (DG),   Special   Category   Crew   and Passenger Information, Three-Letter Codes  Cargoes that have special codes due to their content and have special loading principles due to their content and can be carried as cargo/mail/EIC/baggage in special cases. The special cargoes that require segregation due to Company regulations are specified in  LS.67.044 Special Cargo Segregation Table They are notified to the flight crew with   FR.61.0001 Special Load-Notification To Captain  (NOTOC) if necessary. The details related to the activities of sharing the NOTOC with all respondents and filing of it are available in all requirements in  TL.61.001 Instruction On Cargo NOTOC Preparation and E K.10.63.002 Dangerous Goods Manual. In special cases, special cargoes that can be carried as baggage upon approval must also be notified by preparing NOTOC if necessary. All dangerous goods already have the status of special cargo at the same time. However, some special cargoes such as HUM, AVI, LHO are not in the dangerous goods category. Special cargoes in the form of allowed baggage accompanied by passengers and crew are detailed in   FR.67.0326 Dangerous Goods  Signage and LS.67.051   Table of Dangerous   Goods Passengers and Crew are   Allowed to Carry with Them. Dangerous Goods are the articles that may harm the passengers, crew members, aircraft or other cargo, available on board any aircraft, as well as the environment due to their chemical and/or physical characteristics, as described and listed in DK.41.011  Dangerous Goods Regulations (DGR)/2.3. Table A. Thus, they must only be accepted if found in compliance with “DK.41.011  Dangerous Goods Regulations (DGR )” and the current publications; otherwise, they must never be accepted. The employee who loads hazardous materials must know the segregation conditions and loading procedures and has been certified in accordance with the training requirements of   DK.41.011 Dangerous Goods Regulations (DGR   ) / 1.5. Training Requirements.   The detailed information on the acceptance of dangerous goods and their transportation principles and packaging conditions is described in EK.10.63.002  Dangerous Goods Manual.  IMPORTANT NOTE:   The dangerous goods   to be loaded to the flights departing from and arriving in America are subject to restrictions  and exceptions. Considering the classes, subsidiary risk and UN numbers of the dangerous goods, dangerous goods are loaded to the relevant flights in compliance with the conditions specified in   DK.41.011 Dangerous Goods Regulations (DGR)/section 2.8.2 List of State Variations.  Attention:  Failure to load the special cargoes and/or dangerous goods as per the segregation rules may  jeopardize the flight safety. This situation also causes high level findings in audits. Big Cargo (BIG)  They are the loads that are loaded on two or more pallets due to their dimensions or weights and may require special handling and loading/offloading equipment; and in case of circular flights, they must be loaded by considering the destination of the load. While loading BIG cargoes;  a.   Aircraft loading capacity shall not be exceeded.  b.   Necessary means and labor force shall be deployed for the equipment to be carried in the best way possible. In order to perform the loading procedure in the best possible way, the cargo department shall acquire or inform the weight, contents and loading requirements of each item. Heavy Cargo (HEA)  Except for wheelchair, HUM and COMAT (AOG or EIC) transportation, the maximum weight limit per piece in bulk loads is 150 kg, and the maximum limit for HUM and COMAT (AOG or EIC) transportation is determined as 250 kg. For cargoes with a weight per piece of up to 250 kg, excluding HUM and COMAT (AOG or EIC) transports; if it will be carried on a cargo   aircraft,   approval   must   be   obtained   from   the   Cargo   Apron   Management   Department   via   the   address  CARGOAPRONOPERATIONSMANAGER@THY.COM; if it will be carried on a passenger aircraft, approval must be obtained from the Istanbul Operations and Apron Services Department via the address   HCCRAMP@THY.COM. Loads exceeding 250 kg shall only be admitted to cargo compartments with ULD loading configuration, inside a container or on a pallet.  a.   All exposed machine components must be secured before loading on board the aircraft or on a pallet. (Figure-142: Securing HEA Cargo)  b.   Center of gravity of the load must be clearly specified.  c.   While loading in bulk compartment, supporting materials must be used in order not to exceed the floor load capacity of the aircraft.  d.   If the parts in contact with the ground are not of the same shape (such as engines, pumps, etc.), the equipment must be placed on a wooden pallet, which will be carried by a forklift.  e.   During loading/unloading with a forklift, care is taken not to damage the aircraft and the fork tips are always lowered to avoid damaging the compartment doors.  f.   It must be labeled “HEA”   (Figure-143: Heavy (HEA) Label); and "This Way Up" (Figure-144: This Way Up Label) labels must   be attached on four sides, if vertical loading is required.  Figure-142: Securing HEA Cargo  Figure-143: Heavy (HEA) Label  Figure-144: This Way UP Label  g.   In case of the flights performed with bulk loading only, its loading position and weight is shown in the SI field of the Loadsheet by  using the HEA code; and   FR.61.0001 Special Load-Notification To Captain (NOTOC) is issued.  h.   For HEA cargoes to be carried in ULD, there is no need to issue   FR.61.0001 Special Load-Notification To Captain (NOTOC).  i.   In case of two or more HEA cargoes loaded into the same compartment, each HEA cargo must be shown on the Loadsheet separately. If it is to be lifted by holding from certain points, such points shall be specified clearly. When it is tied down, attention shall be paid while using tie-down devices in order not to damage fragile parts. Ballast Bags (BAL)  Ballast bags must be kept at each station to be used for flights with actual/potential balance problems.  a.   Each bag must weigh 25 kg. Aircraft Spare Part (FKT)  The materials and tools (aircraft tire, Tool Kit Box (TKB), etc.) of the aircraft, which shall be carried in case the airports the aircraft goes to do not have technical materials, and the loading compartment or position of which is constant. Its three-letter code is FKT.  Information on the weights of Tool Kit Boxes by aircraft type is available on   ahm.thy.com.  Attention:  Before each flight, it is necessary to check physically that FKT is secured/tied down in the cargo compartment, and the FKT weight and position must be taken into account and shown on the Loadsheet. The same must also be done for the technical materials (TKB) carried by the assigned technician. FKTs may be carried on board the aircraft or stored at stations, depending on the operational conditions. FKT weight is not included in DOW/DOI values; it is included to the total traffic load manually. They must be loaded and tied-down to be secured by the employee responsible for loading/offloading under the supervision of a technician. Such loads must not be unloaded at the station of arrival. Human remains must be carried in accordance with government regulations and the details explained in TL.69.025 Funeral  Carriage Instruction.  b.   Aded to ULD together with other loads. In that case, the human remain must absolutely be placed on top, in an easily accessible place; no other load must be put on it. Human remains can be stacked one on the top of the other in the ULD by paying attention to the stacking rules, only for international shipments. In bulk loadings and domestic shipments, no load, including other human remains, must be loaded on the human remains.  c.   It shall be accepted as heavy (HEA) load. It shall be fastened and secured. A nylon cover shall be spread to protect the aircraft floor.  d.   In principle, a corpse (not cremated) in a coffin can be transported in any compartment, door or compartment, if it does not exceed the limits.  e.   The coffin shall be loaded horizontally in the flight direction and tied down to the aircraft floor. It shall be loaded and secured on a pallet on aircraft with "ULD" loading configuration.  f.   Human remains in ashes (Human Ashes) are accepted in a special covered container placed into a wooden box or crate and packaged in a shock absorber material providing effective protection against breakage. There is   no need   to issue NOTOC for the human remains in ashes.  g.   The coffin shall be carried inside a special vehicle, which does not attract the passengers' attention.  h.   Shall not be kept waiting at hold, it shall be loaded as soon as possible or dispatched to the cargo handling.  i.   Number of "HUM" that can be carried in the cargo compartment shall be determined by the cargo/station official, taking passenger and baggage reservation entries into account.  j. "HUM" code and loading position is specified in the Loadsheet, and in the "SI" section of "LDM". In the EDP and Manual Weight and Balance Forms, the position of the weapon must be stated in the SI column along with its weight.  5.11.Load Limits  Due to the flexible structure of the aircraft fuselage, contortion/distortion may occur, particularly depending on the load it carries during flight. Contortion/distortion, posing constant risk of damage in the long term, has been defined and limited as "Airframe Structural Loading Limitation" by the airframe manufacturers. In this way, contortion/distortion shall not exceed the maximum limits defined at any point.  Note:   The detailed load limit information by aircraft type is accessible in   LS.67.054 List of Technical Specifications of Aircraft  Compartments and ULDs.  Load limitations are divided into two as Structural and Floor/Panel.  Attention:  Failure to abide by the loading limits and rules may jeopardize the flight safety. Therefore, this situation causes high level findings in audits.  5.11.1. Structural Load Limitations  These are the limits to be complied with to avoid damage to the fuselage structure of the aircraft.  a.   Area Load Limitation  b.   Running-Linear-Load Limitation  c.   Cumulative Load Limitation  d.   Combined Load Limitation  e.   Compartment Load Limitation  f.   Lateral Imbalance  5.11.1.1. Area Load Limitation  Compartment area limitation is the pressure limit in kg/m2, indicating the pressure applied on the compartment floor in m2 by the weight of the load in kg set with the purpose of ensuring that the capacity of the aircraft structure is not exceeded. An example of surface area calculation is given in Figure-156: Surface Area.. Area limitation is checked by dividing the weight of the load by the area defined as the external perimeter represented by the points of contact of the load with the floor.  Figure-156: Surface Area  If the result is higher than the area limitation, the load shall not be accepted as it is. Planks shall be placed beneath the load after making necessary calculations. If plank is required for the load, this means that maximum area limitation has been reached. Thus, no other load shall be placed on the load or plank. Area limitation expressed in kg/m 2 , is found by dividing the weight of the load by the area defined as the external perimeter (projection) represented by the points of contact of the load with the floor. Running-Linear-Load Limitation  Because of its flexible structure, fuselage contorts due to the load it carries during flight. Thus, maximum linear limit, which does not exceed the airframe contortion limit set by the aircraft manufacturer is provided in order to prevent permanent damage to the aircraft. This limit is expressed in kg/m. Linear limit helps to determine the total maximum load allowed in each bulk loading compartment. Linear limit shall be checked by dividing the weight of load by its length according to the direction of the flight.  NOTE:   Linear limit calculation is not required for the load exceeding the area limitation and thus loaded on planks.  Heavy Packages:   Linear limit shall be applied while carrying one or more heavy packages. Any aircraft with a linear limitation of 285 kg/m means that load(s) weighing more than 285 kg per 1 m of the aircraft may not be loaded. Cumulative Load Limitation  The total load limitation that can be carried at the forward and aft of the fuselage, set by the aircraft manufacturer.  5.11.1.4. Combined Load Limitation  This shall be used in checking the total load amount at the "Maindeck" and "Lowerdeck."  5.11.1.5. Compartment Load Limitation  This refers to the maximum load amount permitted by the manufacturer to be carried in compartment section.  5.11.1.6. Lateral Imbalance Limitation  The limitation set by the manufacturer, requiring loading of equal weights to the right and left, taking into account the balance of the aircraft throughout the longitudinal axis (tail-to-nose). In case of wide body aircraft, it is necessary to pay attention to the loads on both sides of the central axis of the aircraft. This is called lateral balance. The limits published by the manufacturer firm for lateral imbalance must not be exceeded. If the lateral imbalance exceeds the published limits, the load cannot be accepted as is, and it becomes necessary to redistribute the load. While loading cargoes into any compartment of wide body aircraft, they must not be loaded only one side (right or left side) of the aircraft.  5.11.2. Determination of Necessity in Bulk Loading Aircraft  Planking;   In order to load the cargo exceeding the maximum space limitation and/or longitude limit set by the aircraft manufacturer without damaging the cargo compartment floor, the weight of the load must be supported by spreading it over a wide area with the help of a plank or platform, and the load must be secured by fixing. Planks must be placed under all loads that have metal bottom (except for category-II and category-III radioactive materials), as they can damage the compartment floor. There is no such obligation for ULD loading. The weights of the tie-down equipment and planks used for bulk loading must be shown on the Loadsheet with EIC code. For load tying methods, see 4.5.7.6. Standard Tying title.  EXCEPTION:   This condition is not required for metallic packages carrying Radioactive Material (RRY). Figure-161: Sample Planking Image  Planking Requirement is determined in accordance with the following issues; Table-55: The maximum base pull of the aircraft compartment to be loaded is determined from the Compartment Base Pulls table. From the relevant table prepared according to the compartment floor pulls (Table-57: Table of Maximum Loadable Weights According to the Length and Width of the Cargo for the Compartment with a Base Weighing Capacity of 415 kg/m 2   or Table-58: The base edge dimensions of the load to be loaded onto the aircraft are intersected by the maximum load that can be loaded according to the length and width of the load for a compartment with a base load of 732 kg/m 2 . If the weight to be obtained when intersected, is more than the weight of the load, the load can be loaded without the need for planking. If the weight to be obtained when intersected, is less than the weight of the load, it is necessary to expand the floor area of the load by planking. Minimum two planks shall be used. They shall be of sufficient thickness and strength. Planks may be placed in two ways  1.   Placing the planks under the actual contact points of the load  2.   Placing the planks by protruding a maximum of 5 cm from the contact points of the load Example-1: When a load weighing 145 kg with floor side dimensions of 90 cm x 30 cm is to be loaded into the rear hall of a B737-800 aircraft, the floor pull corresponding to the rear hall of B737-800 among the compartment floor pulls in Table-55 showing the compartment floor tension is checked = 732kg/m 2   and the relevant width and length measurements for the maximum loadable weights according to the length and width of the load for the compartment with a floor pull of 732kg/m 2   as shown in Table-58: Maximum Loadable Weights According to the Length and Width of the Load For a compartment with a base load of 732kg/m 2 , are intersected = 197kg 145<197 = A load of 145kg, which is 90cm by 30cm, can be carried in the rear hold. In this case, in order to load the cargo, it is necessary to plank by 5 cm from the sides. When loaded by protruding 5 cm from the sides, the new dimensions of our load become 100 cm by 40 cm. The new weight of the load together with the planks is 160kg+2kg+2kg=164kg. The load, which is 100 cm by 40 cm, is intersected from the table with its new dimensions = 166 kg 164<166 with a plank, the load can be carried out 5 cm from the feet and loading can be done in the rear hold. Planning of ground stay durations at stations is carried out in accordance with the procedures specified in the documents LS.67.061 Istanbul Station Ground Times Tables, LS.67.039 Table Of Ground Times At Intermediate Point,   LS.67.40 Exceptional Ground Times and LS.67.041 Outstations Ground Times Tables. The times specified in LS.67.039 Table of Ground Times at Intermediate Point,  LS.67.040 Exceptional Ground Times and LS.67.041 Outstations Ground Times Tables are also the minimum ground times (MGT) of the relevant station, and due to the tariff structure and necessity, the Production Planning Directorate units can make a higher ground time planning without obtaining an approval from the relevant units of the Ground Operations Directorate. However, in order to prevent chain delays in the entire network as a result of the late arrival of the flights to the stations, the station officials shall take the necessary measures to run the flights earlier than the MGT times specified in the documents.  5.14.1. Ground Times at Intermediate Point  For stations that are in the intermediate point position for certain flights, the ground time shall be planned by the relevant units of the Production Planning Directorate, as specified inLS.67.039 Table of Ground Times at Intermediate Point. Ground time planning for stations that are planned to be performed for the first time for commercial/operational reasons and therefore are not included in LS.67.039 Table of Ground Times at Intermediate Point but will be intermediate points is planned according to the procedures specified in LS.67.039 Table of Ground Times at Intermediate Point until the ground time for the specific track determined in LS.67.041 Outstations Ground Times Tables as a result of the studies to be carried out by the relevant units of the Ground Operations Directorate.  5.14.2. Exceptional Ground Times  LS.67.040 Exceptional Ground Times Table includes the routes for which exceptional ground times other than the standard times are planned. In order to ensure the general standard for the ground times in the Company, the officials of the stations specified in  LS.67.040 Exceptional Ground Time Table coordinate with the relevant units of the Production Planning Directorate in order to implement the times in LS.67.041 Outstations Ground Times Tables. The document shall include routes that are assessed by Ground Operations Directorate to contain at least one of the following exceptional circumstances.  The obligations imposed by the agreements made with the handling firm,  Obligations imposed on all airlines as a result of the submission of official letters by the airport authorities,Stations requesting changes in the minimum ground stay duration In order for the stations requesting a change in the minimum ground time to be added to the exception document, the following processes must be followed respectively.  5.14.2.1. Stations Requesting Increase in Minimum Ground Time  The relevant Sales/International Departments determine and manage the works to improve the negative deviations in Ground Time specific to their stations. If negative deviation in station performance persists despite Ground Time negative deviation improvement works carried out at the station by the Sales/International Departments; a benchmark study is conducted by the Sales/International Departments covering the process, service received, planned and minimum ground times of the rival carriers. The stations requesting increase in minimum ground time submit the relevant study and the time they request to Production Planning Directorate through   FR.67.0443 Exceptional Ground Time Offer Form. If the station's proposal is deemed appropriate by Production Planning Directorate, the relevant work and the requested time is proposed to Ground Operations Directorate through F R.67.0443 Exceptional Ground Times Offer Form. After the proposal, Ground Operations Directorate conducts an operational data analysis and, if deemed necessary, an inspection by performing site supervision activity at the station. Loading Control in Cargo Aircraft  In order for the flight to be operated safely, all loads loaded on the aircraft must be fully planned, recorded and reported. The information exchange carried out verbally in the course of Load Control process must absolutely be confirmed in writing before closure of the aircraft doors. The load control process must comply with the national and international rules so that each flight can be performed safely. The load control operation on the Company cargo aircraft has been defined in accordance with the AHM 500   “Load Control” process in DK.41.012   IATA Airport Handling Manual (AHM) and standard procedures have been established for minimum requirements. Implementation details of the load control operation carried out specifically for the company cargo aircraftis defined in the requirements of EK.10.61.005 Load Master Manuel in accordance with the principles under the 5. Load Control heading. The load control operation is carried out by certified Company Aircraft Loading Specialist/Load Controller employees and the employees of the ground handling company from which the service is received are supervised throughout the loading operation. In cargo flights carried out by cargo aircraft, apart from the general information included in 5. LOAD CONTROL Section, the necessary information and existing differences are listed below; Crew Weights Aircraft Loader Weight: 85kg Duties in the Weight and Balance Calculation Process are described in   TL.61.004 Load Master Flight Preparation, Loading and  Unloading Instruction Displaying Trim/Auxiliary Tank Fuel Information on the Loadsheet is described in   TL.61.024 Instruction On The Cargo Aircraft Electronic Loadsheet Software Use Last Minute Changes (LMC) are not made on cargo aircraft. In cases where last minute changes are required, a new loadsheet is produced. The processes to be followed after landings at airports other than the planned destination (divert, technical landing, emergencies, etc.) are followed according to   TL.61.021 Cargo Aircraft AOG and Divert Cargo Application Instructions and PR.10.60.001 Divert Procedure, and the new weight and balance form is prepared according to   PR.61.049 Cargo Aircraft Centralized Load Control  Management Procedure. In the Load Control Process, in case of incidents related to ground safety during arrival and departure flights under the responsibility of cargo operations, a 1.8 HAZ (Hazard) report or a 1.10 CGR report must be filled in through the AQD, which is the Company Safety Reporting System. The requirements for preparing cargo aircraft weight and balance forms for the Cargo Aircraft Loading Specialist (Preparer of the Weight and Balance Form) are included in the   TL.61.024 Instruction On The Cargo Aircraft Electronic Loadsheet Software Use. In cargo aircraft, the   FR.73.0001 Aircraft Security Search Checklist is filled out by the employees listed in the document and delivered to the responsible captain pilot. Just Culture  Just Culture is an environment of trust in which people are encouraged (or even rewarded) to provide safety-related information, while also knowing what acceptable and unacceptable behavior is, and requires identifying safety problems and taking appropriate corrective action. In the just culture climate, human and organizational mistakes are seen as an important opportunity to improve operations and to provide feedback and lessons learned. Adoption of a just culture approach in the creation of all safety-related activities of the Company is guaranteed as a commitment of the management in   PL.10.21.001 Safety Policy. The development of safety in aviation largely depends on the reporting and analysis system of accidents and incidents. For a good reporting, motivation and rewarding, information, feedback, establishing an environment of trust, and dealing with the errors that may occur, except for unacceptable behaviors, with an approach that does not aim to punish are needed. The establishment of Just Culture in a business will have measurable effects such as incident reports and numerical increase in corrective actions taken, as well as intangible organizational and management benefits. In businesses that adopt the Just Culture approach, there is a need to make a clear distinction between acceptable and unacceptable behaviors and to communicate this to all employees. In accordance with   PL.10.21.001 Safety Policy, the following situations have been determined as unacceptable behaviors within the scope of the just culture approach of the Company: i. Gross negligence, ii. Willful violation, iii. Catastrophic acts. For   unacceptable   behaviors,   the   processes   in   PR.10.67.012   Ground   Operation   Safety   Competence   Assessment   Boards Procedure/6.5 Boards' Decision-Making Principles may be used. Voluntary reporting refers to reporting that is completely voluntary and has no specific format, and unlike mandatory reporting, it is proactive. Voluntary reporting within the scope of aviation safety provides us with information that can help us prevent future accidents. Therefore, voluntary reporting makes significant contributions to increasing aviation safety. With a proactive approach, when one of the holes in the 'Swiss Cheese' model is closed, a damage or malfunction will be prevented. Voluntary reporting contributes positively to the Safety League and «Excellence Ground to Sky» score of the relevant station. Voluntary reporting notifications are made through the AQD 1.8 HAZ (Hazard) Report.  6.5.1.2.1. Reporting, Investigation, and Responsibility  EK.10.21.001 Safety Management Manual/6.2.7. Reporting of safety incidents and hazards is encouraged by all management levels, taking into account the "Just" culture approach outlined in the Reporting and Just Culture Philosophy Section. All safety incidents reported in accordance with the requirements of the   PR.10.21.008 Procedure for Safety Reporting System/6. Implementation article are investigated in accordance with the requirements specified in PR.10.21.009 Procedure for Assessment and  Investigation Of Safety Reports. The role of managers (or incident investigators) is to systematically identify organizational weaknesses and safety deficiencies by trying to understand the factors that led to errors occurring. All safety data obtained through the reporting and/or investigation process may be used for no purpose other than to promote and improve safety.  6.5.1.3. Mandatory Incident Reports  The Safety Management System of Turkish Airlines consists of investigation and hazard analysis performed following the reporting process which is one of the main factors. Such process enables each employee to contribute to safety by reporting any kind of incidents, and to help such relevant investigation on complete basis. Shear pin damage occurring during pushback/towing operation with towbar. Forgetting to install the steering pin before a pushback/towing operation with towbarless. Anti-collision lights and beacons not functioning. Missing or wrong cone/chock placement. Erroneous “Marshalling” or “Wing Walker” service. Not performing the fuselage damage checks after arrival/before departure correctly.  b. Damage to Aircraft:  Aircraft-aircraft and aircraft-equipment collisions. Detection of unreported damage on/in the aircraft (e.g. damage from the previous flight). Damage inside the hold (panel, floor, ceiling, detector, lamp, etc.)  d. Refueling Operation:  Fuel spillage. Risk of fire due to fuel leakage. Not complying with the procedures for refueling when passengers are onboard, embarking/disembarking. Closed escape path of the fueling vehicle. Other unsafe conditions stemming from fuel operation  e. Aircraft De-icing and Anti-icing:  Unsafety during de-icing/anti-icing of the aircraft.  f. Hazard Reports  The human is the most important aspect in the identification, reporting, and controlling of hazards. Most accidents are the result of an inappropriate human action, human error, inadequate design, inadequate procedures, loss of situational awareness, intentional action, inadequate ergonomics and human factor consideration.  In order to assess and reduce the risk in the Company's ground handling operations;  Hazards are analyzed to identify existing and potential risks, Safety risks are assessed to determine risk control actions, Where necessary, risk mitigation activities are developed and implemented in ground operations. Any kind of incident which may result in blatantly interrupting safety or which has the potential to cause any damage and/or injury should be reported through the hazard reporting process within the Safety Reporting System (SRS). Hazards are reported through “1.8 Hazard” entry on AQD.  6.5.1.5. Confidential Reporting  A confidential reporting system is also available throughout the organization, via the SRS portal, that facilitates reporting of events, hazards and/ or concerns resulting from or associated with human performance in operations. This system is fully supported by senior management and it is intended to give Turkish Airlines employees an opportunity to report incidents, errors or discrepancies which they would normally be reluctant to report through normal channels. To alleviate the fear of reprisals against the reporter, the Safety Management System initiated and supported by senior management within Turkish Airlines, will guarantee confidentiality and immunity from any disciplinary action unless the regulatory authority independently pursues the incident or if the reporting matter would be categorized as a Mandatory Incident Report which would require such actions. Confidential notifications are made through “1.1 Confidential (CFR)” entry on AQD. Detailed information is in   EK.10.21.001 Safety Management Manual/section 6.2.5.6.   Confidential Reporting.  6.5.2. Immediate Action Planning  In case of an incident or accident, all ground employees must understand and have knowledge of the emergency response including but not limited to the following actions:  Stopping the operation when necessary (e.g. stopping the engines, pressing the emergency button) Removing all unauthorized personnel from the scene. Informing of the concerned parties and all employees directly affected by the incident (for example, flight crew) immediately.  Reporting the incident to the manager, who will take responsibility for initiating the local response plan if necessary, and the emergency department:  1.   The scene of incident is secured.  2.   If necessary, all instructions coming from the emergency services are followed.  3.   Reports are made to the station manager and, if necessary, to local authorities, and constant communication with them is ensured.  4.   Incident/accident report(s) is(are) prepared to collect detailed information on the incident.  5.   Any post-incident investigation, analysis and/or investigation is assisted. The order of the actions listed above may vary depending on the nature and importance of the event.  6.5.3. Aircraft Evacuation  Aircraft evacuation without flight crew and passengers: Duties and responsibilities for evacuation. Aircraft evacuation procedures and different methods (e.g. mobile ladders, boarding bridge). The evacuation slides must not be considered as the primary exit route. The communication means used during evacuation (e.g. radios and audio warning systems).  NOTE:   The employee must receive training to gain experience in evacuation, and participate in periodic drills.  6.5.4. Dangerous Goods  When suspicious damage or leakage related to dangerous goods occurs, the following measures must be taken:  a.   The cause, source, and result of the damage or leak must be identified.  b.   The operational activities near the hazard must be stopped or minimized.  c.   The unauthorized employees must be sent away from the incident area. Diversion Message (DIV)  The type of message sent after deciding on landing at a point other than the planned destination of the flight due to any reason. It is sufficient to send to the departure, planned arrival and diverted point. UTC time and date must be used. Diversion message must be sent by the first station or first department receiving the information in relation to the fact that the flight will divert. Immediately after the aircraft has landed after the diversion message, the arrival message must be sent. Normal departure message shall be sent to all addresses, to which diversion message has been sent, after the aircraft takes off. Ground   Operations   Directorate/Handling   Agreements   Management   (International)   and   Handling   Agreements   Management (Domestic and Station Ticket Sales) forward the requests to the Security Directorate/Aviation Security Management via e-mail in order to evaluate the authority requirement for service procurement, the necessity of the service and the suitability of the company for service procurement. Cargo Handling Agreements and ramp agreements for cargo aircraft are signed by the Cargo Handling Agreements Management based on the approval received from the Executive Committee. An original copy of the agreement agreed upon and signed as a result of mutual negotiations is kept in the Handling Agreements Management (International) and/or Handling Agreements Management (Domestic and Station Ticket Sales) and the other original copy is sent attached to a letter to the firm which signed it with the Company. Besides, if the cargo service cannot be separated from the ramp and passenger handling agreement, the agreement is signed after obtaining the opinion of the relevant Management of the Office of Chief Cargo Officer during the negotiation process. During the approval process, the relevant department’s acknowledgement initials are added. After signing of the agreement as a result of completion of the signature process, the agreement is distributed to the Cargo Global Handling Agreement over EDMS. Handling agreements for cargo aircraft are agreements signed between the Company and ground handling companies to provide ramp services and cargo storage services for cargo aircraft at all stations where the Company operates and will operate. The cargo handling agreements are made on the basis of   PR.61.021 Cargo Handling Agreements Management Procedure.  8.2. Service Level Agreement (SLA)  Service Level Agreements (SLA) are signed in addition to the Annex B Simplified Method formed by reference to all requirements specified   in   DK.41.044   IATA Standard   Ground   Handling Agreement   (SGHA)   and   Standard   Transportation   Document   Service  Agreement (STDSA) depending on the station conditions at domestic stations and outstations. Several stations of the Company do not have SLA agreement. While preparing the service level agreement, attention is paid to the following points: Determining benefits of SLA, Using SLA efficiently, Including the SLA in standard ground handling agreement and/or standard transportation document service agreement, Achieving the on-time takeoff performance goal with SLA that is in addition to the standard ground handling agreement, Preventing fee rise, Ensuring that the competent employees are employed in the specialty fields, Meeting the global service standard, Ensuring the safe tracking of records.  8.3. Supervision and Control of Ground Operation Service Supply Standards  The details of the supervision and control conditions of the ground operations provided by the ground handling agent as per the services   specified   in   the   mutually   signed   DK.41.044   IATA   Standard   Ground   Handling   Agreement   (SGHA)/Annex   B   (and   all requirements specified in its annexed Service Standards Agreement (SLA), if available) are available in PR.67.052 Ground Operations Supervision and Control Procedure. Specified   in   PR.67.052   Ground   Operations   Monitoring   And   Controlling   Procedure,   FR.67.0220   Ground   Operation   Standards  Monitoring Form is filled out once a year by the station officials. Management in line with the data received from the system once a year is forwarded to the Handling Agreements (Domestic and Station Ticket Sales) and Handling Agreements (International) Managements with a cover letter. The Handling Agreements (Domestic and Station Ticket Sales) and Handling Agreements (International) Managements prepare and send by e-mail and/or post a letter of thanks to the ground handling agents at the airports ranked in the top 5 in the scoring system specified in the report sent and a warning letter to the ground handling agents at the airports ranked in the bottom 5. In the event that there are more than 5 airports with the highest score in the scoring system in the report, the 5 ground handling agents serving the most flights in the year of observation will be addressed for the letter of thanks, and in the event that there are more than 5 airports with the lowest score in the scoring system, the 5 ground handling agents serving the least number of flights in the year of observation will be addressed for the letter of warning. As   per   “Station   Handling Agreements   Grievance   Management   Process”   specified   in   LS.67.017   List   of   Processes   of   Ground  Operations Directorate, within the scope of the agreement, any irregularities that cannot be resolved by the station officials are notified to the Handling Agreements (Domestic and Station Ticket Sales) and/or Handling Agreements (International) Managements by e-mail by the station officials. After evaluating the reported irregularities, the relevant ground handling agent is warned by e-mail that it is necessary to act per the agreement. Online and/or face-to-face meetings are held with the ground handling agent and station officials, if necessary, to resolve these irregularities. After all the discussions, if the ground handling agent stills fails to eliminate the irregularities, an official warning letter is written. The check of the service quality of cargo handling agent in cases where cargo services are included in the passenger and ramp agreements is assessed by the Cargo Operational Performance Management against the details explained in PR.61.023 Procedure  for Supervision and Control of Cargo Aircraft Ground Operations.  9. GROUND HANDLING EQUIPMENT  The Company detects whether the purchased product and service comply with the specified purchasing requirements in accordance with all requirements of   PR.01.40.001 Purchasing And Sales Procedure. The Product and Service Management affiliated to Ground Operations Directorate fulfills the requests for ground equipment from all domestic/international stations and various fixtures and modification needs of Ground Operations Directorate managements as per the details of   TL.67.086 Product and Ground Equipment  Investment Planning and Procurement Process Management Instruction.  9.1. Tracking of Maintenance and Repair of Ground Equipment Serving Aircraft  For maintenance-repair of the Ground support equipment serving the aircraft, a program prepared as per the maintenance-repair instructions of the manufacturer of the relevant equipment must be applied. Within the framework of this program, inspections must be made in accordance with the details explained in   TL.67.033 Instruction on Inspection and Maintenance of Equipment; and the process must be followed and secured.  9.2. Layout of Ground Equipment around Aircraft  As long as there is no airport authority restriction, the physical conditions of the airport are convenient, and there is no adverse weather condition, the layout of the ground equipment around the aircraft in routine operation by the Company's aircraft type is based on   LS.67.048 List of Ground Equipment Positions around Aircraft. It is issued on the basis of the requirements specified in LS.67.048  List of Ground Equipment Positions around Aircraft and   DK.41.012 Airport Handling Manual (AHM)/Chapter 9 Airport Handling Ground  Support Equipment Specifications.  In relation to the services to be given to the aircraft (air condition, potable water, lavatory, etc.), the maximum pressure, maximum current values, minimum equipment requirements by aircraft type are available in   DK.41.012 Airport Handling Manual (AHM)/Chapter  9 Airport Handling Ground Support Equipment Specifications.  10. GROUND OPERATIONS OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH, SAFETY AND ENVIRONMENT  The occupational health and safety implementations of the Company are defined in   EK.10.35.008 Occupational Health and Safety  Management Manual and its environmental management implementations in the requirements of DK.41.053 IATA Environmental Assessment Standards Manual, and the said implementations within the scope of Ground Handling are carried out in compliance with the requirements explained in these documents.  The details of management of wastes at all stations are specified in   PR.10.33.006 Procedure for Waste Management.  At the outstations, on the other hand, the rules of the relevant country authority apply.
